Katalog Berita (Halaman 40/58)

#3617. What to Wear When Exercising Outdoors, Based on How Cold It Is

I fell in love with cold weather running while I was training for a spring marathon. It wasn’t a choice at first: Some weeks, the weather was bad for days on end, and if I stayed home, I would fall behind in my training. Everybody else in my training group was braving the elements, so I did too—with no regrets.

I got to run on quiet mornings while snow was softly falling. I signed up for a winter race that herded finishers into a heated barn for hot chocolate and soup. I set a personal record at a spring race, during which I pushed myself hard without breaking a sweat. I now find it sad when somebody tells me they’re afraid of running in the cold, or that they would run in the winter but don’t know what to wear.

No, cold weather doesn’t have to stop you from running, but getting dressed can be a puzzle: How do you keep from freezing your butt off at first and avoid overheating once you start to sweat? Fortunately, it isn’t as tough as it looks. With the right gear, your fingers and ears can stay toasty while you jog through a winter wonderland. Below, I’ll give you a temperature-by-temperature running cheat sheet, and then dive into the specifics on how to buy the best socks, shirts, and more.

When I get dressed to run in winter, I take a look at the “feels like” temperature, not the actual high or low. I also make sure to check the weather for the time I’ll go running, not for the whole day. It doesn’t matter how warm it will be at 2 p.m. if my run will be happening at 6 a.m., before the sun is up. I use the Carrot Weather app, but any app that gives you hourly feels-like temps will work just fine.

Next, use the 20-degree rule. Imagine that the temperature is 20 degrees (Fahrenheit) warmer than it really is. What would you wear then? Here's an example: if it’s 50 degrees out, you should dress as if it were 70: in a T-shirt and shorts, most likely. If it’s 30 degrees, you’d dress as if it were 50: long pants and maybe a light jacket. Get the idea?

Everybody has their own preferences. Some people wear shorts even when it’s snowing, while others will pop a beanie on as soon as there’s a detectable chill in the air. I’m a pretty middle-of-the-road runner when it comes to keeping warm, so here’s what I wear at each “feels like” temperature, starting with warmer weather and working our way colder. I'll give a guide to each type of garment or accessory at the end.

At 50+ degrees Fahrenheit, I’m wearing basically the same things I would for a summer run.

Head and hands: Nothing special. No gloves and no hat, unless it’s a baseball cap to shade my eyes from the sun.

We’re starting to feel the first bit of a chill. This is where I may start bringing gloves, although they’ll probably get stuffed into a pocket by the end of the run. Remember, with the 20-degree rule, it will feel like 60 degrees by the time you're warmed up.

Bottoms: Leggings, lightweight long pants, or shorts.

Top: Something with long sleeves, but ideally made of thin material (think long-sleeved T-shirt, not a full-on sweatshirt or jacket). If you wore a sun shirt in the summer, that's a good layering option for these cool temps. I like my REI Sahara Shade hoodie here, but any long sleeve will do. If you run fall and winter races, you'll probably be handed a free long-sleeved version at some point.

Hands: I usually just pull my shirt's sleeves over my hands, but you could wear knit gloves if you want. Consider something like Flipmits for an intermediate option (they can be folded down into a wrist cuff when your hands warm up).

Head: A headband if you need protection for your ears.

You may see a few snowflakes drifting down, but don’t bundle up in a snowsuit. Once you’re warmed up, it will only feel like 50 degrees—so go for something in “light jacket” territory.

Bottoms: Leggings or running tights. The fleece-lined kind can be nice. (I have these.)

Top: You’ll want some kind of jacket or sweatshirt. A lightweight, reflective rain jacket is great here, or just throw on a regular hoodie over your T-shirt. (I go with cotton sweats in dry weather or light snow, but I'd go for synthetics or wool if there's rain or sleet.)

Hands: Definitely wear gloves. The cheap knit ones are usually good enough, but consider treating yourself to a nice pair of running gloves.

Head: Your choice of hat or headband; I’d stick with the headband.

Feet: This is around the temperature you may start to want warmer socks. That goes double if snow is in play: snow that falls onto your shoes will work its way through the mesh, melt, and make your feet wet. Wool is a good material here, so consider something like these from Smartwool.

This is where I’ll officially say it’s “cold.” Whatever warm-weather gear you were getting away with at warmer temps, you’ll probably have to swap it out now. Shorts people will break out their long pants. Headband people will wear a real hat.

Bottoms: Leggings and shorts. I don’t care if you think it looks goofy to wear both; this is an A+ hack. Or try a puffer skirt.

Top: It’s definitely jacket weather. Rather than getting a warmer jacket, I like to wear the same light jacket as I did at 30 degrees, but this time with a long-sleeved fleece or wool base layer underneath.

Hands: Real gloves, please. You can keep wearing your little knit gloves if you’re able to tuck your hands inside your jacket sleeves, or if you have a pair of mittens to wear over top; otherwise, get windproof gloves.

Head: A hat, and maybe also a buff for your nose and mouth. (If you have any cloth masks still hanging around from the early COVID days, they’re perfect for cold weather runs.)

Feet: Warm socks for sure. If you’ll be doing a lot of running in these temperatures, you may want shoes that are specialized for the elements. Look for ones with Gore-Tex uppers, like the Brooks Ghost GTX.

This is where I tap out. If a run is just barely in the teens, I’ll make do with the 20-degree items I mentioned above, adding an extra layer wherever needed. But if that isn't enough, I opt for the treadmill. You certainly can run in this weather if you are determined. You’ll want windproof everything, some kind of face covering, and you may need eye protection such as goggles.

Whenever the weather gets to your own personal “too cold” temperature, remember that you still have options. The early afternoon is often the warmest part of the day, so a run may be tolerable then. There’s also no shame in using a treadmill (even if you have to join a cheap gym for this reason alone).

Everybody has different preferences, and with practice you’ll figure out if you’re the kind of person who wears three shirts before it hits freezing or the type to run through the snow in shorts. But this should give you a starting point when you head out for your first (or next) cold weather run.

As you continue on your cold-weather running journey, you may need to buy some new gear or repurpose things from elsewhere in your closet. And yes, the first few minutes of your run will feel chilly. But if you’re wearing the right shoes and clothes (and planning routes with a few extra factors in mind, which I’ll discuss below), winter running is not just feasible; it’s actually fun. So here are the items you may want to consider.

Your feet need to be warm and, if possible, dry. Warm socks go without saying, but there are some extra considerations when you’re picking socks to run in. Wool socks are ideal because they keep your feet warm even when they get wet. You may not think of winter as a wet time, but any snow that meets up with your body heat will turn into water. If you don’t have wool socks, synthetic wicking fabrics are a good second choice. Cotton is a no-no

First, the socks have to be able to fit into your shoes. If you’ve been running in super thin cotton or synthetic socks all summer, thick socks may not fit. Smartwool run socks are available in a thin version that can fit no problem—but in colder weather you’ll want some thickness for extra warmth. That thickness, in turn, may mean that your winter running shoes need to be roomier than the shoes you wear in summer. If you’re buying a new pair, make sure to try them on with the type of socks you intend to run in.

If your warm socks fit, you can make do with the same shoes you wore in the summer. Your feet will stay dry if the weather is dry and you stay out of puddles. If you encounter snow and slush, though, your feet will have to endure warm-but-wet conditions for the rest of your run. That can be okay for short runs, but for serious winter running, consider upgrading your shoes.

Some running shoes are available with water-resistant uppers. This level of water resistance will keep stray snowflakes out of your socks, but it isn’t reliable if you’ll be stepping in slush puddles. In that case, you’ll want something more waterproof, like Gore-Tex shoes, many of which are made for running trails.

If you expect to run on a lot of ice or packed snow, especially on trails, spikes can give you a little extra grip.

Yaktrax makes a rubber harness that stretches to fit your shoe, with steel coils and small spikes, for about $40.

Microspikes are a notch up from there, costing around $90 for what look like a miniature version of the chains you’d put on car tires.

And if you’re really dedicated—and are seeking a purpose-built pair of snow shoes—you can attach individual spikes: either these traction spikes from IceSpike, or via a DIY approach using sheet metal screws. (There’s a tutorial here.)

The versions that include rubber, like Yaktrax, can wear out quickly on pavement, so it’s best to save these for runs on trails or on unplowed paths. You’ll also want to be careful about the fit. I tried a pair that were similar to Yaktrax, but they were a tad too big. Shortly into my run, I found that the rubber stretched enough to pull the front set of spikes up over the top of my shoe. I've since gotten better-fitting ones, and they work great.

Spikes and specialized shoes help you go more places, in worse weather—but remember that they’re not required to just head out on a chilly day. Regular shoes are fine if the weather is cold but dry, or if you’re willing to put up with a little moisture.

I actually love when the weather gets cold enough that I need a jacket, because then I get to wear something that gives me extra pockets! Stick with thin jackets that have some room inside. By the time temps dip into the 20s or below, you’ll be doing some serious layering: for example, an undershirt, a long-sleeved warm layer, and a jacket. A great option for that warm layer is a wool base layer like this one. (Don’t worry, it’s not itchy.) If you can’t wear wool, a synthetic fleece is a good alternative.

Before you run out to buy all new clothes, experiment with what’s in your closet. Try repurposing a thin sweater, for example. Some people would never wear cotton for running (it can be cold when wet), but I wear it as my undershirt layer and have lived to tell the tale. Just make sure to shower or change after your run, so you aren't sitting around in cold, wet clothes.

The jacket is the most important layer. You can grab a sweatshirt in a pinch, but to be really well-equipped for nasty weather, you’ll want a jacket that is windproof and water-resistant. Jackets made for running are lightweight, for layering. Consider ones that are visible at night, with bright colors and reflective areas, and that come with zippered pockets.

Once it’s too cold for shorts, you’ll want to start layering your bottoms, too. Loose pants let cold air in, which is why leggings or “running tights” like these are standard winter wear for all genders. Running tights come in different thicknesses; go for something fleece-lined for your coldest runs, or layer two pairs.

You need to keep your ears warm, but don’t reach for a winter hat right away: an ear warmer or headband can cover your ears while still letting heat escape from the top of your head. And if anything is falling from the sky (say, snow), a baseball cap will keep it out of your eyes.

Fleece or knit hats are great for cold enough days, of course. The dividing line between earwarmer weather and hat weather is a personal one, and depends on whether you’re overheating. If you’re wearing a hat but sweating into your base layers, the hat is probably overkill.

Gloves, however, are essential. I keep a pair of cheap knit gloves in my jacket pockets, but windy or very cold days call for something stronger. You can layer gloves; I find gloves under mittens work well. You can also get windproof insulated gloves, which are warmer than any number of layers of holey knit gloves.

Your face will freeze on windy or very cold days, so this is where your old stash of pandemic face masks really shines. Consider a balaclava or even a fleece-lined bandana. A neck gaiter stays on better than a scarf if your neck is cold. At this point, every inch of you is covered but your eyes. Sunglasses can take care of that.

Johnny Depp is an accomplished character actor with a long and wildly successful career. Arguably one of Depp's best roles is as Captain Jack Sparrow in the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which are streaming in their entirety with a Disney+ subscription. I didn't expect the 63 year-old to have jokes when talking about possibly returning to the franchise alongside Orlando Bloom's Will Turner.

While Depp will return to theaters in Ebenezer this month, some moviegoers are hoping to see him return in a future Pirates of the Caribbean movie. During a recent interview with People, the Edward Scissorhands actor was asked about possibly returning to the beloved franchise, and responded with:

Well, I think we should have a contest of who can grow the fastest non-beard. Because neither of us can grow a beard, I don’t think. I can’t, for sure, but maybe he can. I don’t know.

Shots fired. Despite having facial hair in the Pirates of the Caribbean films, it turns out that neither Johnny Depp nor Orlando Bloom can actually grow a beard. While sidestepping whether or not he'd be down to return as Jack Sparrow, the Sweeney Todd actor was sure to poke fun at both himself, and his famous co-star.

Ebenezer marks Depp's first real return to a big Hollywood movie since the verdict of his defamation trial with Amber Heard was revealed. He spent a few years living abroad and getting out of the spotlight, but he's back playing the title role of Ti West's forthcoming holiday movie. Only time will tell if the upcoming book to screen adaptation ends up being considered one of the best Christmas movies of all time, but it seems like a game changer for the actor.

There's been chatter about more Pirates movies for a few years. At one point multiple movies were in development, including one that would star Margot Robbie. Unfortunately, there hasn't been any concrete updates about one of these projects moving forward in the development process. Although with Johnny Depp returning to the big screen, I have to assume that the chatter surrounding the franchise, and his possible return as Captain Jack Sparrow, will get louder.

Depp starred as the protagonist in all five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which ran in theaters from 2003 to 2017. The same can't be said for Orlando Bloom, who was absent for On Stranger Tides. He ended up returning in Dead Men Tell No Tales, which is the most recent installment in the action/adventure property.

All five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies are streaming now on Disney+. Only time will tell if a sixth movie ends up being green lit by the powers that be at Disney, but there does seem to be a ton of chatter about that possibility online.

#3615. 10-Year-Old Killed Teen Neighbor After Mom Told Him to Grab a Gun: Cops

A mother is facing serious charges — including murder — after her 10-year-old son fatally shot a 16-year-old girl during a “chaotic” fight between neighbors over loud music at a New Mexico apartment complex.

According to authorities, Elaina Gomez-Villeda had been fighting with her neighbors when she allegedly told her son to get a gun from their Albuquerque apartment on Saturday, October 31, according to the Albuquerque Police Department.

The boy grabbed the gun and shot a 16-year-old girl, killing her, police said.

A criminal complaint obtained by KOAT-TV identifies the teen as Keinerlein Rangel.

“What we know at this time is that there was a neighbor dispute over loud music. At one point in time, neighbors went next door to advise their neighbor to turn down the music,” Albuquerque Chief of Police Cecily Barker said in a statement to the TV station.

According to the criminal complaint, Gomez-Villeda, 40, asked Keinerlein Rangel and her mother, Susana, to turn down music they had been playing while unpacking items at their home.

After Susana refused to lower the music’s volume, Gomez-Villeda confronted the mother and daughter outside their residence, resulting in a physical altercation involving Gomez-Villeda hitting Susana and Keinerlein, per court records viewed by KOAT-TV.

When Gomez-Villeda’s child tried to intervene during the fight, she allegedly instructed her son to get her gun from their apartment, police said, per KRQE. The boy came back and fired one shot, fatally striking Keinerlein.

Gomez-Villeda and her son went inside their home immediately afterward, according to authorities. Afterward, she told investigators she sent a text to her husband, stating, “I’m probably going to jail right now,” the TV station reported.

She ultimately called 911 and accused a man identified as Keinerlein’s father of trying to pull open her apartment door and breaking her window following the shooting. She told detectives that she shot at him to fend him off, per KRQE.

In addition to murder, Gomez-Villeda is charged with conspiracy to commit a felony child abuse, contributing to the deliquency of a minor, battery and receiving stolen property in connection a firearm, according to Bernalillo County Metropolitan Detention Center records viewed by Us.

Information on whether she retained legal counsel wasn’t immediately available.

Gomez-Villeda;s 10-year-old son wasn’t identified by authorities because he hasn’t been charged, Albuquerque police spokesperson Gilbert Gallegos said in a statement to the Santa Fe New Mexican.

“APD detectives are working with the District Attorney’s Office and state officials to determine potential criminal charges because of his age,” Gallegos noted.

#3614. Drake’s Stylist Juliet Charlotte Has Seen All Your Memes

Stylist Sessions is a series of conversations in which Vanity Fair’s style correspondent, José Criales-Unzueta, unpacks the details, strategies, and Easter eggs on red carpets with the leading stylists. Up next, Juliet Charlotte tells VF about dressing Drake and, yes, reading all your comments about his looks

If you have access to the internet, it’s likely that you’ve seen what Drake wore to celebrate his 40th birthday last weekend in New York City. The rapper opted for a pair of red Versace leather pants and a cheetah jacket, a customized Chrome Hearts jeans and a suede vest, and an archival Chanel scarf paired with gray sweats. But it was an Hermès by Martin Margiela fringed shawl from 1997—a bonafide fashion vintage holy grail—that launched a thousand memes. Drake stepped out, and the jokes poured in: he was dubbed “pumpkin spice papi,” a nod to his nickname and Instagram handle @champagnepapi, described as a Real Housewife on a girls trip to Aspen, and as someone ready for “Christian girl autumn,” another viral trend.

Drake has been the punchline in culture many times, but—online trolls be damned—he’s been dressing better than ever. Chalk that up to his new-ish stylist, New Jersey native Juliet Charlotte. The 27-year-old started her career working with Ye and his fashion brand, Yeezy, as part of his wider styling team. Now that she’s a year into working with Drake, she’s based in Toronto. She also styles the up-and-coming Canadian singer-songwriter Chxrry, whose debut album U, Me & My Ego was released earlier this year.

Charlotte is a singular kind of stylist, particularly in that she prefers to buy pieces—some new, most archival—to build archives for her clients instead of borrowing clothes that any other celebrity could wear. In her first-ever interview, she tells VF about dressing Drake, and addresses the many memes. Spoiler alert: She’s seen them and remains unfazed—she even found some of them funny.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

Juliet Charlotte: I started styling five years ago now. I had just turned 21. Kanye’s team reached out to me, his GM [general manager] at the time, this guy named Laurence Chandler. They were like, “Are you a stylist? Can you come in and do some fittings with us?” I was literally a college student working a retail job, and I was like, Yes, I am a stylist. Of course I can [laughs]. It was around the time of the pandemic, when Ye was at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium and working with Demna. I walked into this room and there’s Demna and all these Balenciaga clothes and Ye. I just wanted to work. I was excited, and I just pretended that I knew what I was doing. I ended up working with him up until maybe two years ago now. I learned a lot from that experience, and then I took on new clients. I worked with [rapper and singer] Molly Santana, and now Chxrry and Drake.

Why do you think they thought you were a stylist?

I was going to school for fashion in New Jersey, and I didn’t actually know which area of fashion I wanted to enter. I just knew that I always loved clothes. When the pandemic happened, all the stores closed, so I had to find a new way to make money. I started to make angel number necklaces, and it just blew up and it was really profitable for me. Looking back, it’s kind of embarrassing, but I was young and it allowed me to buy clothes that I wanted. I would take pictures and post on my Instagram just casually. It wasn’t like I wanted to be an influencer or anything, I just wanted people to see the way I dress. It was a very casual thing, but Yeezy is very reference-based, and I guess I kept showing up on mood boards at that time. So Ye was like, let’s just get this girl in here.

I was part of a bigger team, and Ye would throw me into different roles. So it wasn’t always just styling. Sometimes I was working on e-commerce or doing campaigns, or sometimes it was Bianca [Censori]’s wardrobe. It’s really collaborative at Yeezy. There’s so many talented people that work on everything together.

I was wondering if there was a Ye or Yeezy connection, because I noticed an aesthetic throughline with your personal style. What would you say is your aesthetic, your “thing,” as a stylist?

The Yeezy background definitely helped make me this way, because I want to simplify everything and strip down everything and just be like, let’s just do the absolute best version of whatever you want to do. I’m always trying to declutter. And I really think that came from working with Ye, because he just wants to strip everything back and make it just simple but beautiful and effective.

Drake is a maximalist when it comes to his style, and I appreciate that. I don’t want to just throw my personal style on anybody that I work with. I really want to take what they love and be like, “Okay, let’s do the best version of this.” Working with him, I really just try and keep it in his world and keep it to things that excite him.

Drake out in New York City wearing vintage Hermès by Martin Margiela from 1997.

Hermès by Martin Margiela, fall-winter 1997.

Have you always been into vintage fashion? Or is it something that you’ve developed with Drake to build that into his wardrobe?

Obviously we just had that Hermès by [Martin] Margiela moment, which I really enjoyed and I thought it was fun. But I’m really interested in taking pieces, just random vintage pieces that didn’t get such a moment in the past, because that Hermès piece already had its moment on the runway. It’s fun to bring it back, but the way that I like to shop is finding vintage pieces that didn’t get a moment and reinventing them. Obviously there’s a lot of amazing designers right now, but I’m also not so into over-consumption, and just what we’ve turned into. I’d really rather shop vintage as much as I can.

Drake is someone who has such a wide range of influences and sounds. When you work on looks for him, are you trying to pull from this really wide range of inspirations and aesthetics, or are you trying to be a little more focused? Do you try to speak back to the music or do you just try to be a little more focused on just the look?

Sometimes we’re pulling inspiration from Michael Jackson or Liberace, or another artist. But, for example, we’re in Texas right now. He just bought a ranch in Texas. It’s so beautiful. When I first started working with him and I came to the ranch, I’m like, “You are a ranch owner. You’re not larping this aesthetic. You literally live it.” I was really inspired by the saddle shop that’s nearby and all these different stores because it’s two hours away from Houston. He was already wearing [Western clothing] when I met him. This is just a different variation of it. The Western stuff is heavily in his style now, loves vests. I take what I see in his everyday life and see what we lean on more. Like even this mob boss type of thing—he’s really interested in Italian culture, and I’m Italian, so that influence comes in as well.

He has had such a long and prolific career, and he is often self-referential. Do you ever reference early moments in his career?

We did just pull back in his “FOMO” video. We did a variation of the “Hotline Bling” outfit that he wore. But we really don’t draw back too much, I think because he’s just evolved so much as a person. I’ll still send him some looks and be like, “Oh, you ate this,” [laughs]. I have met him as the person that he is now and I’m like, “Okay, he just turned 40. Let’s just be elevated and grown.”

Chxrry at Paris Fashion Week in September.

Chxrry is building something really strong. What’s it like to work with both an artist that has been working in the industry for so long while also with someone who’s so green?

Chxrry and I have become best friends in the process, so we’re just figuring it out together. We’re the same age. She’s so early in her career that I’m sure she’ll have many evolutions, but for now it’s just about having fun.

With Drake, he just loves clothes and is pretty easygoing, but there’s obviously a lot more pressure that’s involved because he’s so established. It’s very different, but equally as rewarding.

I have to ask about the birthday outfits. I thought they were great, but I’m curious if you planned a birthday weekend wardrobe or if you are more casual about it?

Well, October’s a crazy month, so there’s so much stuff going on so I did a lot of preparation. We knew that we wanted to do a beautiful suit, but we actually had three other suits that fell through before that one. Last minute, our atelier had just made that tux for him, and then I got the brooch, we put on a bow tie. It all came together at the last minute, and that Chanel scarf I had just bought that morning in New York. The Hermès shawl I bought the day before we left for the trip in Canada. Everything is really just down to what he’s feeling like that night. We can do all this preparation, but that night if he’s like, “Actually, I just feel like being more chill or I just want to do this,” we just pivot, and we always figure it out.

Drake wearing gray sweats and a vintage Chanel scarf.

A Chorme Hearts cheetah jacket and Versace red leather pants.

I like that he seems to wear only things he owns, when many celebrities wear borrowed clothing. Do you also do that, or do you prefer to just buy things?

On the record [laughs], I hate pulling. I hate loaning. I hate all of that. It gives me anxiety. I hate if it was my stuff and it was out in the world and you just never know what happens. It could get messed up in travel, and there’s just wear and tear. Things just happen. I know it’s a huge part of styling, but for me, I’d rather just source the pieces myself and have them be a part of our archive and a part of our collection.

With someone like Drake, who is so big, you want there to be an archive of what he’s done and worn, otherwise it’s all lost in brands’ sample closets. I have to ask about the memes. People had so much to say about the Hermès by Margiela. As the stylist, what do you think of that?

I love a joke. I love a joke we can laugh about, but I still love the look. I don’t feel less than or like, “Oh God, it’s a meme.” I still love the look. I think it was amazing. Even when we did “FOMO” and he was wearing that leather jacket with the fur on one side, that was a women’s Saint Laurent piece. I love when men do things that are out of the box, or that isn’t just pants and a shirt. Why not wear a fringed shawl? I was into it, but I could appreciate the joke and I did think some of them were funny.

Pumpkin Spice Papi was really funny. If anything, becoming a meme nowadays adds to the look. It’s already a Halloween costume.

Yes [laughs], I’ve seen that. I was too young, but I always think that if we had the internet the way that we do now, what would people say about Michael Jackson or what would they say about Prince? I’m sure there would be so many memes. There would have to be.

#3613. Anker’s New Soundcore Space 2 Headphones Are Already 18% Off

Anker released the noise-cancelling Soundcore Space One headphones a few years ago, and while they were a more budget-friendly alternative to premium models from Bose and Sony, their performance and fit still fell short in several areas. The brand’s updated Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a major upgrade across the board: They’re comfier, have better ANC, and are currently 18% off at $106.49 (originally $129.99), a rare price cut for a still-new release from a popular brand.

Battery life is one of the Soundcore Space 2’s most attractive features: They last up to 50 hours with ANC on and 70 hours with ANC off, and a five-minute charge gives you up to four extra hours. The noise cancellation is strong for the price, blocking out lower-frequency sounds well. Comfort is also a major upgrade from its sparser predecessor, with roomier, more plush memory foam earcups and a padded headband. They’re also travel-friendly, as the earcups rotate and fold.

The Soundcore app allows you to customize EQ and sound presets, giving you added flexibility if you don’t like the default tuning. Instead of touch-sensitive panels, these headphones use conventional buttons, which help prevent accidental commands while adjusting the earcups and are easy to operate. Along with supporting Bluetooth 6.1, they also have a wired-cable option, which isn’t always the case with modern wireless headphones. That said, they don’t support USB-C audio.

If you want over-ear noise-canceling headphones that perform well but don’t have $200 to shell out for a more expensive model, the Anker Soundcore Space 2 headphones are a comfortable, effective, and long-lasting alternative that hover around $100 at the current discounted price.

#3610. One of the GameCube’s Great Cult Classics Gets the Remaster It Deserves

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee is as clumsy and charming as you remember

When I was a kid, there were some games I only knew through magazines. I never played them, but they were all over the pages of Electronic Gaming Monthly and Nintendo Power, so I knew everything about them anyway. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee was firmly a “magazine game” when it was released for the GameCube in 2002. I even had a free poster of it on my wall as a kid, one I kept hung up even after a wave of middling reviews eventually dropped.

Historically, games like that aren’t prime candidates for remasters. They’re left to become rare collectibles found at retro game conventions while canon classics receive countless double dips on modern platforms. So what a delight it is that Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered now exists, in all of its messy glory. Atari’s surprising revival brings back a quintessential magazine game, rescuing it from its cult-classic destiny with a makeover and online multiplayer in tow.

Does it finally prove 2002’s unimpressed critics wrong? Not exactly. It’s still the same messy and shallow fighting game in some ways. But the purpose of a remaster like this shouldn’t be to engineer a redemption arc; all games, even the ones you never experienced beyond their box art, deserve to be preserved and celebrated.

Developed by Pipeworks in 2002, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee is a 3D brawler where players duke it out with a roster of rubbery kaiju. It’s a mix between arcade classic Rampage and Super Smash Bros., as you brawl your way through destructible cities using directional attacks. Despite receiving a few strong reviews at release from the likes of Nintendo Power and IGN, it largely earned middling scores from critics who took issue with its lack of depth. History has already repeated itself in 2026: the remaster currently has almost exact same Metacritic score as the original game. (73 for the original, 72 for the remaster.) Having spent hours with the Pipeworks’ faithful remaster, the consistent reaction tracks. Despite looking shinier, the new version wears all of its predecessor’s warts like a badge of honor.

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee remains a gleefully silly button masher that’s built for parties. Even now, there’s plenty of immediate pick-up-and-play fun that comes with stepping into Godzilla or Megalon’s rubber boots and smashing up Tokyo. Matches feel as big and exaggerated as professional wrestling bouts, as your monster body slams and tail whips buildings. What can feel a little clunky at first soon comes together as you learn how to block, strategically use your atomic breath to create space between you and your opponent, and duck behind buildings for cover. There’s just enough depth to create a casually satisfying fighting game where punching isn’t your only option.

As someone who never got to spend much time with the original as a kid outside of GameStop demo kiosks, I was smitten with the remaster right away, despite recognizing some obvious flaws. Yes, your grab button is finicky, leaving you struggling to pick up a building or scoop up your opponent. The movement can feel laborious as you trek around open city arenas. Characters can feel wildly imbalanced, with flying monsters like King Ghidorah having some clear advantages over grounded foes. There’s also its disappointingly repetitive arcade mode, which doesn’t bother to give each monster their own distinct story as they go to war against an alien invasion. There’s a good reason that games like Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee were largely enjoyed as weekend Blockbuster rentals in their time; you’re sure to hit the bottom of it in just a few hours.

But however short your fling with the remaster may be, it’s still worth spending some time with a blast from the past that’s so committed to celebrating a goofy piece of GameCube history. I quickly came to admire the brawler for its smart way of adapting old-school kaiju fights into a video game. It really gets across the idea that you’re a guy in a monster suit stomping around a fragile miniature city. The remaster keeps that spirit intact by making the shiny new textures look even more like rubber. I appreciate that the clumsiness of the brawling is preserved too, even if it’s not going to earn any favor with critics; the remaster is at its best when it stands by the original game’s vision.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Conversely, it’s at its worst when it tries to work in arbitrary tweaks. In the original game, you unlocked new monsters and stages by meeting various conditions as you played. The remaster trades that tradition for a long-tailed grind where you gain research points by playing. That approach not only pushes you to replay dull modes over and over again, but it also removes the surprising spirit of unlockables from the experience. Gone is the time-honored joy of getting a new character out of nowhere during a session. It’s one bum choice in a game that otherwise reveres GameCube era design choices.

Despite that flaw, I’m glad Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee has gotten its due on modern consoles — and in a way that isn’t desperate to rewrite history. As a collector of PlayStation 2 and GameCube games, I know that there’s a unique joy in cracking open an old game from an age where developers were still figuring out how 3D games should feel. These days, modern games can feel predictable and uniform, as so many developers have refined what a parry should feel like to a scientific degree. Pipeworks was very much experimenting in 2002 as it tried to crack what a Godzilla game that was faithful to Japanese cinema tradition should feel like. The results may have been messy at times, but it’s always a delight to play an old game that’s filled with deliberate design choices. Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like nothing else in 2026, and that’s what makes it a worthy preservation effort, position in video game canon be damned.

Nintendo kicked and screamed against the PlayStation hegemony and its own fans, but it all worked out in the end

#3609. 10 Shows Like 'A Different World' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The original A Different World was a groundbreaking sitcom in its era, spending six seasons highlighting Black academic drive among a cast of characters so indelible that we're now checking in on them decades later. Spearheaded by Queen Sugar's Felicia Pride, the update has been a critical and ratings hit for Netflix, earning the rarest prize of all in streaming television: a quick second season renewal. While you're waiting for season two, here are some other smart coming-of-age shows that blend heart and humor with realistic drama.

An easy pairing with A Different World, this show follows Black-ish's Zoey Johnson (Yara Shahidi) as she leaves home to attend a (fictional) California liberal arts college (the last couple of post-graduation seasons shift the focus to her brother Andre, played by Marcus Scribner). The emphasis is on driven young people who are capable of making big mistakes on the path to adulthood. A true comedy-drama, Grown-ish feels real(-ish) in a way that few other college shows have managed. Stream Grown-ish on Hulu.

Adapted from and expanding upon the 2014 movie, this show takes us to a (fictional) Ivy League school for a comedy-drama that tackles campus life and politics from a rather different perspective than that of Rooster. Logan Browning leads the ensemble cast as Sam White, who kind of inadvertently starts the titular radio show following a racially charged incident on campus. Far from the racial screed that some bad-faith YouTubers seem to find it, it's never shy about confronting the complicated and occasionally silly contradictions of campus activism, with each episode approaching life at Winchester University from a different character's perspective. Stream Dear White People on Netflix.

Kimberly (Pauline Chalamet) is an endlessly naïve scholarship student; Bela (Amrit Kaur) is an aspiring comedy writer on the make for the hottest guys; Whitney (Alyah Chanelle Scott) is an overachieving athlete and senator’s daughter; and Leighton (Reneé Rapp) is a closeted sorority girl. They're all randomly assigned to room together as freshmen at the fictional Essex College in Vermont. Created by Mindy Kaling and Justin Noble, this comedy-drama isn't nearly as salacious as its title suggests. There's sex for sure, but mostly it's a funny, queer-friendly show that's a little less about one overarching romance than it is about growing up, and the value of female friendship. Stream The Sex Lives of College Girls on HBO Max.

Even though we're backing up a couple of years to follow teens in their high school years, this British import's setting is a decent match, finding its students living away from home and family for the first time in their lives. At the fictional prestigious boarding school St. Gilbert’s, five Black teens are newly attending on scholarships, but their integration into the existing cliques is less than smooth—especially given that they're there largely as a PR stunt. Boarders blends teen romance, coming-of-age drama, and a delightful willingness to take the piss when it comes to the whole "rich private school" thing. Stream Boarders on Tubi.

Another modern take on a beloved '80s/'90s sitcom, this one's a bit different, serving as a total reimagining with no narrative connection to the original. And while A Different World is a comedy with dramatic heft, this one's more of a straight drama. It’s jarring for fans of the beloved original to tune in to find a serious show with the same premise as the Will Smith original—one that often leans into heavy realism. Jabari Banks plays, er, Will Smith, a 16-year-old from West Philadelphia who moves in with his auntie and uncle in Bel-Air following a gun charge and a run-in with a Philly drug lord. Banks is charismatic and believable, bringing a ton of personality to a show that occasionally veers down dark alleys. Stream Bel-Air on Peacock.

Comedian Benito Skinner plays himself, kinda, in this buzzy comedy that sees a former high school jock facing his freshman year in college while desperately trying to convince himself and everyone else that he's as straight as they come (relatable, except for the jock part). Much of the appeal is in its deft blending of tones: It's both a frequently raunchy college comedy and a sweet coming-of-age story about accepting yourself without worrying about what everyone else thinks. The cast includes Adam DiMarco (The White Lotus) and Rish Shah (Ms. Marvel), and, though it's more a story of one young man's coming of age, there's a strong ensemble backing him up. Stream Overcompensating on Prime Video.

The heart of All American (for most of its run) is Spencer James (Daniel Ezra), based on real-life NFL linebacker Spencer Paysinger. A star player for his high school team in Crenshaw, he's recruited by the coach (Taye Diggs) of a team in Beverly Hills to come and play for them, forcing Spencer to navigate two very different worlds while trying to build a life and potential career. Stream All American on Netflix.

Following a family tragedy, the already awkward 15-year-old Devi Vishwakumar (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) has a pretty terrible freshman year of high school, and decides that she’s going to turn things around the following year, hoping that a nearly academic study of sex will get her the boyfriend(s) her raging hormones have begun to demand. It works, to a point—but getting a surprise yes to sex from her crush leads her to question what she’s really ready for. More about burgeoning sexuality than sex specifically, this Mindy Kaling-produced series is both honest and charming. Stream Never Have I Ever on Netflix.

For realism in a show about the college experience, you could do a lot worse than this docuseries following several students at Gallaudet University, a school for deaf and hard-of-hearing young adults. In one sense, it's a specific setting where perspectives on deafness vary wildly, even in Gallaudet's self-contained world (aside from being a show about academically driven and horny college students, this is also a great primer for hearing people about some of the issues). But even for all of that, the challenges in building a life and future away from home are pretty universally relatable. Stream Deaf U on Netflix.

There's a reason A Different World has returned in 2026, and a lot of that has to do with the fact that there was nothing else on TV quite like it back in the late '80s and early '90s. For all of its sitcom sensibilities, the show tried hard (especially after multi-hyphenate creator Debbie Allen arrived to rework things after its first season) to paint a realistic picture of college life and an HBCU. Of the few shows on TV with largely Black casts, almost none would go so far as to highlight achievement and excellence; A Different World managed to do so while building a cast of characters so memorable that we're more than willing to catch up with them nearly forty years later. Stream A Different World on Netflix.

#3608. Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie's Daughter Vivienne Drops Dad's Last Name

Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s 18-year-old daughter, Vivienne, has officially dropped her father’s last name, becoming the fourth of the pair’s shared six children to drop their dad’s famous moniker.

A Los Angeles judge granted Vivienne’s petition to legally change her name from Vivienne Marcheline Jolie-Pitt to Vivienne Marcheline Jolie on Monday, November 2, Us can confirm.

“There being no objections, the petition for change of name is granted,” read court paperwork obtained by Us on Monday. “The Decree is signed and filed.”

Vivienne’s attorney, Peter Kenneth Levine, appeared remotely for a Monday morning hearing, according to the outlet. Judge Virginia Keeny presided over the hearing at Los Angeles Superior Court’s Stanley Mosk Courthouse and read aloud the names of those whose name change petitions had been approved.

“These are name change petitions, which are going to be granted. That means that I can read the information provided and sign a decree, and you’ll be able to get a copy of the decree in possibly one week in Room 112 in the first floor of this building, the Stanley Mosk Courthouse,” Keeny said. “So if you hear your name, you can sign off, and you can get your paperwork in a week.”

The judge reportedly continued, “I’m going to read both the last name and also the last four numbers of the case.”

Vivienne initially filed her paperwork on July 20, eight days after she and twin brother Knox turned 18. The reason for her filing was listed as “personal” in court docs obtained by Us at the time.

“If people knew the whole truth they would have more sympathy for the children and respect them,” a source close to Jolie, 51, told Us at the time. “The fact they aren’t speaking ill or sharing things publicly only shows their decency.”

Prior to her filing, Vivienne had been using her mother’s last name publicly for more than two years. She was credited as “Vivienne Jolie” in the Playbill for the Broadway production of The Outsiders in May 2024.

Vivienne’s older sister Shiloh, 20, was the first of Jolie and Pitt’s six children to legally drop her father’s surname. She filed paperwork in May 2024, and her request was granted that August.

The former couple’s daughter Zahara, 21, followed suit in September, as did their son Maddox, 25.

Knox omitted “Pitt” from his name on his high school diploma in June, although he has not yet filed paperwork to legally make the change.

Jolie and Pitt, 62, also share son Pax, 22. The exes were married from 2014 to 2016. Their divorce was finalized in 2024, although they remain entangled in a separate legal battle over their French winery Château Miraval.
