#3577. I Tested ChatGPT's New 'Slides' Tool, and Here's How It Compares to Gemini

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

ChatGPT's capabilities continue to expand apace, and the latest feature is a fully capable slideshow creator. Announced a few weeks ago, ChatGPT Slides lets you create PowerPoint-style decks from inside your conversations, and it's now appearing for those on the Pro tier and above (meaning right now, you need to spend at least $100 a month to get it).

If you're on the free ChatGPT plan or the $20-a-month Plus tier, you can still get ChatGPT to generate downloadable PowerPoint files from the content of your conversations. However, they'll be more basic than those made in the full version of ChatGPT Slides, and there are no collaboration or native edit options.

ChatGPT Slides is part of OpenAI's push to give users a complete office suite inside the ChatGPT apps. Pages (the word processor) is already available for Pro tiers and above, while a spreadsheet app is on the way—the idea being that you will soon be able to get all your work done without any help from Google or Microsoft.

While Chatgpt Slides is only available on pricey plans right now, it's likely to come to lower subscription tiers in the future. But for now, how does the tool compare to what's available in the free and Plus tiers, not to mention what you can do with Gemini inside Google Slides? I've taken a detailed look.

When it comes to testing out AI tools, it helps to focus on something you're already knowledgeable about so you can spot any mistakes. To test this, I decided to see what ChatGPT could hoover up from the web about the new iPhone Duo. If you're on the free or Plus plans, you can start a conversation, then ask for a slideshow or PowerPoint about it.

Plus accounts also have access to a specific Presentations add-on, available via the + (plus) menu in the prompt box, though I get the impression this feature is in a state of flux since ChatGPT Slides arrived. In any case, you can begin asking about the iPhone Duo specs and early online reactions, and then say "build me a slideshow on the key features and reviews so far".

What I got back on the $20 Plus account was a fairly competent slideshow on Apple's foldable, with accurate information as far as I could see, and a simple series of layouts. It looked like something you might whip up from a template if you were in a rush and didn't have time to properly align all the bullet points or be very selective about which details you included and which you left out. One neat touch is that ChatGPT was able to drop in an official photo of the iPhone Duo at the start of the slideshow, but I had to specifically ask for one.

You can go back and make specific edits to the slideshow, but you have to describe them in the general prompt box—you can't select individual slide elements and make more precise changes. Still, if all you want to do is occasionally convert your ChatGPT conversations into a rough and ready slideshow, there's no real need to upgrade from the free or Plus accounts for now.

Switching to a Pro account, I gave a similar task to ChatGPT Slides hoping for something more comprehensive. To begin with, Slides gets its own dedicated area in the app, so you can start up a blank presentation from scratch—there are some basic image and text features, but the idea is to use prompts to build your slide deck. It's like a really basic Google Slides, with a prompt box.

Creating a slideshow this way feels rather tedious: Typing out what you want to say and then waiting for ChatGPT to do it isn't as intuitive as just throwing in some graphics and text yourself, as you might do in PowerPoint. It also seems to be a bit buggy, at least during the time I spent testing it, with some requests not properly completing.

Starting a standard conversation with ChatGPT and then turning all the information into a deck is much more useful from my perspective. My iPhone Duo slideshow was longer, laid out better, and more informative than the one I created on the Plus plan—there were even charts of battery life and official photos this time.

However, whether I used the free, Plus, or Pro tools, my presentations didn't come across as particularly well thought through. They don't really flow smoothly, either across individual slides or the slideshow as a whole—it feels very much like an algorithm, rather than a person, has decided what information to include and where on the slides to stick it.

Whether you create presentations in chats or through the ChatGPT Slides space, you're able to click on individual elements and do some basic manual resizing and repositioning. You can also request edits via prompts: "Drop in an image of a cat", "make this pop more", "center all of this information", or whatever it is.

ChatGPT Slides does offer collaborative tools, which I wasn't able to test, and I can see that being useful for teams heavily invested in ChatGPT's ecosystem. I can also imagine ChatGPT Slides coming in handy when you've got a lot of information you need to quickly dump into a slideshow that looks vaguely presentable.

In general though, I think I'd much rather stick to the traditional way of making slideshows for now. These old methods are more precise and more manageable, and give you full control over what's shown and where—even if they do take a bit longer. What's more, modern-day presentation tools come with so many templates and other layout aids that it's not difficult to put together something that's easy on the eyes while including all of the information you think is most critical.

Google is, of course, also all the way in on AI (and then some), and if you pay for Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) or above, you can have Gemini pop up right inside Google Slides to give you some assistance with your presentation-making. To compare the tools, I gave it the same task as I did ChatGPT, asking for a slide deck on the new iPhone Duo.

Gemini actually asked some questions along the way: about wht visual style to use, the audience to aim the slideshow at, and the details to highlight. Though it's always possible to put this sort of information manually into a prompt, this would be a helpful additional to ChatGPT Slides.

What Gemini and Google Slides produced was impressive in terms of the layout and overall vibe of the presentation: It felt much more like a human being had put together the slide deck compared to what ChatGPT had produced, in terms of the information chosen, the way the slides were laid out, and the color picks.

However, Google's result had its faults too: The presentation got the facts on the maximum brightness of the iPhone Duo screen wrong, and produced an "iPhone Duo" graphic that looked like two iPhones from around 2021 stuck together. ChatGPT Slides at least managed to pull official imagery from the Apple website.

You can't attach individual edit prompts to specific parts of your presentation in Google Slides as you can in ChatGPT Slides—you have to mention them in the general prompt box. That said, Google Slides is obviously a much more mature and established slideshow tool compared to the OpenAI equivalent, in terms of its features and layout options (it has been around for a decade, after all).

Given that extra software structure and the lower cost of entry, Gemini and Google Slides is the better option for AI-assisted slideshow making at the moment—though I wouldn't bet against OpenAI catching up. For now, ChatGPT Slides is something that's good to have available if you're already paying a lot for ChatGPT every month, but not a feature that makes it worth your while to swap your AI allegiance.

#3576. Dead by Daylight Fans Are Uninstalling the Game in Protest

Behaviour Interactive is under fire following Halloween livestream fail

Some Dead by Daylight players are expressing disappointment with developer Behaviour Interactive — and vowing to uninstall the game — after the studio appeared to show support for divisive streamer TheBurntPeanut.

During TheBurntPeanut's Halloween livestream, a Behaviour Interactive employee gifted the VTuber all available DLC for Dead by Daylight. Given the streamer's controversial nature, fans did not take this lightly. To show how displeased they were with the situation, some players uninstalled the game and requested a refund in protest.

Dead by Daylight is a multiplayer survival game where a player takes on the role of a killer and tries to track down and eliminate survivors. It features an array of well-known characters from all sorts of horror franchises alongside original creations. Thousands of players logged in to play this Halloween weekend, including VTuber TheBurntPeanut. During the stream, he received all of Dead by Daylight's paid expansions in his inbox — a gift from someone at Behaviour Interactive.

TheBurntPeanut is a controversial streamer, so many fans were immediately unhappy to see Behaviour Interactive supporting him. Seeing this, Peanut offered to return the items; the employee responded, "We can take the heat! They are yours to keep." The way that they dismissed fans' reaction only made matters worse.

Players were particularly upset over the fact that many Dead by Daylight content creators have been waiting for a long time to get approved for the Creator Program. All while controversial streamers continue to get accepted and receive support from the developers. This has resulted in Dead by Daylight veterans voicing their disappointment and uninstalling the game.

After quick backlash from the community, the official Dead by Daylight account responded, underlining that the anonymous employee's decision was made without proper approval and that their comments and conduct were not a reflection of Behaviour Interactive's values. The studio apologized for letting down the community and promised to review internal processes to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

TheBurntPeanut responded to the situation during a Minecraft stream, denying the accusations made against him. The streamer is known for not sticking with games for long, so it is entirely possible that he will not return to Dead by Daylight. Nevertheless, for many, the damage is still done.

One of Natalie Portman’s most iconic roles, even twenty years later, is V For Vendetta. How can one forget how great she looked with a shaved head? She just shared her personal takes on what it was like to be without hair for awhile, I didn’t see this recommendation coming from her.

Portman first rocked a buzzcut in 2005 at the premiere of Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith at Cannes Film Festival. It had been freshly shaven on set when she hopped on a plane to go to the glitzy event in between filming. As she recalled about attending the event with the fresh cut in her words:

Everyone was like, ‘Oh wow, she has no hair.’ And then I went back, got on a plane and went back to Berlin and started shooting again on Monday. It was pretty wild to be out in public exposed like a baby bird. I feel like it's something every woman should do at least once in her life. It feels so amazing to have rain on your head for the first time.

Wow, what a glowing review from Natalie Portman about shaving one’s head! While speaking to Harper’s Bazaar, the actress suggested that “every woman” give it a try at some point in their life. She loved it because it felt amazing to feel the rain on her head – which funny enough is the same thing Millie Bobby Brown pointed out about going bald for Stranger Things. Portman had a really positive review for shaving her head, but there is something she didn’t like so much:

I did not love growing it back. I have curly hair, and so when it grows back you just look like a little boy for a very long time.

Another solid point. I guess there’s always a baseball cap for those awkward growing pains? In V for Vendetta, Portman’s character of Evey has her head shaved against her will when she’s captured, imprisoned and tortured in the dystopian thriller. The moment when her head was shaved off had to be captured in one take with three cameras at once. During rehearsals for the scene, Portman said a bunch of men on the crew offered to have their heads shaved in order for it to be tested and ready for Portman.

Portman is one of quite a few actors who’ve left their hair behind for a while for a role. Emma Stone is the most recent example for her film Bugonia, but in her case, she made her director Yorgos Lanthimos do so too “in solidarity”. Though, the pact wasn’t as satisfying as Stone thought it would be. Florence Pugh also shaved her head for We Live In Time, and has talked about how she was worried she might look like “an egg” before officially committing to it, and embracing the haircut wholeheartedly.

You can check out Natalie Portman in V For Vendetta with a Paramount+ subscription. It’s still arguably one of her best movies, so her bold haircut was absolutely worth it.

#3574. This New Garmin Feature Is Draining Battery Life, but There's a Quick Fix

Garmin users are taking to the company's support forums with a common grievance: The newly introduced "OK Garmin" hands-free voice feature appears to be eating through battery life. The feature arrived through Garmin’s September software updates, bringing hands-free voice activation to the Fenix 8, Forerunner 570 and 970, Venu 4, and several other models. Here's how to make sure Garmin's new updates aren't slashing your watch's battery life.

Last month's updates for select watches also brought all-day fall detection, a set of new Quick Workouts and Garmin Run Coach plans, as well as that "OK Garmin" hands-free voice command feature. It's exactly what it sounds like: Instead of pressing a button, users can simply say “OK Garmin” to activate voice commands. However, it looks like "OK Garmin" in particular is what causes some watch's projected runtimes to drastically drop, allegedly by roughly 35% to 50% in some cases.

Garmin does acknowledge that enabling these settings shortens battery life, though it doesn't say by how much. The tradeoff makes sense, since the watch has to listen constantly for its wake phrase. Even so, giving up several days of runtime is a steep price for a feature that many people may seldom use. Luckily, the fix is simple: Turning off "OK Garmin" should restore your battery life estimates right away.

If your watch has been draining faster since the update, go to Settings > System > Voice and disable "OK Garmin." If needed, you can also switch off the Phone Assistant wake word from the same area. The good news is that turning this feature off won't even take voice commands away—you can still trigger them manually using the watch's physical controls.

Keep in mind that these numbers are battery estimates rather than independently tested, real-world runtimes. Some of the battery complaints that surfaced after the update may also stem from unrelated issues. Still, trading away as much as half your battery life just to avoid pressing a button is a difficult bargain to defend.

With November here, some people are already making Thanksgiving plans and watching Hallmark Christmas movies. But, I’m personally going to need five business days to mourn the end of spooky season. One of Universal Orlando’s masterminds, Michael Aiello, is totally on my wavelength, as he reflected on making this year’s landmark Halloween Horror Nights happen.

Aiello is the Senior Director of Entertainment Creative Development at Universal Orlando Resort and has over thirty years of experience at the theme park to his name. Since this year was the park’s special 35th anniversary scaring us with Universal’s beloved seasonal festivity, he had a lot to say about bringing it all to life. In his words:

For me, one of the greatest rewards of doing what we do is watching all of you experience the worlds we’ve created. Seeing your excitement, hearing your reactions, and knowing these stories mean as much to you as they do to us is something I’ll never take for granted.

I know HHN has become one of my favorite traditions, and it’s great to hear from the designer that it’s all about our reactions and enjoyment of it. The 2026 edition had a lot of highlights, from the Sinners haunted house, an especially bloody attraction with cannibals and an awesome ode to the Hellraiser franchise. In a post on X, Aiello said creatives like himself only get so many anniversaries in their careers, and doing the one this past season has been really rewarding for himself and his team. He continued:

There’s also something incredibly special about seeing Jack the Clown, Oddfellow and our legendary HHN icons and characters come together to celebrate 35 years of Halloween Horror Nights. These characters represent decades of imagination, artistry, and extraordinary talent, both behind the scenes and in the spotlight. They’ve become so much more than personas in a Halloween event. They’re part of its history, its identity, and the memories of generations of horror fans. Watching audiences embrace them again this year has been an absolute joy.

This year’s event was called Jack & Oddfellow: Chaos & Control. It brought about a crossover between two of HHN’s most popular icons, Jack the Clown and Dr. Oddfellow. Both characters debuted during the tenth Halloween Horror Nights back in 2000. They have become so popular that they’ve made multiple appearances in Orlando. With the season having ended, Aielo took some time to thank everyone involved for basically making it possible.

HHN definitely wouldn’t exist without the many hands and minds that create it every year. Aiello shouted out every division that works on the event including the scareactors and performers "who tirelessly bring the fear night after night”. The Halloween Horror Nights senior director also added this to his message:

I’ve always looked at our anniversary years as a chance to celebrate the stories we’ve told, the characters we’ve created, and the memories we’ve made along the way. Perhaps when the 40th rolls around, we’ll pull that book off the shelf again and discover a few more chapters worth telling. Or perhaps the story takes us somewhere entirely unexpected. That’s part of the magic of what we do. We never really know what the future holds.

The future can indeed be uncertain, but if history is any kind of indicator, the talented creatives at the park will find a way to spook audiences in unexpected ways down the road. Aiello also left fans with this last bit:

As our Infernal Carnival and all horrors within comes to close… Somewhere in the darkness, we direct our focus on the next nightmare… Happy Halloween Horror Nights…Till the fog rolls once again.

Oh, I’m so looking forward to the next nightmare! Before we know it, HHN will be celebrating its 40th anniversary, and we expect even more special surprises. Even though we're heading into the holidays, I feel like I’m already counting down the days for the next scary season!

#3572. Heat Director Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself at LA Gun Range

Michael Mann was rushed to the hospital Saturday, after the director of films such as Collateral, The Insider, and Ferrari accidentally shot himself at a Los Angeles gun range. According to People, the bullet from Mann's gun struck his leg while the 83-year-old artist was returning the firearm to its holster.

“On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered, resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann. He was treated and is being released,” a spokesperson for Mann said in a statement to media.

In a separate statement that did not name Mann, the Los Angeles Police Department confirmed the incident, which TMZ reports occurred at The Range LA, a members-only shooting club on the Westside region of Los Angeles.

Robert DeNiro, Al Pacino, and Michael Mann at the world premiere of Heat.

“Yesterday at around 4 p.m., officers responded to the 11000 block of Missouri Avenue for a radio call for shots fired at that location," the LAPD statement reads. "Responding units’ investigation determined the shooting to be accidental. The subject was transported to a local hospital in stable condition. An injury report was completed.”

According to Deadline, the incident is not expected to delay work on Heat 2, which is scheduled to begin production in January, 2027. The director, who has been nominated for four Academy Awards and is the winner of two Emmys and a BAFTA, is also responsible for films including Hunter (1986) and The Last of the Mohicans (1992); he is also known for creating the acclaimed television series Miami Vice.

Michael Mann's latest film, the sequel to 1995 crime classic Heat, will explore the origins of the characters played by Al Pacino and Robert De Niro in the original film. Its cast reportedly includes Leonardo DiCaprio, Christian Bale, and Adolescence creator Stephen Graham.

#3571. This Is the Robot Vacuum I Use Every Day, and It's 50% Off Right Now

I live in a 1,600-square-foot home, and vacuuming and mopping it by hand takes a considerable chunk of time. Passing that labor off to a robot vacuum was a great decision. I decided to go with the Roborock Qrevo CurvX since it seemed like a great fit for my circumstances. If you also have a dog, a mix of different floor types, and a gym with a workout mat, this robot vacuum might work for you, too. Amazon currently has it for $749.99 (originally $1,499.99), a 50% discount, and the lowest price it has ever been, according to price-tracking tools.

One of the main things I was looking for in a robot vacuum was suction power. The Qrevo CurvX has 22,000 Pa, which is stronger than most options at its price and is powerful enough to pick up anything that needs vacuuming in my house. I like that it has a self-lifting chassis so it can climb over my workout mat, rugs, obstacles like cables, or anything else that might be in the way, so I don't have to babysit it while it's doing its job. I also like the extendable mop pads and side brushes that allow it to reach corners and crevices it might not be slim enough to fit into. (Speaking of which, it's only 3.14 inches tall, so it can fit under most couches and beds without issue.)

My experience with the Roborock app has been great. It's easy to use and gives me enough control to clean my house how I want without a hassle. "No Go Zones" are easy to set up, as is the schedule. The main issue I've had is the size of the internal dust bin: It's small, so it needs to be cleaned after basically every scheduled use (though that shouldn't be as bad if you don't have a pet that sheds a lot).

Take it from me: If you're looking for a reliable hybrid robot vacuum that can clean multiple types of floors, mop, and comes with a great app, the Qrevo CurvX makes a compelling case at the current $750 discount.

#3570. Tomi Adeyemi Does Not Want to Talk About the Children of Blood and Bone Movie

“You are a once in a generation talent,” says Tomi Adeyemi, tears in her eyes. The author is not paying me a compliment; she is reading a line from one of her numerous fan letters.

Adeyemi is a New York Times bestselling writer, a feat she accomplished at twenty-four with her 2018 fantasy debut novel Children of Blood and Bone—the first in her Legacy of Orïsha trilogy, which marries old-fashioned American YA with West African mythology. Her new novel, The Siren—released in September—follows Emery, a freshman at Dartmouth desperate to find her place as she undertakes a series of trials to join the titular group of powerful girls on campus.

This is Adeyemi’s first time since childhood not writing fantasy; maybe her first time period, since she says the first book she ever wrote was a Parent Trap fan fiction. But it’s also an attempt to move past the widely successful young-adult fantasy with which she made her name—as well as the drama surrounding the film adaptation of Adeyemi’s debut novel, an experience she has called the worst thing she ever lived through.

In now-deleted TikToks, Adeyemi said that she’s distancing herself from the film, she won’t watch it, and that she blocked one of its leads, Amandla Stenberg, on social media. Sources indicated to VF this summer that Adeyemi got more creative control over the film than most first-time authors do, including a co-screenwriting credit; they also noted that she's switched talent agencies multiple times since striking an initial deal with ICM. “There must be something [going on] because she’s burned every bridge,” one insider who works in the book-to-film space said.

When we meet, Adeyemi says that she doesn’t want to talk about that.

Instead, she talks about how she used to exclusively write fantasy because the world wasn’t safe enough for her to write anything else. Now, though, she no longer feels like she has to hide behind magic. “I’ve become someone who can inhabit it fully,” she says. “When you allow a woman to grow her claws, I am more akin to a jungle cat than I am a house plant.” She breaks into a chorus of Frank Sinatra’s “My Way,” adding a Jackson 5-esque run: “Da-da-da, oh, baby, yeah-yeah.” She tells me that sometimes, when she connects with certain people—like me—she just can’t help herself from singing. “The stars, the moon!” she belts—lines from Florence + the Machine’s “Cosmic Love.”

Adeyemi’s a musical person. She saw Florence play at Lollapalooza: “Somehow, Florence wielded her magic so I was able to get to the very front row, and she’s singing to me. I’m like, Look at this wild woman, howling to the moon.” This reminds her of a scene from her new book: when Roux, the girl Emery idolizes, is introduced. Adeyemi writes Roux dancing on a table, kicking glasses, alive and wild. Emery wants to be like that; so does Adeyemi. She explains this before singing some more: “You woke up like that, you woke up like that.”

Adeyemi’s admiration for Roux is almost tangible. She smiles dreamily when she speaks about her creation, leaving you to wonder if there was a specific person this character was based on.

Though Adeyemi started working on The Siren in 2020, she says the novel’s published version was written entirely last year. She’s gotten used to trying, and trying again; while applying for fiction writing classes in college, Adeyemi says, she was rejected five semesters in a row. One professor actually told her he couldn’t teach her to write, an anecdote she’s happy to relate now: “Hello! So many bestsellers later.” She spent four and a half years writing her first, unpublished novel, which she says was rejected 63 times. Only then did she write Children of Blood and Bone.

Adeyemi says she writes to free herself—and while one can’t be sure exactly what she had to free herself from last year, the film adaptation of Blood and Bone was shot in 2025. That’s also when Adeyemi allegedly fell out with Stenberg. And while they’re spelled differently, it’s notable that Roux—The Siren’s charismatic villain—has the same name as one of Stenberg’s most popular characters, Rue in the first Hunger Games movie.

Female authors are often asked, unfairly, whether they are writing their own lives into a story. Yet it’s also impossible to ignore the parallels between Emery and Adeyemi herself. Both are Ivy-educated writers and self-proclaimed outsiders. Adeyemi also doesn’t shy from comparisons between herself and her most recent main character: she says that all authors write themselves, because doing so is a vehicle for understanding. Reading The Siren is like stepping into her consciousness.

So is interviewing her. Adeyemi has a tendency to go off on tangents about astrology, tarots, mystical energy. “Do you remember how it felt when the entire universe came alive? All these spindles, nerve endings rise,” she asks me at one point, holding out her arms. “If you could feel the stars and taste the wind?”

The novel is wrapped up in themes of belonging, identity, and loneliness—a narrative Adeyemi tells me she relates to. “I think if you don’t belong to yourself, you don’t belong anywhere,” she says—though Adeyemi also thinks that her Aquarius placements mean people like her will never fit in, because they are not designed to. Take “our most iconic Aquarius rising, Audrey Hepburn,” or SZA, who famously wears fairy wings onstage and on red carpets. “How painful must it have been when you were on land?” Adeyemi asks her fellow Aquarius rhetorically. “How painful must it have been to learn how to fly? How painful is it for the butterflies inside before they become their butterflies?”

Adeyemi herself appears on the cover of The Siren—something that “has never been done before,” she says. “But a lot of what I do has never been done before. I remember choosing the image because I saw the darkness, that power in Emery. I’ve never seen that look in anyone else’s eye.”

There was a time where having her books adapted for the screen felt like the epitome of Adeyemi’s work. The author no longer feels that way: “I am the epitome of my work,” she says. And as she said on those now-deleted TikToks, she really would rather not talk about the film adaptation of her first novel at all.

We avoid the topic during our initial conversation. When our time runs out, though, Adeyemi tells me she’d like to talk more at a later date. When I do eventually speak to Adeyemi again—and ask about the Blood and Bone film—she shuts down physically. Her smile drops; the question throws off the energy of the conversation, almost like a betrayal has occurred. I ask another question, and Adeyemi tells me that she is getting a call. She turns off her camera, and I sit in silence for seven minutes.

Eventually, Adeyemi returns and asks if I am still there. She tells me, “The Siren is number three, New York Times.” She’s feeling the hot flash version of goosebumps, she says, like she just finished a marathon.

Adeyemi says that all of this—her career, her work, her writing process—was inspired by extreme fear. She speaks about it in the second person: “An agonizing understanding that you’ve been taught to work so hard to build a better life, [but] you might not get to build that life. It could be snapped away from you like that. I live in that terror.” She’s gone through her own trials: not just the long journey to publishing Blood and Bone, but the internet’s scrutiny over the comments she made about the Blood and Bone adaptation. “I’m exceptionally proud of who I am today,” she says, though “life is terrifying.”

In our first conversation, Adeyemi had said The Siren might be her last book—that she might be finished with writing altogether. “You can depart from all these previous eras of your life with a gentle sort of ruthlessness,” she said, “and then tomorrow can actually be a new day.” Now, she seems reenergized by the idea of work, telling me that she’s met children’s literacy organizations that try to inspire kids with the work of James Baldwin, Octavia Butler, and herself. “I’m proud of writing this from a really hard time and place,” she says, “and I wanna continue Emery’s journey.”

I ask her what changed between that interview and this one. Her smile freezes; she laughs awkwardly before hesitantly replying, “I think it’s interesting talking to you in the summer and then talking to you post this tour. I don’t know how the piece will end up, since you’re getting two very distinct cross sections.”

She takes another beat. “So that quote felt more… there was more of a resonance the first time we spoke. As I’m sitting here with you now, I just have a vision of myself writing deeply.”

The time between our talks seems to have given her space for deep reflection. I remind Adeyemi what she’d told me about feeling more like a jungle cat than a houseplant, and ask if she felt she had to be a jungle cat during her journey with the Blood and Bone film. “I think all women have to be in tune with their power. I think Black women have to be in tune with their power, dark-skinned Black women especially,” she answers. “There’s a sense of gravity that wouldn’t have been there without knowing what it is to step into my power and voice. You owe it to yourself to feel safe, and if you’re the only one there to defend yourself, you have to have the claws.”

As the film’s January release inches closer, one has to wonder if Adeyemi has a desire to retract her claws—and her statements about the movie. Or at least whether everything that’s transpired has changed her relationship with her debut novel. “I think my relationship with myself has changed more than anything,” Adeyemi answers. When narrating the audiobook for The Siren, she noticed that Emery doesn’t recognize her own genius. That broke Adeyemi’s heart, because the character’s insecurities came from a personal place. The difference between her character and her own feelings also shows Adeyemi’s own growth: “You don’t feel that way anymore,” she told herself.

When asked whether she might try to make another movie someday—or adapt The Siren—she answers firmly: “I’ve already done that journey. It’s a lot of work, but it’s not work that is for myself. When you commit to doing something on screen, it’s more about everyone else on the other side of that screen. I think because I have such a directorial and cinematic approach to my writing, I do value having experienced everything.” Selling the rights to your novel means essentially giving it away to other people, she says. That was extremely difficult for her. “I don’t need anyone in this world.”

Maybe Adeyemi’s film future lies instead in front of the camera. She did film a cameo in Blood and Bone, and one in the second Devil Wears Prada film: “At the beginning of the year, I thought, Oh, I would like to try acting,” she laughs now. “By the end of the year, I had a cameo across from Viola Davis and another across from Meryl Streep.” In the future, she’d be interested in voice acting and animation. Or live-action—but maybe only if, say, Jon Chu asked her to star in a Bollywood rom-com with Dev Patel.

“SASUKE!” She yells the name of a Naruto character in a high-pitched voice, then adds in her normal voice, “I’m clearly a very animated person.”

Warning! Spoilers ahead for the Season 3 premiere of St. Denis Medical, “He Ain’t Noah Wyle." If you haven't tuned in for the NBC show, don't fret as this isn't a huge spoiler, but I will talk about the episode in this story.

St. Denis Medical’s third season finally premiered on the 2026 TV schedule, and it was so entertaining. On top of addressing some of the romantic twists left off in the Season 2 finale, the medical mockumentary continued to bring the comedy. This included some fun references to The Pitt, and I had to ask the creator why the direct mentions happened.

Following Ron’s surgery in the Season 2 finale, Damon Wayans guest starred as his temporary replacement, Dr. Highland. While Highland's a good doctor, it’s not hard to see his mannerisms and the way he dresses are similar to that of Dr. Robby from the Emmy-winning drama The Pitt. Alex even makes it a point to say Dr. Highland has a “big performative” energy and thinks he’s in a medical drama. However, “He ain’t Noah Wyle,” as she says (and as the title of the premiere also notes).

Between the way he acts, dresses, and talks, with one speech pulled directly from The Pitt, it was very clear the episode was not attempting to be subtle. St. Denis has in the past had no trouble spoofing other medical shows. That said, references can be tough, and Eric Ledgin told CinemaBlend why it’s easier to mention some shows, like The Pitt, and harder to mention others:

I always feel most connected to the show when the characters are living in the same world I'm living in. So, that gets a little tricky in the sense that they can't be fans of In Living Color because that would cause some kind of time portal warp that would ruin the show, I suppose. But they can know about The Pitt, you know, and they can comment on it, as that's a popular show; it's in the zeitgeist.

I love it when my favorite shows are name-dropped in my other favorite shows, especially when there’s a clear reference, such as Dr. Highland acting like Wyle’s Dr. Robby. It’s understandable why it can get tricky to bring up other shows, particularly ones that have featured the actors on St. Denis Medical themselves, but this time the whole show reference within a show thing worked.

Meanwhile,The Pitt is only two seasons in, but plenty of healthcare workers have praised the drama for its accuracy. It's also one of the most talked-about shows, and that's another reason why Ledgin felt the need to reference it, telling CinemaBlend:

I feel like there probably aren't many hospitals where people are working there and not talking about The Pitt from time to time. And, you know, as I think Alex says, or at least said it in an early draft of the script, it was like, ‘I watch The Pitt, I love The Pitt. But this ain't The Pitt.’ And so it's nice to be swimming in such different waters from them that we can still be fans of that show and comment on it in a fun way.

Since Ron is back at work following his surgery, Dr. Highland seems to have been dismissed (or at least is out of the picture for now). I'm a little sad to be saying goodbye to the St. Denis Medical version of Dr. Robby already. But here's hoping we still get some other shoutouts to The Pitt from time to time. (Especially since Alex has stated she loves Noah Wyle and would leave her husband for him, so I just know she’s gonna be watching Robby's Season 3 return.)

Meanwhile, fans can look forward to more from Season 3 of St. Denis Medical now that it’s finally here. Aside from fun references to other medical shows, there is a lot to look forward to on the plot front. We've got guest stars coming. We've got more chaos coming. So, stay tuned, as new episodes air on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET on NBC, and are streaming the next day with a Peacock subscription.

#3568. How To Watch Robert Pattinson's Primetime At Home

The year of Robert Pattinson will continue until morale improves — and, hopefully, for some time after that, too. While fellow "The Odyssey" co-stars Zendaya and Anne Hathaway have stolen the spotlight for similar reasons throughout 2026, the "Primetime" actor has quietly appeared in quite a few high-profile roles throughout the last several months. A24's "The Drama" (also co-starring Zendaya) left quite the impression on audiences and at the box office, as did the aforementioned retelling of "The Odyssey" by Christopher Nolan. And, as if his memorable line about getting "these beggars out of here" wasn't enough, he's set to follow all that up with a turn in "Dune: Part Three" later this December.

But don't sleep on "Primetime," the other major production by "You Can See Everything" co-director Lance Oppenheim this year. Starring Pattinson as Chris Hansen, the host behind the controversial TV show in the early aughts "To Catch a Predator," the film takes an unflinching, stylish, and occasionally surrealistic approach to the real-life figure who publicly shamed and embarrassed so many troubled minds with nefarious intent. But was this done for heroic and well-intentioned reasons? Or is there more to be uncovered beneath that bleached hair, distinctive voice, and wild-eyed chase for ratings and pop-culture buzz?

Well, audiences will now get a chance to decide for themselves, as "Primetime" is being made available to watch at home. The news comes a little over a month after its release in theaters, where it's actually still playing in certain locations. But for those who may have missed it the first time around, read on for all the details about how to catch it from the comfort of your living room.

The dark and unsettling satire that is "Primetime" is officially coming home, which is certain to lend a strong sense of irony to anyone watching this A24 movie about one of the most notorious television shows ever made. Based on the real-life controversy surrounding host Chris Hansen and his "To Catch a Predator" reality series, the film comes from director Lance Oppenheim and stars Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever, "Superman" breakout Skyler Gisondo, Bokeem Woodbine, Tony Revolori, Anna Faris, and even singer/songwriter Phoebe Bridgers.

But, for now, audiences can look forward to experiencing "Primetime" in all its unsettling, R-rated drama at home.

#3567. The Garmin Cirqa Finally Got a Much-Needed Feature

This week Garmin's screenless Cirqa smart band received a firmware update that fixes one of its most obvious gaps: the lack of alerts from your phone. With Version 4.20, you can now set up your smart band to buzz your wrist for texts, calls, and other smart notifications from your phone. The addition is listed on Garmin's forums as "Support vibration for smart notifications/incoming calls." Reaction has been upbeat, too—users on the Garmin subreddit have been glad to see the feature arrive.

Amusingly, Garmin's own FAQ still states that the Cirqa does not vibrate for text messages, phone calls, or other smartphone notifications. Clearly that page is now out of date, so Garmin will want to correct it. Since Garmin doesn't yet have step-by-step instructions, I tested the text-message vibrations myself. Here's how you can set up your Cirqa smart band to vibrate for calls and texts, in addition to a number of other promising updates to check out.

To receive these alerts, your band must be running firmware 4.20 or later. Here is how to get everything configured.

Update the firmware. Open your Garmin Connect app and sync your Cirqa, so the app can check for and install version 4.20 or newer.

Grant the necessary phone permissions. In your phone's settings, make sure Garmin Connect has permission to access SMS, Contacts, and Phone.

Configure notifications in Garmin Connect. Back in Garmin Connect, tap the Menu (or More) tab. Select Garmin Devices, then choose your Cirqa Smart Band. Go to Notifications & Alerts (or Smart Notifications) and turn on text and call alerts.

Troubleshooting tip: If alerts aren't coming through, check that Do Not Disturb, Sleep Mode, and any aggressive Battery Saver settings are turned off on both your phone and the band.

For most a lot of Cirqa fans, the phone alerts are the headline, but the 4.20 update carries a solid list of other improvements and bug fixes:

Trail Run: Run/Walk detection is now available for Trail Run activities.

Timestamp fix: Resolved a problem where an activity's recorded time didn't match the time on your phone.

Distance calibration: You can now calibrate distance for Treadmill Run, Indoor Rowing, and Indoor Cycling before saving the activity on the device.

Duration alerts: Duration time alerts for speaking out now accumulate.

Stress alerts: Stress alerts are now blocked while Auto Activity Detection is recording.

Bedtime reminders: Fixed an issue where the bedtime approaching notification sometimes failed to trigger.

Live Activity: Heart rate now appears on the Live Activity screen before recording begins.

Pinned activity bug: Fixed an issue where the pinned activity reverted to Timed Activity after changing the phone's language.

Workout editing: Fixed a problem that prevented editing reps during a workout.

Stability: General system stability improvements.

#3566. Nintendo Officially Comments on Zelda Remake's Divisive Graphics

Link, Zelda, and others have a distinct style to them

Nintendo's upcoming remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time looks drastically different from the Nintendo 64 original. That's understandable, given the nearly 28 years that have passed since the first 3D Zelda debuted. Beyond the graphical advancements, however, the Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time makes some bold character design choices, some of which have divided longtime Zelda fans.

In a new interview with the developers of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, we finally get, we finally get some explanation of why Nintendo made certain aesthetic choices, including the decision to make Link, Zelda, and others look more like puppets than strictly photorealistic people.

Nintendo developer Aya Shida, who served as art director on The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, said that, "When we first considered how to leverage the capabilities of Nintendo Switch 2 to explore new forms of visual expression, a fairly natural direction seemed to be to create a richly detailed world that felt as though it could truly exist. But our goal wasn't simply to make everything look realistic."

Shida noted the contrast between the dark but beautiful setting of Hyrule and the game's colorful, quirky characters in the original game.

"I felt that this contrast was what gave The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time its mysterious, almost dreamlike charm," Shida explained. "So for this game, we wanted to rebuild Hyrule as a rich, dense world that felt as though it could truly exist, while retaining the feel of the original. At the same time, we wanted its colorful and quirky characters to feel like a natural part of that world. Figuring out how to strike the right balance became one of the main themes of the art development."

Shida revealed that some of the game's art direction was guided by certain keywords: "a puppet-show feel" and "the analog feel of practical effects films." Those phrases refer to creating "a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds."

"We also felt that there was some overlap between these forms of expression and the distinctive nostalgia evoked by the original game," Shida explained. "We began by drawing sketches of Link, Zelda, and the other characters. At the same time, to show the kind of world they would inhabit, we created a 3D model of the Great Deku Tree that looked truly alive, carefully adjusting the lighting and textures. We then presented the concept to Aonuma-san, explaining that we wanted characters like these to blend naturally into a world like this."

Longtime Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma weighed in on that choice, highlighting how nostalgia for the original Ocarina of Time played into the remake's visual style.

"Back when we were developing the game for Nintendo 64, we thought we were making something cutting-edge for the time," Aonuma said. "We weren't trying to create anything nostalgic. But after all these years, the current development team feels a certain sense of nostalgia when they look back at the original. And their efforts to express that nostalgia led them to an analog, puppet-show-like feel. As one of the original developers, that progression made sense to me."

Players will get a chance to immerse themselves in the reimagined Hyrule later this week, when The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time arrives on Nintendo Switch 2.

Nintendo’s new version of a Zelda classic is sharp, streamlined, and plays better than ever

#3565. How To Watch Zach Cregger's Resident Evil At Home

This has been a wonderful year for video game movie fans. We've seen both big productions and even indie movies translate the world of video games to cinema with much success (check out our list of the best video game adaptations of 2026 here).

The best movie based on a video game this year is Zach Cregger's "Resident Evil," which actually ignores the exact plot of the long-running Capcom franchise. Instead of being a faithful game recreation, it actually tells an original story that understands the true appeal of the best games in the "Resident Evil" franchise. Cregger crafted a horror comedy that's all about the frustration of finding yourself in an impossible situation where absolutely nothing works in your favor, and the comedy that comes from everything going wrong at the worst possible moment.

After dominating the box office, "Resident Evil" is finally coming home, with platforms like Fandango at Home listing the film with a release date for November 3, 2026 (you can of course choose another platform like Prime Video, or Apple TV). That means you can purchase or rent "Resident Evil" to watch from the comfort or horrors of home as soon as tomorrow, for the typical VOD price of $24.99 to purchase.

We don't know if "Resident Evil" will arrive on digital platforms with any bonus features just yet. That being said, we have seen and heard plenty about the making of the movie. When /Film had the chance to speak with Weta's Kevin Smith, one of the visual effects supervisors in the movie, he talked about how ridiculously complicated the sewer zombie was — especially with all the blood and goop coming out of his guts.

"Resident Evil" does what the best video game adaptations do — makes you feel like you're in the world of the game, even if it's telling an entirely different story than the familiar source mateiral. The film often feels like one of the journal entries you find in a "Resident Evil" game, a tragic story of a poor schmuck who messes around and finds themselves turned into a zombie.

Based on some of his comments about making the film, it seems unlikely Zach Cregger will return to make a sequel, but given how successful it's been at the box office, it's only a matter of time before we return to Raccoon City again.

#3564. Substack’s Cofounder Might Not Know How to Save the Media—But He Knows How to Outplay It

As recently as a few years ago, Substack was struggling to shed the perception that it was radioactive. “Substack Has a Nazi Problem,” read the headline of a 2023 Atlantic story that surfaced “scores of white-supremacist, neo-Confederate, and explicitly Nazi newsletters” on the platform, which was, in some instances, taking its standard 10% profit from them. Over 200 Substack writers wrote an open letter opposing the company’s hands-off approach to content moderation, and several high-profile writers and publications migrated to competitors.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Charli xcx publish there—Kylie Jenner has said she’d like to—as do new media phenomena like Feed Me and The Free Press. The platform has significant footholds in fashion, AI, politics, literature, celebrity gossip, and most everything in between. In the opening pages of his book, How to Save the Media, McKenzie recalls drinking whiskey at the Chelsea Hotel alongside former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown, who now publishes the popular Fresh Hell newsletter on Substack. The United Kingdom–born Brown, like McKenzie, came to America from abroad, only to rise to the highest rungs of its media world, and she seemed now to see him as a peer.

“You’re a New Zealander, aren’t you?” she asked McKenzie. “There’s something to being an outsider.”

In a recent interview with Vanity Fair, speaking from the Toni Morrison Conference Room at Substack’s San Francisco headquarters, McKenzie appeared uncomfortable with the idea that his book, liberally sprinkled with such encounters with the cream of the Substack crop, amounted to a victory lap. He was, despite a generally mild manner and steadfast earnestness, relentlessly on message. “I’m always going to be like a broken record coming back to the importance of direct relationships,” McKenzie acknowledged. It’s the Substack theory of fixing an ailing media ecosystem: replacing the ad-based chaos sown by the internet with a more nourishing connection between writer and reader, and having consumers pay for the media they want to see in the world rather than subject themselves to the whims of an attention economy controlled by big social media companies. McKenzie admitted his book’s title was a provocation, but “for me, it’s backing up the gospel that I’m trying to preach.”

Still, we could agree that something about the controversies that dogged the platform in recent years now seems quaint—that Substack has achieved some fundamental conquest. Instead of reactively responding to the “Nazi problem,” the company chose to stick with its hands-off approach to content moderation, and the outcry dissipated: Substack remains the go-to home for your established journalists striking out on their own (Jim Acosta, Nate Silver) as well as your upstart media operations repurposing the expertise once best associated with legacy outlets (The Bulwark, The Ankler). I suggested to McKenzie that the platform today is akin to Instagram or Grindr: a tech company, yes, but also an undeniable element of the fabric of contemporary life.

From a writer’s perspective, one knock-on effect of the Substack boom has been the rising cachet around writing itself, despite the spree of recent news stories declaring the end of reading. There are so many—too many?—personal essayists and gift guide impresarios emerging seemingly out of nowhere. (“I’m not snobby about that,” McKenzie said. “I think everyone should try to write and no one should be discouraged through peer pressure from writing.”) And then there is the ever-increasing atomization across media, with political discourse splaying out across countless newsletters that are only intermittently in conversation with one another. Is this new cacophony strictly better than the ones we encountered on Facebook and Twitter? Part of the reason the open letter concerning Nazi Substack newsletters didn’t stick, perhaps, was that no one is reading the same things anyway.

McKenzie is currently chipping away at Anna Karenina. “I honestly think writing is good and reading is good,” he said, echoing the kind of unadorned aphorisms he sometimes issues on X. As far as the purported literacy emergency, he says, “I don’t see many centuries of progress on this fundamental communication form being undone overnight.” Our “cultural crisis,” McKenzie thinks, has more to do with the distribution mechanisms of writing, and “is intrinsically tied to the state of the media system.”

After departing small-town New Zealand to pursue a career in journalism, McKenzie, 44, tried his hand at tech reporting in Hong Kong and San Francisco. Later, while working at the messaging app Kik, he and the company’s chief technology officer Chris Best hatched their plan to reroute the flow of publishing profits away from social media companies and toward writers. (Best is Substack’s CEO, while McKenzie works as its “chief writing officer” and heads up the company’s partnerships and talent acquisition efforts.)

“We had more direct relationships in the traditional media system,” McKenzie said, referring to, for example, a subscription to a print newspaper. “But then it got broken by the internet and replaced by something that corroded the direct relationships and gave all the power to Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg instead.”

As it happens, one of the touchstones in McKenzie’s own writing career is his dust-up with Musk. He worked for a time in communications at Tesla, and Musk, McKenzie writes, threatened to sue to block a book that he wrote about the company after leaving. (Insane Mode was published in 2018. Musk and Tesla didn’t return requests for comment.) Later, McKenzie and Best would turn down acquisition offers from Jack Dorsey’s Twitter and Musk’s X.

It was a choice they made, in McKenzie’s telling, to preserve the company’s independence—to prevent the Substack ecosystem from going the same way as those social platforms, which tend to leave their consumers more exhausted and frustrated than enlightened. I proposed to McKenzie that the company’s endurance in the face of its detractors has something to do with the shifting shape of online discourse, and that Substack itself has had a key role in making the tools of mass censure weaker in the age of media fragmentation. “I wonder if a lesson we are all learning,” he suggested, “is that the heavy-handed censorship approach can often backfire.”

“Did it do any good to kick Trump off Twitter and Facebook for two years?” he asked.

In How to Save the Media, McKenzie reflects on an evening he spent at the Biltmore Hotel in downtown Los Angeles in 2021. He was there to support Bari Weiss, who had struck out on Substack after leaving The New York Times about a year earlier. The schism would go on to shape the future of journalism from the newsletter economy all the way up to the highest echelons of Hollywood and television news after Weiss was appointed editor in chief of CBS News last year. (Of the common criticisms that Weiss has made the network overly Trump-friendly and lacks the requisite TV experience for the role, McKenzie says, “I think for the most part, the media industry is experiencing Bari Weiss as a media gossip story. And I think the more interesting story is the structural story and what it suggests about what’s possible in this emerging media economy. So I’m mostly watching from that perspective and I still think it’s too early to draw grand conclusions about what’s happened so far.”) In her resignation letter from the Times, Weiss wrote that Twitter had become the paper’s “ultimate editor.” On Substack, she built The Free Press, an outlet that has largely defined itself in opposition to what it sees as mainstream media orthodoxies.

That night, the Los Angeles Press Club was honoring Weiss. McKenzie took the accolade, he writes, “as validation of the nascent direct-relationships model”: Despite the ongoing and widespread opposition to her politics, Weiss had identified a journalistic niche that required no traditional media backing. Yet, The Free Press ultimately brought Weiss back to the legacy press—the new Substack class has its eye on some of the old media rewards, to the extent that they remain available.The night served as a sign, McKenzie writes, that “independence can still deliver prestige.”

“I don’t think what we’re going through here,” he told me, “is a moment of change where all the benefits from the old things have to be thrown out.”

#3562. Thor Director Taika Waititi Slams Critics After His Jenna Ortega Sci-Fi Movie Flops

Director Taika Waititi isn't too happy with critics of his latest movie, "Klara and the Sun." The filmmaker behind "Thor: Ragnarok" and "Jojo Rabbit" recently took to social media to share his thoughts on the matter after his sci-fi movie starring Jenna Ortega flopped at the box office.

Posting on Instagram, Waititi shared a screenshot of a Screen Rant article highlighting the movie's audience score on Rotten Tomatoes, which sits at a decent 74%. The problem? It holds a lousy 24% critical approval rating. It's those critics that Waititi took issue with, writing:

"I haven't read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people. So, this Halloween, let's spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn't achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics. The same people who also hated 'Jojo Rabbit.' Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin."

"Klara and the Sun" is based on the 2021 book of the same name by Kazuo Ishiguro. It centers on Klara (Ortega), an Artificial Friend who meets Josie (Mia Tharia) and begins to heal her family, bringing light into the latter's complicated world with her innocent wonder and unwavering loyalty. For most critics, though, Waititi's movie failed to live up to the potential that existed on the page in Ishiguro's novel.

However, that wasn't at all the case with 2019's "Jojo Rabbit," despite what Waititi implied in his post. On the contrary, that movie was generally well-liked and became one of the big winners at the 2020 Oscars, taking home the Best Adapted Screenplay prize (on top of being nominated for Best Picture). It was a hit in theaters, too, bringing in $90 million against a $14 million budget.

It's one thing for a filmmaker like Taika Waititi to be disappointed that a movie didn't perform well. Indeed, "Klara and the Sun" hasn't even made $2 million at the box office against a $20 million budget. It's not an expensive movie, but with a cast that includes "Wednesday" star Jenna Ortega and Oscar-nominee Amy Adams, Sony Pictures had much higher expectations.

Recall that Waititi was on top of the world after "Thor: Ragnarok" saved a "dying" Chris Hemsworth, becoming a huge hit and reviving the "Thor" franchise within the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Waititi's sequel, "Thor: Love and Thunder," was also a success, but its reception was far less warm. Sadly, it's been a downhill slide since then, with Waititi's "Next Goal Wins" becoming a box office bomb in 2023.

That said, this is far from the first time that a high-profile filmmaker has taken aim at critics. "Gods of Egypt" director Alex Proyas really hates film critics, but he hasn't had a meaningful hit in some time. Elsewhere, "Clerks" director Kevin Smith rather publicly took aim at critics in the 2010s. Smith later made peace with movie critics, but it was a much-discussed issue at the time. It happens, but it's rarely a great look for the director doing the complaining.

The issue is that critics can slightly help a movie, but they rarely move the needle all that much in terms of selling tickets. If critical opinion mattered more, a great many acclaimed films would make a lot more money. But that's not the reality we live in. Either way, Waititi has big feelings about all of this, which he's opted to air out in public.

#3560. 5 Best Sci-Fi Movies Where The Hero Dies

Needless to say, this article will be full of spoilers.

There are many things the "Star Trek" and "Star Wars" franchises have in common, not the least of which is hope. The former is set in a utopian future wherein human prejudice, capitalism, and war have all been dispensed with in favor of a society built on diplomacy, peace, and sharing. Similarly, all "Star Wars" stories posit that fascism is an impermanent state that's constantly being batted back down by the forces of good, no matter how often it tries to reassert itself. Heck, the first "Star Wars" movie was subtitled "A New Hope," showing the cycle at work.

But for every "Star Trek" and "Star Wars" film, there are lots of other science fiction movies that end on notes of sacrifice, death, or despair. In our darker moods, we humans often don't feel very good about the future, and that hopelessness can be reflected in our sci-fi tales. For every utopia, there is a dystopia. For every instance of humankind uniting to save their planet, there is a tale of humanity failing to stop its own self-destruction.

Indeed, the following five sci-fi movies feature protagonists who die. Some of the deaths are tragically noble. Others, however, are wasteful and harrowing, providing lessons for audiences about the dangers of various sins. All of them leave viewers in a poignant state, though, so let's look into the shadows of what is to come.

Ted Post's "Beneath the Planet of the Apes" was the first follow-up to Franklin J. Schaffner's 1968 classic "Planet of the Apes." If the original film is an on-the-nose satire of human interaction (transposing apes and humans in the planetary pecking order), then "Beneath" just pushes things into more obvious territory. The movie stars James Franciscus as Brent, a human astronaut who, as part of a rescue mission, somehow ends up on the same distant-future Earth that Taylor (Charlton Heston) did in "Planet of the Apes." Once there, Brent discovers that the apes are gearing up to take over the Forbidden Zone under the command of the gorilla Ursus (James Gregory), which Dr. Zaius (Maurice Evans) objects to.

In "Planet of the Apes," all the humans of the future appear to be mute and feral. Its sequel, on the other hand, reveals there is a subterranean enclave of surviving, ghoul-like humans who've developed psychic powers. The human psychics also worship an unexploded nuclear bomb, admiring its power. Taylor and Brent eventually meet up, but Taylor is naturally terrified when he sees the bomb's Alpha Omega markings, knowing that this particular bomb is capable of, just by itself, ending all life on the planet.

As it so happens, this is Chekhov's doomsday bomb. Once the bomb is introduced, we know that "Beneath the Planet of the Apes" can't possibly end well. Sure enough, when Taylor is mortally wounded at the end of the film, he curses and collapses on the bomb's detonation switch. In this case, the hero dies, along with everyone else on Earth. It's one of the bleakest endings in sci-fi history.

Douglas Trumbull's 1972 film "Silent Running" is so good that it made /Film's Jeremy Smith a lifelong sci-fi fan. More specifically, it's something of a dystopian movie and shows what happens when an idealist with principles butts heads with an uncaring, commercialized future that doesn't care about the calm, complexity, and beauty of the natural world. Everyone ought to watch this one, especially if you liked "Project Hail Mary" (and I know you did).

In the dystopian future of "Silent Running," humans have ruined Earth to the point of killing all its forests. Specimens of many planet species have been kept alive on spacebound repositories, which exist in giant greenhouse-like geodesic domes. Bruce Dern plays Freeman Lowell, a botanist who has been tasked with looking after the samples on a ship called the Valley Forge. The Valley Forge is owned by American Airlines.

When the ship is ordered to jettison its plants and head back to Earth (as it's needed for commercial purposes), Freeman turns on his corporate bosses and proves that he's willing to kill his human crew mates to protect the forest domes. Shockingly, he actually manages to escape with one of the domes, although he loses others in the process. By the end of the movie, Freeman even makes the ultimate sacrifice to keep the forest protected.

Of course, "Silent Running" is a commentary on modern-day environmentalism and how horrible commercialism always seems to outweigh the needs of our planet. Is "Silent Running" preachy? Yes. Is it tragic and great? Also yes.

John Carpenter's 1988 film "They Live" stands as a vital criticism of the United States under Ronald Reagan. In the film, the nameless protagonist, "Nada" (Roddy Piper), finds a pair of alien-constructed sunglasses that allow him to see through all the secret alien disguises on Earth. Certain citizens are revealed to be creepy aliens in disguise, but more so, billboards, magazines, and advertisements are shown to be masking subliminal messages that make human consumers more complacent by ordering them to "OBEY," "STAY ASLEEP," or "CONSUME."

Nada is hardly the best person to make this alien discovery. He's a blue-collar drifter without the means to handle this weird revelation, and when he tries to tell someone else about it, they end up fighting for a really, really, really long time. That's not a joke, either, as Piper and his co-star Keith David beat the hell out of each other for what feels like 20 minutes.

Luckily, Nada has connections within the local shanty town. There, he learns the aliens have been mingling with Earth's wealthy and using brain-scrambling signals to keep the impoverished docile. "They Live" then ends with a raid on the alien compound with Nada, David's Frank Armitage, and a few others trying to shut down the alien signal once and for all.

Although a sci-fi movie, it's easy to believe that "They Live" might very well be a documentary. The ultra-wealthy, we seem to inherently understand, are deliberately controlling us through media and money. It felt true in 1988, and it definitely feels true now. Nada ends up taking care of business, but not before being mortally wounded. In the film's most inspiring scene, his final act on this planet is to flip the middle finger to the aliens, spitting his last breath at them.

In 2011, Lars von Trier released the second entry in what might be considered his "Depression Trilogy," a series of movies that began with 2009's "Antichrist" and ended with 2013's "Nymphomaniac." The second film, "Melancholia," is just as much a metaphor for depression as it is a sci-fi apocalypse flick. "Melancholia" takes place in a world where a rogue planet, known as Melancholia, is going to slingshot around Earth before looping back in space and colliding with it, ending all life. The gravitational loops are a little dance of death, a preview of the apocalypse.

With this impending doom looming in the background, the movie centers on Justine (Kirsren Dunst), a newly-married woman who finds herself sliding back into the depression she has long fought off. When she learns that all life on Earth will end, Justine finds herself grimly pleased. She asserts that all life on Earth is evil, there is no other life in the universe, and that human extinction would be a blessing. Death cannot be stopped, and its coming is a release. Meanwhile, eerie things start to happen as Melancholia approaches. Electricity begins behaving weirdly. Certain characters flee, but where should they go? Justine doesn't panic. She's apathetic.

In the end, no one in the film lives. "Melancholia" is a beautiful, harrowing, and shockingly accurate portrait of a depressed mind. Justine has simply stopped caring about anything because it feels like there is no escape. Because, in the mind of Lars von Trier, there isn't.

You already know if "Melancholia" is your kind of movie. Just be sure to follow it with something more optimistic, like "Apocalypse Now."

Coralie Fargeat's 2024 horror hit "The Substance" is hardly subtle. Demi Moore stars as Elisabeth Sparkle, a celebrated actor who's recently made her living by hosting a TV workout program. Her disgusting boss (Dennis Quaid) fires her early in the film, all but saying out loud that she's too old to be a heartthrob anymore. From there, Elisabeth is put in contact with a shadowy pharmaceutical company that mails her doses of "The Substance," which promises to make her young again ... in a sense.

Sure enough, when Elisabeth injects herself with The Substance, she passes out, her back splits open like a cocoon, and a younger woman (Margaret Qualley) crawls out. These two women are the same person, but the younger one decides to take the name Sue. According to the rules of The Substance, Elisabeth and Sue have to take turns being conscious, one week each, with Sue feeding off Elisabeth's spinal fluids. Naturally, though, "Sue" doesn't want to go back to being the "old" Elisabeth she resents, and the consequences of what happens when the rules of The Substance are broken are quickly made horrifically clear.

By the end of the movie, Elisabeth has become a literal puddle of dead puffy flesh on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. "The Substance" is openly about the callowness of Hollywood and its dogged tendency to cast aside women "of a certain age" in favor of youthful ingénues. It should be recalled that Moore was nominated for an Oscar for Best Actress for "The Substance" but lost to a youthful ingénue, Mikey Madison. The message of "The Substance" played out in real life. How darkly poetic.

#3559. The Jewelry at the Center of Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall’s On-Set Romance

In many photographs from the 1950s, Lauren Bacall appears alongside Humphrey Bogart with a small golden object between her lips. Curiously, it is a small gold whistle hanging from a bracelet. Not exactly the kind of accessory one would expect to find in a Hollywood star’s jewelry box. Yet, for Bacall, that particular piece held a very special meaning. Bogart himself gave it to her, inspired by a line the actor delivered in the film where the two met and fell in love.

In 1944, Bacall was just 19 years old when she made her film debut alongside Bogart in To Have and Have Not, directed by Howard Hawks. Bogart, 44 at the time, was already one of Hollywood’s most famous actors. On set, their relationship developed into something more than professional. They fell in love, and in May 1945, got married.

It was here that the origin story of the unusual bracelet began, with a line from Bacall that became one of old Hollywood’s most memorable: “You do know how to whistle, don’t you Steve? You just put your lips together and blow.” The scene, a candid moment of trust between the two characters, was a standout in the film, and it was this line that inspired the idea for the bracelet.

The result was a 14-karat-gold bracelet with a small pendant whistle, also made of gold and fully functional. The piece has a rather minimalist look, with smooth, polished surfaces and no particular decorations, except for a few personal engravings.

On one side of the tag are the words “Betty Bacall,” a reference to the actor’s original name, Betty Joan Perske, and on the other, “The Whistler.” On the whistle itself, the initials “B&B”—for Bogart and Bacall—are engraved, along with the number “21,” the meaning of which is still a mystery.

Bacall wore the bracelet in her daily life, carrying with her that small memento of the film that marked the beginning of her relationship with Bogart. In 1954, during a television interview with journalist Edward R. Murrow, the actor herself revealed the meaning of the whistle, explaining its connection to the famous line from To Have and Have Not.

Decades later, in September 2023, the bracelet made headlines again, when it was auctioned by Julien’s Auctions. The initial estimate ranged from $100,000 to $200,000, and on September 8, it sold for $158,750—a substantial sum for a small gold whistle. Though, considering who it belonged to—and especially who gave it to her—it’s not all that surprising.

Originally published in Vanity Fair Italy.

60 Minutes looked a lot different when it returned to the 2026 TV schedule for its 59th season back in September. That was in great part due to a creative overhaul that took place over the summer and saw several key employees fired from their positions. Since then, a few of those former staffers have spoken out about their oustings and the state of the news magazine under the leadership of CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss. Now, Cecilia Vega is sharing her take and revealing one detail that still bothers her.

Since its season premiere, 60 Minutes has been at the center of various headlines, with a number of those pertaining to low ratings compared to past seasons of the show. On top of that, there have been ongoing claims of editorial interference on Weiss’ part. Vega made such claims in July and alleged that she was pressured to exude what she considered to be bias into her stories. As for her feelings on the show now, Vega said during a talk in Washington D.C. (via The Daily Beast) that she wasn’t pleased:

It pains me. It hurts to watch, from afar. It hurts to talk to my colleagues who are still there. It hurts to see the ratings slump that is happening right now.

Regarding the ratings, it was recently reported that the October 25th broadcast of 60 drew 5.6 million viewers. That marked a notable decrease for the show, which reportedly averaged 9.1 million viewers during Season 58. Weiss recently addressed the concerns during a tech panel and asserted that the show was still doing “tremendously well.” The Free Press founder, who’s denied editorial bias, also said she’d been aiming to block out the backlash against CBS News and her changes on the previously mentioned news program.

The staff firings took place on May 28, 2026, which apparently became known as “Black Thursday” internally. On that day, Vega was fired alongside others like fellow correspondent Sharyn Alfonsi, former 60 Minutes executive producer Tanya Simon and executive editor Draggan Mihailovich. Shortly after, veteran correspondent Scott Pelley was fired as well after accusing Weiss of “murdering” the show. As for Vega, one thing still gives her pause about her exit from the series and the media company as a whole:

I still don’t know why I was fired. I was not given a reason. I was fired without cause. I just find it exceptionally disturbing.

Pelley recalled the staff meeting that was held shortly after his 60 Minutes colleagues and others were fired. The veteran newsman recalled everyone expecting Weiss to be at the meeting but were surprised to find that only series EP Nick Bilton was present. According to Pelley, employees were even more unhappy after Bilton started reading a statement from his phone without looking up at anyone. Months later, Vega seems to have a lot of respect for Pelley and others who have “held the line” or those who are still trying to at CBS:

I held the line, and Scott held the line, and Sharyn held the line, and I think people are still holding the line over there. But what they are having to go through, or what we had to go through, should never happen in a newsroom.

Questions remain in regard to what lies ahead for 60 Minutes and CBS News as a whole under Bari Weiss’ leadership. Additionally, there are more variables to consider following the merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, which has birthed Skydance. Cecilia Vega, for her part, says she’s unaware of the “endgame” and thinks “it’s a real mystery.”

Erik Swann is a Senior Content Producer at CinemaBlend. He began working with the publication in 2020 when he was hired as Weekend Editor. Today, he continues to write, edit and handle social media responsibilities over the weekend. On weekdays, he also writes TV and movie-related news and helps out with editing and social media as needed. He graduated from the University of Maryland, where he received a degree in Broadcast Journalism. After shifting into multi-platform journalism, he started working as a freelance writer and editor before joining CB. Covers superheroes, sci-fi, comedy, and almost anything else in film and TV. He eats more pizza than the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.
