#3525. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace is officially an Emmy winner.

Wallace won the Editing for a Daytime Studio Program category at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys for his work on Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables.” He accepted the award during the ceremony at the Hollywood Palladium on Friday, October 30.

IndieWire was also nominated for a Daytime Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Daytime Studio Non-Fiction Series for IndieWire executive producer Mary Pelloni’s work on the show. The two nominations and one win, in categories that also included broadcast talk shows, reflect IndieWire’s increasing presence in the traditional video spaces in addition to our written coverage. Wallace works on IndieWire’s staff as a video producer, where he also produces and edits video content across brands like Filmmaker Toolkit, Future of Filmmaking, and other editorial and sponsored projects.

Season 1 of “IndieWire Craft Roundtables” highlighted the below-the-line artisans on many of the biggest films of the season. Hosted by IndieWire’s Jim Hemphill, the season consisted of four episodes, each centered around a different filmmaking department: cinematography, editing, production design, and casting. Shawver (“Sinners”), Andy Jurgensen (“One Battle After Another”), Pamela Martin (“Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere”), Saar Klein (“Dead Man’s Wire”), and Luke Lynch (“BLKNWS: Terms & Conditions”).

The cinematography roundtable featured Adolpho Veloso (“Train Dreams”), Malik Hassan Sayeed (“After the Hunt”), Michael Bauman (“One Battle After Another”), and William Rexer (“The Testament of Ann Lee”).The production design roundtable featured conversations with Cara Brower (“Hedda”), Sam Bader (“The Testament of Ann Lee”), Alexandra Schaller (“Train Dreams”), Scott Chambliss (“Kiss of the Spider Woman”), and Dylan Cole and Ben Procter (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”).

The casting roundtable also featured casting directors Nina Gold (“Jay Kelly”), Margery Simkin (“Avatar: Fire & Ash”), and Jessica Ronane (“After the Hunt”).

“IndieWire Craft Roundtables” returned for Season 2 in June 2026, with six episodes devoted to the biggest TV shows of the year.

#3523. An Unlikely Frasier Episode Earned Death Threats For Daphne Actor Jane Leeves

The "Frasier" revival probably should have been a one-off special, but  we'll always have 11 seasons of classic comfort sitcom hilarity regardless. "Frasier" ran from 1993 to 2004, maintaining a remarkable consistency over the course of 264 episodes. Kelsey Grammer's lovably snooty Dr. Frasier Crane and his family, friends, and co-workers will remain beloved by a generation raised on the NBC sitcom — unless, that is, you're oddly offended by cruelty against rubber eels. Yes, as Daphne Moon actor Jane Leeves reveals in her book "Daphne & Me: My Life on Frasier (And a Bit More)," her character whacking a rubber eel against a countertop earned her death threats from enraged viewers.

"The Innkeepers" is a fondly remembered episode from "Frasier" Season 2 in which the titular psychiatrist and his brother Niles Crane (David Hyde Pierce) decide to take over a failing restaurant and restore it to glory. Of course, nothing goes to plan, and the boys end up enduring an opening night from hell wherein their family and friends are all recruited to help keep the restaurant running as things fall apart in dramatic fashion.

"Frasier" had already ventured into farce with Season 2's "The Matchmaker." But "The Innkeepers" stands as a farcical triumph — despite, as Leeves points out in her book, some viewers believing it strayed too far from the show's otherwise sophisticated humor. But for other fans of the show, it wasn't the shift of comedic styles that was at issue. Instead, it seems Daphne's treatment of an eel in the kitchen of Les Frères Heureux (The Happy Brothers, as Niles and Frasier christen their culinary venture) was a crime worthy of death.

"The Innkeepers" single-handedly makes Season 2 one of the best seasons of "Frasier." In the episode, as a harried evening in Les Frères Heureux becomes even more fraught, Niles Crane — conscripted to chef duty alongside Daphne Moon — tries to bludgeon a tank of eels so as to not have to handle one of the live creatures. Meanwhile, Daphne's patience wears out. "Oh, for heaven's sakes," she exclaims before marching over to the tank, yanking out an eel, and slamming its head on the countertop. She then hands the lifeless fish to a stunned Niles in one of the episode's many moments of broad slapstick humor.

Turns out, it wasn't just Niles who was stunned. In "Daphne and Me," Jane Leeves reveals that she received threatening letters wishing her a torturous death for this transgression. "What I could never have anticipated were the death threats," she writes. "Yep, you heard me. I got death threats for my mistreatment of the clearly rubber eel. As explained in the scene-opening title card, 'No eels were harmed during the making of this episode.'"

Granted, Daphne gave the thing a good whack, and whoever was in charge of providing the rubber eel certainly delivered a fake fish with some convincing heft to it. But as Leeves goes on to point out, her killing the pretend fish was hardly the most egregious example of small screen violence. "At the time, shows like 'NYPD Blue' and many crime procedurals of the present day got away with, or even overtly endorsed, so much unconscionable carnage and brutality," she writes. "I wonder if they ever got letters?" Just in case you doubt the maliciousness of these missives, Leeves goes on to provide an example.

It might sound unbelievable that Jane Leeves received letters wishing her a painful death simply for clocking a rubber eel with a wooden counter. But in her book, the actor actually provides the text of one such letter. "Miss Leeves," it begins. "Every time I see the 'Frasier' episode where you smash the eel's head for a laugh I wish you'd get an agonizing terminal disease. It doesn't matter if the eel is real or fake. It ain't funny. I pray that you get smashed on the head, too." Bearing in mind this was long before the internet age, which means somebody had to sit down, write the letter, find the correct address, then mail it out. Maybe we were doomed before the internet subsumed our lives after all.

Interestingly enough, "The Innkeepers" was a moderately controversial episode of "Frasier" when it first aired. The show itself had debuted to stellar reviews and outstanding ratings. David Hyde Pierce might have felt the "Frasier" pilot was "terrible" at first, but the series premiere earned Emmy wins for Kelsey Grammer, writers David Angell, Peter Casey, and David Lee, and director James Burrows.

"The Innkeepers," however, prompted what Leeves called "mixed reactions." As the actor writes, "Some thought it strayed from the refined, sophisticated humor that was 'Frasier.' I disagree wholeheartedly. In my mind, 'Frasier' was one of the only shows capable of pulling off an ambitious, expertly-written slapstick comedy with such flair and sophistication, adding another tantalizing flavor to the show." Of course, now "The Innkeepers" is recognized for everything Leeves highlights — though whoever wrote her that letter probably never came around to it.

#3522. Google Is Using Data From Gmail and Drive to Target Ads, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

"Marshals" continues to tease a crossover with "Dutton Ranch," with Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton name-dropping his sister in the latest episode. By this point, however, fans are surely tired of the references and eager to see the "Yellowstone" cast reunited.

With its Season 1 finale, "Dutton Ranch" gave itself the perfect excuse for a "Marshals" crossover. Meanwhile, "Marshals" did the same, ending its debut season by having Brecken Merrill's Tate Dutton kidnapped and taken to Texas, where, it just so happens, Kelly Reilly's Beth Dutton and Cole Hauser's Rip Wheeler now live. Meanwhile, Hauser and Reilly spoke positively about a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, suggesting that's exactly what fans would soon be getting — especially considering Reilly referred to the lack of such a thing as a missed opportunity.

Alas, when "Marshals" Season 2 arrived, not only was there no crossover, but Kayce didn't even have to go to Texas, as it turns out Tate was taken to a Wyoming ranch instead. Now, we have the latest example of "Marshals" referencing Beth, which more than anything else serves only to remind us that we're yet to receive the crossover we've been waiting for.

"Marshals" Season 2, Episode 5, "Secret Weapon" picks up in the aftermath of Rudy Carpenter (Braxton Hale) exploding a bomb and taking himself out in the process. After the Marshals track down his accomplice, Derek McCoy, Kayce chases Derek's brother, Will McCoy (Keean Johnson), into a barn that collapses, trapping the pair below ground. It's here that Kayce decides to bring up his family and once again tease audiences with a crossover that is yet to materialize.

In "Secret Weapon," after the barn floor collapses, Will McCoy's leg is badly injured. While trying to find a way out of their predicament, Kayce tries to convince Will to give up details about his brother, who evidently treats Will like a "punching bag." Kayce takes the opportunity to talk about his own brother, Jamie Dutton (played by Wes Bentley on "Yellowstone), and his sister, Beth Dutton, who also treated Jamie like a punching bag. Of course, Beth ultimately kills Jamie Dutton in the final season of "Yellowstone," but Kayce stops short of mentioning that still buried crime.

"You remind me of my middle brother," he tells Will. "Never quite fit in, always on the bad end of a beatdown. My sister made his life hell." Will replies with antagonism. "Picked on by his sister? I'm not that pathetic." But as Kayce quite rightfully points out, "She'd eat you for lunch," adding, "Meaner than any of your brothers, guaranteed."

It's true that Beth Dutton is a force of nature, and that only makes it even more frustrating that she hasn't shown up in "Marshals," which could do with a jolt of energy at this point. Beth and Rip are too busy setting up shop in Rio Paloma, Texas, in the far superior "Dutton Ranch." But this brief mention of Kayce's sister and how she'd eat Will for lunch is a reminder of just how good we once had it with "Yellowstone," and how much "Marshals" is struggling to match the excitement of its predecessor. Of course, "Yellowstone" lost its way at one point, but Beth was never anything less than electrifying, and "Marshals" would benefit from having anyone in its cast with half as much charisma.

For now, these brief references in "Marshals" to beloved "Yellowstone" characters aren't doing the CBS procedural any favors. In "Secret Weapon," Kayce Dutton recalls how fighting wasn't in Jamie Dutton's nature. "He had to be smarter, more cunning," he says, "And eventually he broke from the family, forged his own path." Of course, that path ultimately ended in his death, with Beth taking a knife to the middle Dutton brother's stomach and exacting revenge for the controversial death of Kevin Costner's John Dutton earlier in "Yellowstone" Season 5.

The thing is, being reminded of the "Yellowstone" years is bad enough on a show that clearly struggles to match the quality of Taylor Sheridan's original neo-Western. But when you take into account the anticipation for a "Dutton Ranch"/"Marshals" crossover, it's just downright frustrating.

The "Marshals" Season 1 finale seemed to set up a perfect crossover with "Dutton Ranch," but in the end we got nothing of the sort. We could still see Beth show up later in the season, but for now all we know is that another "Yellowstone" fan-favorite character will be appearing in "Marshals" when Jefferson White's Jimmy Hurdstrom makes his return to the Montana plains. In the meantime, let's hope the show finds a way to keep the "Yellowstone" connection alive without reminding us of what we're missing out on.

#3520. ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 13, 2026 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.]

You’re going to see the hits coming with this one. When Anthony Ippolito first utters the title of Peter Farrelly‘s “I Play Rocky” — it’s an admission and an ask, a demand and a plea — the moment is primed for stand-up-and-cheer crowd-pleasing. Such is the case with Farrelly’s entire film, which tracks Sylvester Stallone’s wild, improbable Hollywood success story through the lens of his creation of “Rocky,” often functioning as its own version of that underdog story, presumably because “Rocky” proper isn’t available to be remade and Stallone was not formally involved with the production of this one. Related Stories IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’ ‘The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins’ Is the Funniest Series of the Year

Stallone has long mythologized his rise to greatness, and that’s no knock on him; his rise to Hollywood royalty was crazy and filled with eye-popping twists and turns. The guy sold his dog when he didn’t have enough money! But Peter Gamble’s script sands down those hard edges into something much more made-for-the-movies, a distinctly knotty treatment for a movie that is meant to be about how hard it is to get original movies made.

While the lightness of the film — including an awkward dinner in which Frank Stallone, Jr. (Matt Dillon) giddily admits to beating his kid, mostly played for chuckles — can detract from the much darker stuff that really happened to Stallone, it’s hard to deny the power of a feature so genuinely built to delight. You can see the strings being pulled (the ropes being strung?), but that means it works more often than not. With a big crowd — a man behind me at the film’s second public screening at TIFF guffawed and hooted with such abandon throughout the film that I could only embrace his joy — “I Play Rocky” does exactly what it’s trying to do.

Stallone’s life story has been threaded through the period just before he started writing scripts and the opening night of “Rocky,” an essential time in the career of a man so dedicated to acting and his craft that it could have ruined him forever. And there’s some light ruin here, including a short stint sleeping on the street (we see literally one night), bonkers financial decisions, and grievous financial choices. Embodied to an almost disarming degree by actor Anthony Ippolito — most people are probably going to get hung up on his impersonation of Stallone’s signature voice, but I’ve never seen anyone make their cheekbones look like Sly’s unexpectedly sunken ones — what feels most real about the film exists because he’s so fully committed to the bit.

And it’s very much to the breakout star’s credit that it doesn’t feel like a bit. While Gamble’s script doesn’t get much further than “this dude just really loved acting,” Ippolito gets pretty soulful here. His Sly (or, as we first meet him during a run of demeaning auditions, “Mike”) is a striver who would likely never call himself “ambitious.” Self-taught, self-educated, and self-aware to a fault, Sly knows he’s not the ideal Hollywood star, but he’s hellbent on showing the world what he’s got.

When his eventual first wife Sasha (a wonderfully calm AnnaSophia Robb) encourages him to just “write a fricking script” worthy of his talents, he does. The first is not “Rocky.” Neither are the seven that follow, but Sly and Sasha still pull up stakes for Hollywood and to chase his dream. No one is buying what he’s selling, though, and even some promising meetings (including one with Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff, both played to the absolute hilt by P.J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell, respectively) end nowhere. A chance encounter — the film’s script lives and dies by those — with a seminal boxing match gives him fresh inspiration, and after just three days, the kid has “Rocky.”

But is he going to be Rocky? Of course, everyone on Earth who sees this film (and plenty who don’t) knows that answer, but what the film lacks in tension, it makes up for in pure grit. Sly learns all about Hollywood negotiations, blustery studio men (a role Tracy Letts was born to play; no one has more fun yelling “Fuck Paramount!” than this guy), and holding fast to seriously deluded dreams. And while the film can flag as we chug through those paces, once “Rocky” is greenlit with Sly in the lead role (and a mess of stipulations, all of them seemingly designed to trip him up), things really start zipping along.

Part of that is due to smart casting. Jay Duplass is a stellar pick for director John G. Avildsen, though anyone who knows anything about Stallone’s on-set approach will chuckle at how much these two seemed to get along (Stephan James should get his own Carl Weathers film now). But more of it comes from the film’s eventual bent toward the mechanics of moviemaking. Come for the high jinks involving beating back union reps (but also, ew?), stay for a subplot about the genius of the Steadicam that is genuinely moving to observe.

That “Rocky” will be a hit is a given — and a fricking huge one at that! — but “I Play Rocky” is far more invested in getting the audience on board with the road it took to get there. And while Farrelly’s approach to this material, extremely glossy and built to delight a wide array of audience members, doesn’t quite speak to the real pain that went into the making of “Rocky,” there’s still plenty here that will make people stand up and cheer. It would, however, be nice if this Hollywood story didn’t feel quite so, well, Hollywood.

“I Play Rocky” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide later in the month.

#3518. ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on February 13, 2026 at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. IFC Films will release it in select theaters on Friday, November 6.]

For the final 20 or so minutes of an early screening of Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson‘s Berlin-bound “Mouse” that I recently attended, the woman sitting behind me in one of NYC’s smallest screening rooms sobbed. Like, really sobbed. I could hear her gasps in between her cries. Yes, I thought to myself, one of my people.

While I’m not sure there’s yet a cult assembled around the deeply empathetic and uniquely humane cinema of O’Sullivan and Thompson (partners in both film and life), God willing, there will be after more audiences see the pair’s third effort. I’ve been banging the drum on their wondrous output since 2020’s “Saint Frances” (which Thompson directed and O’Sullivan wrote and starred in) and their deep-feeling follow-up, 2024’s “Ghostlight” (written by O’Sullivan, who also joined Thompson in co-directing duties). Around these parts, any O’Sullivan and Thompson joint is an event. Related Stories ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser IndieWire’s Trevor Wallace Wins Daytime Emmy for Editing ‘IndieWire Craft Roundtables’

“Mouse” is no exception, and their best effort yet.

As is typically the case with the pair’s films, its logline does not quite do it justice. “Saint Frances” was about a disaffected nanny who bonds with her young charge. “Ghostlight” followed a fractured family as they found unexpected healing in live theater. “Mouse” is about a shy high school senior looking for ballast after the sudden end of her lifelong BFF-ship. These are all “small” stories, but they are also crucially about people, and thus contain the wild multitudes of humanity itself.

O’Sullivan and Thompson reunite with their “Ghostlight” star, Katherine Mallen Kupferer (whose own parents starred alongside her in the previous feature), who is cast here as our titular Mouse. Well, sort of. Her name is Minnie, but her shyness leans toward the mousy, though no one would ever say that to her, least of all her beloved and extremely outgoing best friend, Callie (Chloe Coleman). But when Minnie’s itchy nickname is (wrongly, it turns out) attributed to the flashy Callie, it’s hard for her to shake its deeper meanings.

When the film opens, Minnie and Callie are wrapping their final day as high school juniors in the early summer of 2002 (cue the Michelle Branch soundtrack, perfect). The stage is being set for their senior year — and, quite literally, for the very talented Callie’s next big high school musical moment and her eventual plans to attend Juilliard — and it’s obvious that they’re not about to have the same experience. Callie is popular and vivacious, perpetually surrounded by admirers and various hangers-on (Audrey Grace Marshall’s Cara is hellbent on usurping Minnie’s place in Callie’s life, while her himbo-esque boyfriend Brad is given wonderful dimension through Beck Nolan’s sneaky-good performance).

Minnie? She’s much more reserved, orbiting around Callie and company, not quite ever the star of her own show. But this is not a story about two best friends who break up because of the vagaries of popularity, and Coleman’s Callie is not a villain who breaks Minnie’s delicate heart. Well, not on purpose.

It’s clear that Minnie is out of touch with lots about her life — though not her affection for Callie — including her own sexuality (Iman Vellani as cute local video store clerk Kat happily cracks through that) and her fraught relationship with her overworked mother (Mallen Kupferer’s own mom and “Ghostlight” co-star, Tara Mallen). Callie’s friendship and trust are the best things in her life. Her nice house with a fully stocked kitchen is a bonus, as is Callie’s very-put-together mom Helen (a heartbreaking Sophie Okonedo), who wisely seems to like the steady Minnie a whole heck of a lot more than the rest of Callie’s coterie.

That will prove to be the one saving grace of what comes next. When Minnie and Callie’s friendship comes to a sudden end, it’s only through bonding with Helen that Minnie finds any sort of ballast in her life. But as point-A-to-point-B as that might sound, O’Sullivan and Thompson remain uniquely attuned to the ebbs and flows of real life and how real people respond to it. Mallen Kupferer, so outspoken in “Ghostlight” and so wonderfully goofy in “Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret,” here sinks into the far harder-to-crack Minnie. That’s not to say that Minnie isn’t prone to the emotional wilds of any teenage girl, but the young actress’ finely tuned performance is never broad or silly.

Instead, we get to know Minnie during one of the worst times of her life. So too does Helen, who handles her own feelings about Callie through her own coping mechanisms, some of which work, most of which don’t, and many of which center on building her own friendship with Minnie. The pair of them has a lot in common beyond Callie, including a general sense of wisdom beyond their years that has not always been beneficial to them.

Early in the film, Cara insists that Callie’s group of friends (including both Cara and Minnie) partake in a horrific little parlor game she likens to “Personal Feedback.” Mostly, it’s an excuse for the teenagers to say terrible things about each other under the guise of honesty and friendship. Even our golden girl, Callie, doesn’t escape unharmed, though Minnie almost does, because Cara simply can’t be bothered to remember she exists.

“Mouse” is, at its heart, a wonderful rebuttal to just that sort of cruel thinking — for all the Minnies out there — and a reminder that everyone matters and everyone deserves to be seen. Lofty as that might sound, it’s one of the most basic tenets of humanity, and the kind of thing too often forgotten on the big screen. O’Sullivan and Thompson never forget, however, and their films reflect exactly that. Our only request: more, please, our people need this.

“Mouse” premiered at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival.

#3516. 34 Episodes Of Netflix's Longest-Running Sci-Fi Show Deliver A Masterclass In Anthology Storytelling

One of the best shows on Netflix is also the streaming service's longest-running science fiction series, and every one of its 34 episodes is a masterclass in anthology storytelling. Netflix has some great sci-fi shows in its extensive catalog, from Cyberpunk: Edgerunners to Stranger Things. The streamer also has some great anthology shows on offer, like Love, Death, + Robots and Beef.

The absolute best sci-fi anthology on Netflix, however, is also one of the streamer's oldest flagship programs: Black Mirror. While it only has seven seasons to date, Black Mirror began back in 2011, and Netflix has been in charge of the series since 2016. It's even set to go on longer, as Black Mirror season 8 has reportedly started filming. All told, the anthology series has produced 34 episodes, including one short-lived interactive film titled Bandersnatch.

The fact that Black Mirror has survived 15 years and seven seasons is impressive in its own right, but the reason for its longevity is even more noteworthy. Black Mirror is one of the greatest sci-fi anthology shows ever made, second only to The Twilight Zone, and certainly the best of the 21st century. The best episodes of Black Mirror have won Emmy Awards, been called some of the best short films ever made, and more. It's simply a masterclass in anthology storytelling.

Over the years, Black Mirror morphed from a small but acclaimed series on Channel 4 in the United Kingdom into one of the juggernauts of the biggest streaming service on the planet. While it may not earn as much viewership as shows like Wednesday or Squid Game, Black Mirror is Netflix's workhorse. Shows like Stranger Things end after a few seasons, but Black Mirror is still going strong well over a decade after it began.

13 years after its release, one of the bleakest Black Mirror episodes about artificial intelligence is gradually starting to become an eerie reality.

All of that dependability is because Black Mirror is so consistently good. Every season brings at least one standout episode that sets social media buzzing. Even the worst episodes in the show are still good because they all serve the central idea of critiquing technology. A lot of people resonate with those critiques, which in turn makes Black Mirror all the more popular.

Unfortunately, despite its cultural ubiquity and 15-year run, Black Mirror may soon have some struggles with remaining relevant. The central idea of the show, an anthology critiquing technology and modern life, is just as timely as ever before, but Black Mirror is being outpaced. The modern world and technological advancements like generative AI move so much more quickly than Black Mirror, the show can't keep up.

For instance, Black Mirror season 7 came out in April 2025, and season 8 likely won't be here until late 2027 at the earliest. Technologies that seemed speculative back in 2025, like AI that can recreate faces and voices nearly flawlessly, won't be speculative anymore by the time season 8 is here. Black Mirror is supposed to be a warning about the future of technology, yet the future of technology may beat that warning to the punch.

Even the world itself may have moved on from Black Mirror. Back when the show was starting out, it was the only series willing to take punches at the tech industry and tell a cautionary tale about the near future. Now, with the rise of AI, everyone is taking punches and telling cautionary tales. Black Mirror may not have any bite in a world that has already taken its warnings about technology to heart. If it doesn't have any bite, it's hard to imagine how Black Mirror will remain relevant.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3515. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses

Lionsgate‘s “Hunger Games” prequel “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” will be available in 3D when it opens in theaters on November 20. That on its own isn’t strictly news, but the 3D conversion on the film is coming from a new and unlikely place: Facebook parent company Meta.

Meta is partnering with Lionsgate to convert “Sunrise on the Reaping” to 3D, with director Francis Lawrence working to adapt the film for 3D viewing. Meta worked with VFX giant DNEG and their internal 3D conversion branch Stereo. This is the first time Meta has partnered with a Hollywood film studio on such an undertaking, and it also won’t be the last Lionsgate movie that will get the 3D treatment down the road (other titles will be announced at a later date). Related Stories ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Sylvester Stallone’s Wild Hollywood Underdog Story Gets a Punchy Crowdpleaser

In addition to “Sunrise on the Reaping” being in 3D in theaters, the movie will eventually be available on Meta VR Glasses when those VR devices hit the shelves in spring 2027. IndieWire got to demo those recently, and they’re designed to be lighter and less obtrusive than other VR headsets that can be tougher on the eyes while not sacrificing any of the immersive qualities (they feel and look like slightly larger sunglasses that you might get at the dentist rather than a bulky, wraparound headset that weighs on your face).

The demo we saw included a snippet of the Billie Eilish concert doc co-directed by James Cameron, as well as a clip from “Avengers: Endgame” that added an extra expanded screen effect to fill your line of sight. It’s clear that Meta wants to expand into the entertainment space and compete with the likes of YouTube and Google and other tech giants, and they need premium content like a new “Hunger Games” movie in order to do that.

“From the beginning, we wanted ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ to feel visceral and immersive, pulling audiences deep into Haymitch’s experience,” Lawrence said in a statement. “Adapting the film for 3D gave us another creative tool to bring audiences even closer to his perspective. I’m excited for people to see the film on the big screen and ultimately experience it in an entirely new way on Meta’s VR glasses.”

“As we continue to explore new ways for audiences to experience ‘The Hunger Games,’ we’re thrilled to partner with Meta on this first-of-its-kind collaboration,” said Jim Packer, Chief Revenue Officer, Lionsgate. “Francis Lawrence has created an incredible 3D experience for ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,’ and we’re excited for audiences to experience it in theaters and then on Meta VR Glasses. This is a compelling example of how technology can transform existing formats to create fresh, new experiences.”

“With our upcoming VR Glasses, we’re proud to create premium entertainment the way it’s meant to be felt, and Lionsgate is an ideal partner because of the artistic strength and global appeal of its franchises,” said Sarah Malkin, Head of Entertainment for Meta’s Reality Labs. “’The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ is exactly the kind of cinematic experience that will be phenomenal in theaters, and also showcases what this technology makes possible at home. We’re delighted to work with Lionsgate and Francis Lawrence to bring the film in 3D to audiences around the world.”

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is the sixth “Hunger Games” film and the second prequel after “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” from 2023, which brought in $363 million at the worldwide box office. This film stars Joseph Zada as a teenage Haymitch Abernathy, who is the District 12 character portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the original series of films. The film also stars McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Whitney Peak, Kelvin Harrison Jr., and Ben Wang.

#3514. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 26, 2026 at the 2026 New York Film Festival. GKIDS will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Asked to explain the goofy title he gave to his globally successful 2023 kaiju smash “Godzilla Minus One,” writer-director Takashi Yamazaki explained that it was meant to convey two co-equal things: 1.) That the movie took place before Ishirō Honda’s original “Godzilla,” and 2.) That “people rise up from a postwar Japan that is at zero, and then Godzilla arrives, making the situation even worse and more tragic.”

Continuing the story of its Oscar-winning predecessor while also doubling down on everything that made it the most acclaimed film in its franchise since the King of the Monsters first lumbered out of the Pacific Ocean in 1954, Yamazaki’s thunderously loud and frequently spectacular direct sequel has in turn been saddled with an even sillier title: “Godzilla Minus Zero.” To paraphrase the scene from “Sideways” where Paul Giamatti’s character reveals that his novel is called “The Day After Yesterday”: Isn’t that just… “Godzilla?” Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses ‘Mouse’ Review: ‘Saint Frances’ and ‘Ghostlight’ Filmmakers Bring Their Singular Humanity to a Coming-of-Age Tale

Yes and no. Sure, the title is absurd on its face, but — in keeping with Yamazaki’s logic — it also rather eloquently speaks to the premise of a film about a fragile people who are struggling to maintain (and build upon) the new equilibrium they’ve fought so hard to achieve in the years since their country became the epicenter of Earth’s nuclear era. Another mid-century melodrama with very occasional monster sightings, the more thematically coherent and emotionally affecting “Godzilla Minus Zero” expands on the naive grassroots nationalism of its predecessor by reframing that movie’s characters from victims to survivors, an emphasis that forces ex-kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) and his friends to confront a series of impossible questions. How do you balance grief with growth? Vengeance with peace? Self-sacrifice with self-preservation?

By way of answering those questions (or at least asking them in a variety of increasingly anguished ways), “Godzilla Minus Zero” also forces Shikishima and co. to confront a flying, IMAX-sized, three-headed asshole they come to know as King Ghidorah. Possibly the single most hateable kaiju who’s ever eaten innocent civilians on screen before, King Ghidorah is a real piece of work even before he earns his crown. He first rears his ugly dragon head in Matsumoto circa 1949, which is two years after the events of “Godzilla Minus One,” and maybe two weeks after this scaly destroyer of worlds crash-landed into the mountains of Japan on the back of a meteorite (an arbitrary point of origin that feels like a missed opportunity to freight Ghidora with more human-facing pathos). Seeing as how Godzilla was obliterated and left to rot at the bottom of the sea at the end of the previous film, Ghidora is free to terrorize the countryside whenever he isn’t taking cute little naps in the Nagano hills.

Lucky for Japan, and for all of the other nations that are still living under the delusion that none of this monster business will ever be their problem, at least one of the key heroes who “defeated” Godzilla in 1947 has been preparing his people for the possibility of another kaiju attack. Government higher-ups are still nowhere to be seen, but Einstein-haired Naval engineer Noda (a sweet and eccentrically professorial Hidetaka Yoshioka) has been appointed to the head of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau, where he’s joined by newcomer Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), a preternaturally gifted meteorologist whose ability to predict the weather proves crucial in the fight against Ghidorah, and also embittered biologist Kanji Murakami (“Twilight Samurai” star Min Tanaka), who survived the bombing of Hiroshima, the attack on Ginza in “Godzilla Minus One,” and the assault on Matsumoto that opens this film — a detail that evokes the terribly remarkable story of Tsutomo Yamaguchi.

Thanks to Noda’s hard-earned wisdom, “Godzilla Minus Zero” is able to skip over the part where everyone has to discover that kaiju like Ghidorah are immune to conventional weapons — if not also strengthened by them. That ignorance is reserved for the occupying Americans, who were entirely absent from the previous movie (which nostalgically privileged the self-reliance of Japan’s civilian population at the expense of a more historical view of the post-war struggle). Here, the U.S. Army is represented by a unit of square-jawed, power-hungry jerks who are only interested in helping Japan so far as it helps themselves. They don’t bear the wounds of nuclear devastation, and so they see kaiju as more of an opportunity than a threat.

The opposite is true for our pal Shikishima, who has absolutely no interest in ever climbing back into the cockpit of a fight plane. Now married to the angelic Noriko — Minami Hamabe, who miraculously escaped “Godzilla Minus One” with a new eyepatch and some big secrets — and embracing his role as adoptive father to the devastatingly cute Akiko (returning champion Sae Nagatani), Shikishima just wants to wear his cool brown leather jacket and messenger bag combo in peace.

If only it were that simple. If only Shikishima were convinced, as he tries to convince himself, that staying out of the fight is the best way to protect the women he loves. If only Noda’s plan of electrocuting Ghidorah to death in the skies above Matsumoto were as successful at killing the kaiju as it is at blowing our hair back.

There are only two sustained monster sequences in “Minus Zero,” which adheres to a similar cadence as its predecessor, but they’re both among the most gripping setpieces of their kind in all of moviedom; they match the grandeur — if not the majesty — of those from Gareth Edwards’ “Godzilla,” and eclipse their violent intensity. The ridiculously thrilling aerial sequence above Matsumoto is lifted by the Wagnerian strings of Naoki Satō’s visceral score, kept aloft by special effects that exponentially improve upon the resourceful but weightless CGI from “Minus One,” and seared into your retinas by IMAX razzledazzle of the highest magnitude. And while the final showdown between Ghidorah and Godzilla is slightly weakened by grayscale atmospherics and a few missing beats (one of them very bizarre), it goes without saying that the climatic brawl is one for the ages, as Yamazaki earns the franchise’s first “R” rating with an elegantly choreographed monster mash that rattles with Darwinian force.

Oh yeah, I suppose it also goes without saying that Godzilla is (eventually) in this Godzilla movie. Somehow, the King of the Monsters has returned — if Palpatine had infinitely regenerative flesh, perhaps his resurrection would have been similarly unsurprising. But fans of Honda’s original film, Yamazaki’s previous one, and/or Edwards’ failed 2014 reboot have come to expect and appreciate that Godzilla is most effective when framed as more of a recurring weather phenomenon than a dramatic engine in his own right, and “Godzilla Minus Zero” doesn’t suffer from its title kaiju’s limited screentime.

On the contrary, his absences are crucial to the construction of a florid tear-jerker about a traumatized country trying to move forward in the atomic shadow of a world that will never feel safe again. While a cursed biologist like Murakami might see vengeance as his only path towards peace, a former kamikaze like Shikishima — the guilt he once felt over not killing himself for Japan now bent towards the responsibility he feels towards living for Noriko and their daughter — is left to wrestle over the best way to protect his family: fighting the monsters, or fleeing from them.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is hardly the most nuanced or effective film to explore its country’s post-war despair (the original “Godzilla” still towers above it in that regard, to say nothing of “Drunken Angel,” “The Human Condition,” “An Inn at Osaka,” or any number of other cornerstones of Japanese cinema), but the anger it assigns to Murakami is provocative on its own terms, and the path that it contrives for Shikishima is considerably more nuanced and well-earned than the one he stumbled through before. While the future is still uncertain by the end of this latest Godzilla movie (which feels very much like the middle chapter of a trilogy), “Minus Zero” makes rewarding sense of why the series’ numbers are starting to add up.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” premiered at the 2026 New York Film Festival. GKIDS will release it in U.S. theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3513. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

But when her daughters Ella (Bella Ramsey) and Jo (Odessa Young) arrive unexpectedly and become drawn into the group’s seductive world, Rita is forced to choose between the family she left behind and the life she believes can save her.” Related Stories ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Will Be in 3D in Theaters — and on Meta’s New VR Glasses

#3510. 4 Planet Of The Apes Movies Are Now Streaming On HBO Max, Including Sci-Fi Masterpiece Dawn Of The Planet Of The Apes

Showcasing the evolution of Earth as its predominant species shifts from humans to intelligent apes, watching all four films in the modern Planet of the Apes franchise, which first began 15 years ago, is quite the experience. From Rupert Wyatt's Rise of the Planet of the Apes (2011) to Wes Ball's Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes (2024), few franchises have been as consistently impressive in both story and visuals as this one (each movie has a Rotten Tomatoes score above 80%).

Although all four films have earned generally positive reviews, one sequel absolutely stands above with Matt Reeves' Dawn of the Planet of the Apes. Not only does it remain the best of the entire modern franchise, but it also sits as one of the best sci-fi sequels ever made.

The modern series begins with 2011's Rise of the Planet of the Apes, directed by Rupert Wyatt and starring James Franco as scientist Will Rodman, whose experimental Alzheimer's treatment grants a chimpanzee named Ceaser (Andy Serkis) and more of his fellow apes increased intelligence, while conversely serving as a deadly contagion for a massive percentage of the human population. The movie also stars John Lithgow, Freida Pinto, Brian Cox, and Tom Felton.

Then there's 2014's Dawn of the Planet of the Apes from Matt Reeves, following Ceaser's growing community of apes 10 years after the events of Rise and their clashes with a colony of human survivors. Starring Jason Clarke, Gary Oldman, Keri Russell, and Toby Kebbell, Dawn was an exceptional follow-up (but more on that later).

Reeves returned to direct 2017's War for the Planet of the Apes, set only a couple of years after Dawn. Tensions with the remnants of humanity have only become worse, as Caesar faces a ruthless (and desperate) military leader played by Woody Harrelson in the face of new human crises. Beyond Harrelson, notable stars include Steven Zahn and Amiah Miller.

Lastly, the most recent entry in the franchise is also streaming on HBO Max: 2024's Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes. Directed by Wes Ball, Kingdom is set multiple generations after the time of Ceaser, with apes having transitioned from basically a Stone Age era to more of a structured Bronze Age-type society. The movie stars the ape known as Noa (Owen Teague) and his encounters with a human woman named Mae (Freya Allan), as well as Proximus Ceaser (Kevin Durand), a ruling ape who's taken the name of the legendary ape and his teachings to secure power and build an empire.

Overall, the modern Planet of the Apes franchise is well worth revisiting if you've seen it before, and there's no better time for those who haven't seen it to check them out now that they're all streaming in the same place.

While all four modern Planet of the Apes movies are worth watching, the one I would most recommend personally is Matt Reeves' Dawn of the Planet of the Apes. Taking the foundation of the world and status quo established by Wyatt in Rise, Reeves expands the scope of the narrative into something far more complex and compelling, surpassing most expectations in terms of its depth.

Rather than being a straightforward clash between intelligent apes and human survivors, Dawn also features major struggles within both communities and rising tensions, undermining Ceaser attempts to forge peace with Jason Clarke's Malcom. As the movie progresses and violence becomes inevitable, the action sequences are on another level as the apes storm the humans' defenses.

One notable scene in particular sees Ceaser's rival Koba (Toby Kebbell) leading a force of apes against the humans' community in San Francisco and personally hijacking an armored vehicle. This results in an incredible extended single-take sequence centered on the vehicle as its firing turret rotates, showcasing the full scope of the major battle with a continuous, 360-degree shot.

While the motion-capture work is extraordinary in the entire franchise, it's particularly captivating in Dawn of the Planet of the Apes. This is largely due to the personal conflict between the peace-seeking Ceaser and Koba, who believes the ape leader should wipe out all the humans. Remarkably, the visuals impressively enhance the performances rather than distract. All things considered, Dawn is easily the best chapter in the modern Planet of the Apes franchise (though it really hasn't yet had a bad entry). With all four now on HBO Max, the timing couldn't be better for a full marathon.

Planet of the Apes is a multimedia sci-fi franchise that began in 1963 with Pierre Boulle's novel, which was later adapted into a film in 1968 starring Charlton Heston. The success of the movie led to four sequels, two TV shows, a remake from Tim Burton, and a reboot trilogy. The Planet of the Apes franchise has also seen success in video games and comic books.

#3509. Ridley Scott’s 118-Minute Sci-Fi Thriller Officially Crowned #1 Movie on Prime Video

Widely known and celebrated as one of the greatest directors of all time, most fans and critics would agree that Ridley Scott is losing steam in the later stage of his career. Back at the end of 2024, Scott returned to the colosseum for the legacy sequel to Gladiator, but the film was not met with the same glowing reception as its predecessor. The movie struggled at the box office under the weight of its $250 million production budget, but it has gone on to become one of the most-watched movies of the last few years on Paramount Plus. Just one year before the release of Gladiator II, Scott reunited with Gladiator veteran Joaquin Phoenix for Napoleon, which was also a historic bomb at the box office — the film barely earned back its $200 million budget, and is estimated to have been a major loss for the studio.

Coming into the year, Scott was fresh off a few box office bombs, but the Oscar-nominated director sought redemption with the debut of The Dog Stars. Led by Josh Brolin and Jacob Elordi, The Dog Stars was Scott’s first sci-fi movie in almost 10 years — he last directed Alien: Covenant in 2017 — so there was some anticipation for the film. However, mediocre reviews out of the gate left not much desire for fans to make the trek to the theater, leading to The Dog Stars wrapping up its theatrical run after falling just short of $40 million at the global box office. Now that the film has been completely removed from all theaters, it’s only available to watch on VOD, where it’s now the #1 movie in the world on Prime Video.

The Dog Stars is based on the acclaimed sci-fi novel of the same name by Peter Heller, who also produced the film with screenwriter Mark L. Smith and director Ridley Scott. Additional cast members include Margaret Qualley (Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood), Guy Pearce (The Brutalist), and Benedict Wong (Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness). The official synopsis for The Dog Stars, which earned scores of 41% from critics and 69% from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes, reads as follows:

“Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars is a riveting, epic thriller set in a world where survival is instinct, but humanity is a choice. Scott tells the story of Hig, a young pilot who, together with a military survivalist, Bangley, has carved out an efficient but isolated homestead in a brutal post-apocalyptic world until a mysterious radio transmission spurs Hig to venture into the unknown in search of the hope and humanity he still believes exists.”

Check out The Dog Stars on VOD platforms like Prime Video and Apple TV and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Ridley Scott’s future projects.

#3508. The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

When long-time producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped away from the James Bond franchise last year and Daniel Craig made it clear that he was finished playing agent 007, new producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman were faced with an unenviable task: finding a new actor to step into one of the most iconic roles in all of cinema. In the last few weeks, it’s been reported that Pascal, Heyman, and new Bond director Denis Villeneuve have zeroed in on a few final contenders including Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

Whoever the filmmakers choose, it’s likely to be controversial; Bond fans are very loyal to their particular favorites, and have been ever since Sean Connery was first replaced in the role back in 1969. The general consensus seems to be that Connery was the best Bond (though Craig runs a close second in most polls), but often one’s preference depends on which Bond was one’s first; as someone who grew up with Roger Moore, he’s always been my favorite, and I argued for his supremacy in an earlier IndieWire piece. Related Stories ‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Is Lured Into Lily James’ Cult in a Gut-Wrenching Drama ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

The casting of a new James Bond has always set off a media furor, even in the days long before social media and Letterboxd. When Connery decided he had had enough as 007 after shooting the fifth James Bond movie, “You Only Live Twice,” the press followed producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman’s talent search with bated breath. Once the role was cast, they scrutinized the choice with an intensity that no actor could have survived — certainly not a male model whose only screen credit was a series of chocolate commercials.

After Connery quit, Broccoli, Saltzman, and director Peter Hunt spent over a year interviewing, auditioning, and screen testing hundreds of actors — including a young Shakespearean thespian named Timothy Dalton, who would go on to play Bond nearly 20 years later — to play Bond in “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” Anthony Rogers (“Camelot”), John Richardson (“Black Sunday”), and stage actor Roy Marsden were considered before the filmmakers landed on George Lazenby, whose previous acting experience was limited to those chocolate commercials.

Lazenby lied at his initial meeting and said he had been acting in movies in Germany and Hong Kong, figuring the producers wouldn’t be able to check, but came clean to Hunt the next day. Hunt and the producers were concerned about Lazenby’s chops but loved his look, so they took a chance on the newcomer and put him through hours of voice coaching (to lose his Australian accent) and stunt training before deciding to pull the trigger a few weeks before production was scheduled to begin.

The question then became how to frame Lazenby’s onscreen introduction to make the transition as seamless as possible for audiences. One of screenwriter Richard Maibaum’s drafts began with Bond surviving an explosion that required him to undergo reconstructive surgery, but this was scrapped in favor of a more conventional prologue involving Bond encountering love interest Diana Rigg and fighting foes on the beach and in the water. When Rigg leaves Bond behind instead of making love to him as was customary for Bond’s leading ladies, Lazenby looks in the camera and says, “This never happened to the other fellow.”

It’s a very funny and very efficient way of acknowledging the change in personnel and then moving on, and the opening credit sequence further eases the transition by utilizing clips from earlier Bond movies. It also helps that the creative team on the movie consisted of Bond veterans including Maibaum, production designer Syd Cain, composer John Barry, and Hunt, who made his directorial debut with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had been an editor and second unit director on earlier Bond films.

As a result, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” still looks and sounds so much like a Bond film that the introduction of Lazenby is less jarring than it might have been, though what’s interesting about the movie is how much better it is in just about every way than the previous Connery pictures. One can argue about the relative merits of Connery vs. Lazenby, but there’s no debating the visual elegance of “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” which eschews the somewhat bland high-key lighting of the earlier Bond films in favor of something more atmospheric and glamorous.

Audiences at the time might not have appreciated Hunt and cinematographer Michael Reed’s efforts, being distracted by debates over Lazenby, but contemporary directors like Steven Soderbergh and Christopher Nolan have referenced “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” as an influence and made a case for it as the best of all James Bond movies. On his website, Soderbergh wrote that “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was cinematically “the best Bond film and the only one worth watching repeatedly for reasons other than pure entertainment (certainly it’s the only Bond film I look at and think: I’m stealing that shit).”

Aside from containing several of the series’ best set pieces (including some awe-inspiring ski chases that inspired Nolan when he made “Inception”), “On Her Majesty’s Service” is also the most emotionally resonant Bond film to be made before the Daniel Craig era, with a genuinely moving love story between Lazenby and Rigg. Although composer John Barry scored a lot of 007 movies, his talents were never put to better use than in this film, which fully took advantage of Barry’s skill for sweeping, romantic themes that would later win him an Oscar for “Out of Africa.”

Lazenby gets some of the credit here too; he may lack Connery’s icy charm, but he’s a more human Bond. Displaying a slightly goofier sense of humor than Connery, he’s a transitional figure between the original 007 and the more overtly comic one Roger Moore would introduce in “Live and Let Die” four years later. According to Lazenby, he could have expressed even more emotion had Peter Hunt allowed it; when the actor played one particularly devastating scene with tears in his eyes, Hunt ordered a second take, arguing that Bond shouldn’t cry.

As good as he is in the part, Lazenby’s experience shooting “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” doesn’t seem to have been pleasurable, though whether or not the blame rests on his shoulders depends on who’s telling the story. According to Lazenby, Hunt went cold toward him early in shooting over a misunderstanding and was too preoccupied with the technical side of things to give him much attention; Cubby Broccoli, on the other hand, said Lazenby was spoiled and entitled and alienated many of his colleagues.

Although Broccoli was ultimately happy with Lazenby’s performance, by the time the movie opened, there were a lot of lingering hard feelings — a situation that wasn’t helped by the fairly lukewarm reviews Lazenby received, or by one of his representatives making a statement that Lazenby would not be returning to the role of James Bond. This was the first Broccoli or Harry Saltzman heard of any plans for Lazenby to abandon the part, and they quickly announced that Lazenby had been fired to make it seem as though his departure was their decision, not his.

Although Lazenby later stressed that he wasn’t the one who made the announcement he was quitting, he also clearly didn’t have any great desire to stay on as Bond. His contract was for seven years and had multiple clauses that he felt would restrict his career and lifestyle, and he still hadn’t signed it when “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” wrapped. Lazenby figured he could make more money doing one film in Italy than he could in five years on his Bond contract; he also, in one of the great errors in judgment in movie history, assumed that the James Bond franchise was dying in the era of “Easy Rider” and wouldn’t last much longer anyway.

In fact, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was a sizable hit, grossing $82 million on a production budget of $8 million. It wasn’t as popular as the last Connery film, however, and the mixed reviews gave it the aura of a failure. Broccoli and Saltzman began another worldwide search for a new Bond, considering American stars like Clint Eastwood, Burt Reynolds, and Adam West before convincing Connery to return. The result, “Diamonds Are Forever,” was a monster hit, and Lazenby went on to scattered work around Europe, acknowledging years later that his decision to quit Bond was a major mistake.

Lazenby didn’t completely leave 007 behind, however. After “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” he played a James Bond-esque character in the “Alfred Hitchcock Presents” episode “Diamonds Aren’t Forever” and, in 1983, Lazenby appeared in the TV movie “Return of the Man from U.N.C.L.E.” as a spy with the initials J.B. (who drove an Aston Martin, no less). The actor made a handful of interesting films after he played Bond, most notably Brian Trenchard-Smith’s great action film “The Man from Hong Kong” and Peter Bogdanovich’s exquisite Paul Theroux adaptation “Saint Jack.”

Lazenby was never more memorable than he was as James Bond, however, and it’s a shame he didn’t play the character in more pictures and further develop his variations on the persona. It remains to be seen where Villeneuve’s selection will place in the pantheon of Bonds, but whoever is cast would best be advised to ignore the inevitable social media firestorm that’s coming their way.

Lazenby’s saga proves that no matter how capable an actor is stepping into Bond’s shoes, it takes a while for history to render a fair assessment. 57 years after critics dismissed it, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” has stood the test of time — it’s Soderbergh and Nolan’s verdicts, not those of the contemporary press, that have proven correct.
