Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3505. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3504. In Just 1 Panel, Superman's New Logo Changes Everything About His Lore With New Release

It's surprisingly fun to ask others what they make of the "S" on Superman's chest, and it usually tells a lot about what corners of the fandom different people are drawn to. For those who assume it stands for Superman, they'd be right in the simplest contexts rooted in his history. But others may recognize it as the symbol for the House of El, especially those who saw the 1978 Superman movie. Other movie fans and readers of Mark Waid's Superman: Birthright, or viewers of Man of Steel, grew to understand that emblem as a symbol of hope for his people. This is all a fair perspective to have, but in his most recent retelling, one version of Superman's logo has a darker origin.

The S featured in Superman: The Stranger understandably represented the superhero in his Golden Age iteration, but one key feature from the upcoming issue teases a significantly harrowing pledge behind taking it on as his symbol. Shown in Superman: The Stranger #3, the S symbol appears to represent the company he once worked at before his powers fully developed, trapped helplessly inside when a blaze broke out, killing everyone inside but him. In this case, the S stands for "Saturn", as if to say he carries the guilt of surviving that day.

Superman: The Stranger has been doing well to keep readers enthralled with every aspect of this retelling, including consistent teases of Clark Kent's traumatic past. Rather than the symbol being tied to alien origins or designed by the Kent family based on how he was found, the "S" logo appears to be the same one used for the Saturn Building which caught fire when Clark, alongside potentially others from his orphanage, were working. When the traumatic disaster breaks out, claiming the lives of everyone around him, Clark is physically unable to open a door that was bolted shut, pry the bars off the window, or break down the wall. Beyond the question of who would allow such a chain of events, this memory has understandably lingered with him ever since.

One of the best current Superman stories shows a strong appreciation for his core traits, including his penchant for protecting all innocent life.

Moments like this have had a precedent in Superman: The Stranger, namely in how issue #2 starts by alluding to this fire. Superman clearly takes this incident with him wherever he goes, appearing to carry the building's logo with him as a reminder of what was lost. This is all that readers have to go with until the release of issue #3 this Wednesday, November 4, 2026. Although more context will almost certainly shed light on this connection, it's already a fascinating development, making the "S" logo far more personal and tragic for this version of Superman. It begins to show just the sort of hero he'll soon become for the people of Metropolis.

It's fairly clear in each of the issues currently available that Superman: The Stranger portrays its Clark Kent as one racked with guilt, whether it's as a survivor of a horrific tragedy, or the notion of stopping criminals for the mere crime "of being hungry." It's clear that Superman in a world currently devoid of aliens or supernatural threats must decide how to productively use his gifts, but it also makes his story a lonelier one.

Clark is seen consistently preoccupied with injustice, interrupting an intimate moment with a woman he just met to answer a nearby disturbance, ruining his evening (on Christmas, no less.) He recognizes that the people potentially seeing him as a means to enforce order for the city are upholding their own hateful views toward the downtrodden or demonized immigrants. But above all else, Clark worries his powers could leave just as suddenly as they appeared, and he feels compelled to use everything he has to make a difference in the city. But as the flames from Superman's turn from orange and yellow to green with voices calling out to him, he'll soon have to sort out how exactly he'll answer them.

#3503. 8 Near-Perfect Prime Video Thriller Series That Hooked Us in the First 5 Minutes

Ben Brewster is a filmmaker, critic, screenwriter, and actor whose work sits at the intersection of film culture, craft analysis, and storytelling.

He is a movie list contributing writer at Collider and a contributing writer for High on Films, where he covers contemporary cinema, independent film, and festival releases with an eye toward narrative structure, performance, and visual language.

Ben is an active film festival participant, having worked with Newport Film, the Nantucket Film Festival and as a screener for the Austin, Boston & Woodstock film festivals.  He brings to that work a programming instinct shaped by years of close engagement with independent and documentary cinema. This comes with a deep investment in the kinds of films that rarely find their way into the mainstream conversation without someone willing to advocate for them.

His background spans documentary and narrative filmmaking, film marketing, and production, including work with award-winning directors. This as well as developing his own indie production company, Lilac Creative Studio, through which he develops and produces original work across fiction and nonfiction forms.  His debut documentary, Diamond in the Rust, is an examination of economic redevelopment and displacement in the Queens area of New York City. The film was recently accepted to the Unisphere Film Festival, the Defense of Democracy Film Festival, and the Urbanite Arts & Film Festival. This would mark his first festival recognition as a director.  In addition to his writing and programming work, Ben hosts Beneath the Bloom, a film podcast exploring the work behind the scenes in cinema, and the struggles one can face to make a movie become a reality. The show reflects the same sensibility that runs through all of his work. A conviction that film is not merely entertainment but one of the most powerful tools human beings have for understanding each other.

Across mediums, his work is driven by a deep belief in film as a communal, transformative art form.

It's a good rule for show-runners to follow in the modern entertainment landscape: try and hook viewers within their first five minutes. That might seem short, but so are attention spans nowadays. It is a harsh rule to follow, but it also tells you a lot about the inner makings of a quality thriller. However, Prime Video has a strong record on that front.

The platform has made its name with large-scale action and the Chris Pratt-led, The Terminal List, returned in October with all eight episodes of Season two at once. Reacher is coming off a season four that pulled 66 million viewers in its first 28 days. Fallout has finished filming season three, though it will sadly not arrive in 2027.

Every series here opens with something specific, an image or a scene or a question that sticks. However, the best entries on this list open with small subtleties like a funeral, a birthday party, or even a slice of pie. The genre stretches from spy comedy to a supernatural mystery, but all still bring a stereotypical thriller's infrastructure of high stakes, tense physical confrontations and an atmosphere of narrative uncertainty.

Jack Ryan creates its opening premise on a rather mundane but clever idea, which is that its hero finds the threat in a money transfer spreadsheet. The series opens in Lebanon in 1983, where two brothers dance around their bedroom until bombs fall on their village. The boys grow into the man John Krasiniski's Ryan will spend the first season chasing. Carlton Cuse and Graham Roland ask the audience to understand the villain first before meeting the hero. That narrative technique alone brings a moral depth and weight rarely seen in Tom Clancy adaptations for the screen.

Krasinski plays Ryan as an analyst first and an action hero second, which makes his reluctant move into the field believable. Ali Suleiman and Dina Shihabi as his wife, Hanin, get nearly as much screen time as the American characters. That lifts the first season out of the standard spy manhunt procedural. Wendell Pierce gives Ryan's boss James Greer a rumpled authority that anchors every scene he is in. The series ran four seasons and in the later ones it chased bigger set pieces at some cost to that earlier character work. Although it might settle into a familiar rhythm, the opening hook still lands.

Donal Glover and Francesca Sloane open Mr. & Mrs. Smith with another John and Jane Smith, played by Alexander Skarsgård and Eiza Gonzalez and then promptly kill them off. The scene, of course, winks at the 2005 movie with Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie while promising a very different take. Donald Glover's John and Maya Erskine's Jane each sit down for an interview with a faceless agency, where a terminal greets them with a cheerful "hihi." Jane's terminal even asks for her nail clippings, a detail that helps to set that dry and strange tone. Hiro Murai directs the pilot with his usual sharp eye for awkward silences and comedic undertones.

Glover and Sloane built each episode structurally around a single idea, much like Atlanta did, which keeps the missions fresh. Erskine and Glover trade awkward banter as each episode turns into a test of their relationship. The first season ran eight episodes and a second season began filming this past April under a new show runner.

Short on time, long on suspense. Five Netflix miniseries you can finish before the weekend ends.

Chris Pratt stars as Navy SEAL Lieutenant Commander James Reece and the show does not waste a second before putting the audience in front of its rather grim circumstances. The Terminal List begins at a funeral, with Reece smashing a SEAL pin into a coffin. This cuts between flashbacks of Reece leading an Alpha Platoon into a tunnel in Syria on a mission that nobody believes in. They go underground searching for a chemical weapons terrorist and walk into an ambush. The explosion that follows kills nearly everyone and Antoine Fuqua's (Training Day) slick direction makes the opening sequence feel like a feature film.

Jack Carr's novel supplies the revenge plot, and Pratt trades his usual charm for a hollow stare that suits a man who loses everything. Riley Keough plays Reece's wife, Lauren, and Taylor Kitsch plays his friend Ben Edwards, and they give the family and friendship at the center of the story a real lived-in warmth. A prequel, The Terminal List: Dark Wolf, followed in 2025. Season 2 just hit Prime on October 21st and takes Reece across the world. A third season has not yet been confirmed. The show operates as a single-minded thriller though its pleasures narrow after the opening hour.

Titus Welliver's first scene as the now iconic Harry Bosch was in an undercover car, watching the weather and muttering under his breath about how the rain will wash the city clean. Within minutes, he is chasing a suspect on foot which ultimately ends with a fatal gunshot. Later on in Bosch, he is sitting in a courtroom defending that shooting against a wrongful death suit, while a dog in Laurel Canyon has dug up a child's bones. The pilot juggles the psyche of Bosch, the trial and a dark cold case without overwhelming you.

Eric Overmeyer developed the series with Michael Connelly, and the pilot's mix of courtroom drama and cold case work set the template for seven seasons. Jamie Hector as partner Jerry Edgar and Mimi Rogers as his fierce opponent in court, Honey Chandler, give the opening hour a sturdy supporting cast. The success of the show led to Bosch: Legacy and opened the door for Bosch: Start of Watch. Start of Watch is the new MGM+ prequel with Cameron Monaghan as a rookie Harry set in 1991 and adds a full reboot of the cast to the franchise. Bosch, much like its lead character, is more patient than explosive and uses that unique approach to its advantage.

Stefano Sollima opens ZeroZeroZero with a shock, showing Gabriel Byrne's Edward Lynwood wounded on the ground under falling glass and gunfire. The camera then rewinds, and a single cocaine shipment becomes the thread that connects a Calabrian crime family, a Mexican cartel, and a New Orleans shipping company. Sollima directed the first two episodes, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival in 2019. Andrea Riseborough and Dane DeHaan play Lynwood's grown children, who inherit the family business and its dangers. Dehaan's Chris carries Huntington’s disease, a diagnosis that colors every decision that he makes.

Harold Torres plays Manuel Contreras, a Mexican special forces sergeant pulled toward the cartel he is supposed to fight. Each storyline has its own unique mood, with Janus Metz and Pablo Trapero directing later episodes, which gives the series this relentless international feel. Robert Saviano's book about the global cocaine trade supplies the foundation. ZeroZeroZero is the entry most demanding of your full close attention here, yet it is also one of the most rewarding for that reason.

Peter Capaldi's convicted killer Gideon shows up in the very first scene of The Devil's Hour questioning a bruised Lucy Chambers about whether her life feels like her own. Gideon has an unsettling calm about him that makes every scene feel like a trap. Jessica Raine plays Lucy, a social worker who wakes every night at exactly 3:33 from the same nightmare. In the dream, a woman presses a shotgun under her chin, and Lucy believes the woman is her mother.

The time-bending mystery includes Nikesh Patel as Detective Inspector Ravi Dhillon, who investigates the murders that overlap with Lucy's life. By the end of the first episode, the detectives find a message scratched on a window that asks where Lucy Chambers is. Tom Moran created the series for Amazon, and the story slides between horror, procedural and family drama fairly seamlessly. Lucy's son, Isaac, speaks of people nobody else can see, which adds an extra eerie element to every domestic sequence. The Devil's Hour returned in 2024 for a second season and the first premiered on October 28, four years ago, which makes it a natural pick for this time of year.

Alan Ritchson's Reacher opens with a man being shot at midnight outside the small Georgia town of Margrave, then beaten and hidden under cardboard. The next morning, Reacher steps off a bus and walks into a diner for a slice of peach pie. He never gets the first bite, since the police burst in and arrest him for the murder. By the time the cuffs go on, a killing and a mystery stranger are already in play.

Ritchson's physical presence sells the premise alone, and the writing gives him just enough dry humor to keep the character from becoming a full brute. However, the detective who questions him upon his arrest (Malcolm Goodwin), quickly realizes that the giant in front of him sees the case more clearly than his own fellow officers. The show works directly off its simple but effective narrative and precise manner of execution. Season four premiered on August 12th and Prime has already renewed the series through season six. A spin-off, Neagley, released its first season in September.

Fallout starts in Los Angeles in 2077 with Walton Goggins in a cowboy hat, performing rope tricks for the kids at a rich family's birthday party. The great late Nat King Cole's "Orange Colored Sky" plays over the sinister radio reports of an impending nuclear war. Adults whisper about the news, a radio crackles, and Goggins' Cooper Howard, a fading movie star, declines to give the thumbs up that made him famous. Then the sky changes when a mushroom cloud rises over the city and families race for their private shelters as the bombs fall.

Jonathan Nolan directed the first episode, and few openings in recent television have set such a distinct tone so quickly. The same episode introduces Ella Purnell's Lucy, a vault dweller whose wedding goes wrong, and the Ghoul, the mutated version of Cooper who gets dug out of a grave. Season two aired from December 2025 into early 2026, and season three has finished filming with Aaron Paul, Manny Jacinto, Emily Mortimer and Thomasin McKenzie joining the cast. Fallout stands out amongst such a talented and crowded field due to an introduction that promises a well-defined and designed universe and the series keeps delivering it.

#3502. ‘Okinawa Saudade’ Review: A Moving Documentary About the Okinawan-Brazilian Community Explores the History of Displacement

The Kasato Maru ferried 325 Okinawans to Brazil in 1908, making it the first immigrant ship from Japan to do so. That history is highlighted by the opening of the documentary “Okinawa Saudade,” (“saudade” being a Portuguese word for bittersweet longing, typically around a memory or place). The film looks at the results a century later, now that an estimated 200,000 Brazilians of Okinawan descent are living in Brazil today, and director and cinematographer Yoju Matsubayashi finds a specific and emotionally straightforward route into complicated history. The director has covered the subject to some extent before in 2020’s “Okinawa / Santos,” a film which collected testimony on the forced deportation and even internment of Japanese immigrants in Brazil in the 1940s.””Okinawa Saudade”” narrows that focus to the families of two third-generation Okinawan-Brazilians, specifically ones with an interest in — and a longing towards — the island their families came from, something partially explored through the arts. Related Stories AT&T and IndieWire’s Filmmaker Party at AFI Fest Celebrated Filmmakers and Those Who Champion Them The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

A visual motif of waves viewed from above punctuates different segments of the film, typically as its subject reflect on the previous movements of their families. In the first instance of the shot, a dissolve to a young girl practicing a traditional Japanese dance on her family’s farm in Brazil immediately communicates that feeling of “saudade,” a soft and gently expressed shadow hanging over much of the film. That feeling of “saudade” is seen in the incidental details the director chooses to include, like how one subject’s grandfather grew dragonfruit with Okinawan seeds, as well as his capturing of more outwardly emotional moments, like a tearful reaction to photos not seen in a long time.

The teenage girl Yumi practices Ryukyu Buyo, while a man named Everton practices Eisa, an Okinawan folk dance involving drums. By unspooling their enthusiasm for the history of such Okinawan heritage arts and the history of their families, Matsubayashi also orbits a history of displacement. This emerges in an accumulation of lots of small personal stories, like how one characters recounts their family’s war-motivated exile from Santos. Yumi and Everton also learn more of these details for themselves, the film following them on their travels to Okinawa through exchange programs and traineeships. (In some delightful cases, the learning cuts both ways, as Everton reunites with estranged family, and Yumi’s Okinawan relative marvels at the dialect being preserved halfway around the world.)

Capturing their subjects’ respective journeys with occasional and mostly spontaneous interviews, Matsubayashi prioritizes personal histories over the big picture,as the assembly of the footage and the occasional interjection of archival material makes the relationship of this diaspora a bit clearer. Some of these families left Okinawa to avoid the military draft as well as starvation. Others were divided because of land seizures by the US military in the wake of the war (“I’ve learned that this is a sad place,” Yumi reflects, a quote placed over footage of lingering American military bases on the island). Some viewers might be dissatisfied with how Matsubayashi never quite engages with World War II and the full history of Okinawan annexation directly, but the context feels like plenty for the stories which he is telling, choosing instead to focus on the feelings which all children of immigrant backgrounds have felt: an uncertainty about their connection with the homeland of their parents and grandparents, and a yearning to understand it. The glimpses are enough, as “Okinawa Saudade”gradually paints a picture of how the historical struggles of the island have translated to the diaspora.

Everton outright says why he engages in Eisa drumming, saying that “we are Brazilians, but we don’t look like Brazilians, so we are always looking for belonging,” and his engagement with these traditional artforms becomes a part of this. Both learn the different nuances of their respective practices at home compared to in Okinawa, though both are graced with teachers who refuse to be super didactic about what is “authentic” (“We are always adjusting,” Yumi’s teacher says, “there is no such thing as perfection”). It’s also simply moving seeing, through Matsubayashi’s rather unvarnished camerawork, how the connections and feelings embodied in performing arts can have such far reach across time and place, highlighting the community found by the Brazilian Okinawans who preserved a little piece of the island for themselves.

“Okinawa Saudade” premiered at the 2026 Tokyo International Film Festival. It is currently seeking U.S. distribution.

#3501. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3500. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3499. Dungeon Crawler Carl Officially Returns November 23

Dungeon Crawler Carl fans are waiting with bated breath for an official announcement on Book 9's release date, though it may take a while considering author Matt Dinniman recently released a few teaser chapters and has a ton of story left to tell. That said, the author has proven he can turn out releases like they're going out of style, with Book 8, A Parade of Horribles, releasing in May 2026, just a year and a half after This Inevitable Ruin debuted in November 2024.

Looking at the larger series, Dinniman has released eight full-length novels since Dungeon Crawler Carl first arrived in 2020, an impressive pace considering the increasingly ambitious scope of each installment. With Book 9 set to kick off a two-volume finale, fans could be in for a lengthy wait before Carl and Donut's story reaches its conclusion, but there's plenty to keep them busy until then.

Fortunately, there's another major Dungeon Crawler Carl release officially arriving on November 23, giving fans something new to look forward to in the meantime.

Renegade Game Studios is preparing a massive new wave of Dungeon Crawler Carl releases for November 23, 2026 alongside the larger launch of the upcoming RPG and Unstoppable deck-building game, including the official Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG: Loot Packs, which are currently available to preorder through retailers like Game Nerdz.

These collectible mystery packs are part of the franchise's larger tabletop RPG expansion, with each containing a seven-piece polyhedral dice set and a collectible temporary tattoo. There are 20 different themed dice sets and 20 possible tattoos, with the dice divided into 12 common, five rare, and three legendary designs. Rare sets have advertised odds of one in six packs, while legendary sets are considerably harder to find at just one in 100.

The three legendary designs reference some of the series' most recognizable characters and catchphrases, including Samantha's infamous "I Will Kill Your Mother," Princess Donut's "Non-Alcoholic Dirty Shirley, Extra Cherries," and a special Princess Donut the Queen Anne Chonk set. Fans can preorder individual Loot Packs or an entire unopened display box containing 20 packs, although the randomized assortment means duplicates are possible. The full contents and details are here:

These collectibles accompany Renegade's highly anticipated Dungeon Crawler Carl Roleplaying Game, which allows players to create their own Crawlers and attempt to survive the World Dungeon. The Starter Set covers the first two tutorial floors, while the 300-plus-page Core Rulebook explores floors three through five (or roughly through Book 4), introducing extensive character customization, quests, monsters, familiar locations, and more.

Meanwhile, November also marks the retail debut of Dungeon Crawler Carl: Unstoppable, a separate deck-building game from designer John D. Clair. This solo or two-player cooperative experience lets fans play as Carl or Princess Donut, battling enemies and upgrading their cards as they progress through the dungeon's first three floors. Two expansions, Crawler Chaos and The Iron Tangle, are also arriving this month, introducing additional playable characters and the fourth floor.

All of these releases follow Renegade's record-breaking crowdfunding campaign, which raised over $13.29 million from approximately 55,000 backers. Fulfillment began in October, and some supporters have already received their games and collectibles. However, the official retail release is scheduled for November 23, meaning Dungeon Crawler Carl fans who missed the original campaign will soon have their chance to join the crawl.

#3498. Shrinking season 4 just got exciting release timing update

Shrinking just aired season 3 earlier this year, but all signs point to a refreshingly quick return, as one of the show’s stars just confirmed season 4 is officially done filming.

TV’s streaming era has brought a lot of advantages over linear TV, but undoubtedly one drawback is that shows tend to have much longer waits between seasons.

Traditional broadcast television usually schedules shows to premiere in the fall and run through the spring, then return after a short summer break for a new season in the fall.

In streaming, viewers are shocked when a show comes back after only a year.

Apple TV has slowly been getting better at this. Slow Horses is the best example, but another recent one is Your Friends & Neighbors. And we’re seeing signs of other series getting quicker turnarounds between seasons, including Shrinking.

Shrinking aired its season 3 finale this April, and by May we heard that filming on season 4 was about to start.

Now Jessica Williams, the star who plays Gaby, has confirmed that season 4 has officially wrapped production. This means the series will almost certainly return in early 2027.

On a show like Shrinking, post-production is a much quicker process than with series that are heavy on CGI and other special effects. So we could see Shrinking season 4 premiere in late January, exactly one year after season 3 debuted.

More conservatively, the show returning by spring 2027 seems a safe bet.

You can watch Shrinking seasons 1-3 here on Apple TV.

#3495. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 adding two new features soon

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 are here, and later this year they’ll get even more powerful with two new features: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Here are the details.

Siri AI is a major tentpole of watchOS 27, and later this year there’s a powerful Siri addition coming to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. It’s called Siri Recap.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

Live Rewind is another ‘Audio Intelligence’ feature coming to the new Apple Watch models later this year. It provides a more direct way to revisit something that was just said.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Apple is expected to introduce both new Apple Watch features in watchOS 27.3, which should launch in beta very soon.

#3494. iOS 27.2 just upgraded Apple Photos in two ways, here’s what’s new

Apple Photos got a lot of new features in iOS 27 last month, but this week’s release of iOS 27.2 brought even more improvements. Here’s what’s new.

Shared Albums are among my favorite features in the Photos app. I don’t post on social media often, but I love using Shared Albums because they provide a social media-style experience in a private way that lives right inside Photos.

iOS 27 brought a variety of big improvements to Shared Albums. And now iOS 27.2 has introduced four more.

Per Apple’s release notes, here’s what’s new:

To get these new features, you’ll need to make sure your Shared Albums have been upgraded for iOS 27.

One complication introduced by AI is that it can be hard to know if an image is real or AI-generated.

This challenge extends to AI-edited photos too, which might have key details changed by tools like iOS 27’s Extend, Reframe, and Clean Up features in Photos.

Apple is tackling the issue with its new Reference Image feature in iPhone 18 Pro, and also through a software enhancement that rolled out in iOS 27.2.

Per Apple, its latest software update adds the following:

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground

SynthID is a cross-platform standard developed by Google that embeds unnoticeable digital watermarks into AI-modified photos. Users won’t see a visible watermark, but anyone who checks for a SynthID marker will find it.

#3493. You Can Get These 'Nothing' Over-Ear Headphones for $55 Right Now

Nothing, the upstart U.K. brand that makes products like phones, smartwatches, and headphones, has quickly become one of my favorite players in tech. Its products offer unique features and designs, and the prices are competitive. For example, right now, Nothing's latest budget over-ear headphones, which were released in October 2025, the CMF Headphone Pros, are just $55 (originally $99). This is a great option for anyone looking to get reasonably priced over-the-ear headphones that punch above their weight when it comes to performance.

Much like Nothing's CMF Buds Pro 2 earbuds, the CMF Headphone Pros are budget headphones that don't feel like it. They're an affordable alternative to the popular Headphone 1 (currently $199), and seamlessly integrate into the Nothing/CMF ecosystem, which includes smartphones, watches, and other audio products. There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). On the other side, you'll find an "Energy Slider," which tunes your sound in real-time, instantly adjusting the treble and bass balance.

You'll get an impressive 100 hours of playback on a single charge (reduced to up to 50 hours with ANC turned on) as well as AAC, SBC, and LDAC support. They have an IPX2 rating for resistance against sweat, and there is a 3.5mm audio jack for wired listening.

Nothing is known for its minimalistic design, but these headphones do a bit more by allowing you to mix and match the earcups with different colors (sold separately for $25). These are a good option for those looking for stylish, budget over-ear headphones that have great battery life and excellent audio quality for their price point.

#3491. The Star Trek Franchise Officially Reunites Kirk And Spock On November 13

For 60 years, Star Trek has been home to some of science fiction's most iconic characters, but few have left a greater impression than Captain James T. Kirk and his loyal first officer, Spock. Portrayed by William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy, respectively, the two became the heart of Star Trek: The Original Series, developing a friendship that helped define the franchise for generations.

While Kirk was known for his bold leadership and emotionally charged decision-making (not to mention his occasional disregard for protocol) Spock's unwavering commitment to logic provided the perfect counterbalance. Their relationship evolved throughout The Original Series and subsequent films, culminating in some of the franchise's most emotional moments, particularly Spock's sacrifice in The Wrath of Khan.

Both Shatner and Nimoy left an extraordinary legacy that continues to influence Star Trek today, with their characters being reimagined by new actors across various films and television series. Now, as the franchise celebrates its 60th anniversary, Kirk and Spock are officially being reunited once again in a highly anticipated new release arriving November 13.

Captain Kirk and Spock are officially reuniting on November 13, 2026, although their latest adventure won't be taking place on television or the big screen. Instead, the legendary Star Trek duo will return as part of Magic: The Gathering's upcoming Universes Beyond crossover, which features four Commander decks celebrating different corners of the science fiction franchise.

Of particular interest to fans of Star Trek: The Original Series is the new Landing Party Commander deck, which brings Kirk, Spock, and several other familiar faces from the original USS Enterprise crew together in one release.

The 100-card deck is primarily built around Commander Spock, who serves as its featured commander, although players can also choose Captain Kirk, Boldly Going as an alternative. This allows players to have both characters in the same deck, effectively reuniting William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy's iconic characters for another adventure.

Landing Party is an "exploration-focused" deck, with Spock's abilities allowing players to draw additional cards and potentially cast spells for free depending on the number of differently named lands they control. Meanwhile, Kirk's abilities revolve around the Starship Enterprise, offering a different approach to commanding.

Beyond these two legendary characters, Landing Party includes cards featuring several other recognizable members of the original crew, including Lieutenant Nyota Uhura, Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu, Chief Montgomery Scott, Pavel Chekov, and Dr. McCoy. There are also cards depicting Christopher Pike, Christine Chapel, the Shuttlecraft Galileo, and several iconic locations, including Vulcan and Earth.

Of course, Landing Party is only one of four Commander decks arriving as part of the November 13 crossover. The remaining three include Federation Fleet, led by Jean-Luc Picard; Klingon Fury, featuring Worf as its commander; and We Are the Borg, which puts players in control of the Borg Queen.

Each deck includes 100 cards, with 32 new-to-Magic cards, alongside several familiar reprints. Special Collector's Edition versions featuring surge foil treatments will also be available.

The larger Magic: The Gathering x Star Trek crossover officially launches on November 13, 2026, bringing decades of franchise history into the trading card game. For longtime fans of the original series, however, the chance to command Kirk, Spock, and their Enterprise crew together again may be one of its biggest attractions.

One of my favorite streaming traditions is checking out what each platform has added at the start of a new month. The very first day of the month is when the majority of the best streaming services refresh their libraries with major movie drops, and Prime Video is no exception.

In fact, Prime Video typically drops more movies on the first day of a new month than any of its streaming rivals, and on Sunday, November 1, 2026, Prime’s back catalog is getting a major boost with 103 movies arriving.

That’s an overwhelming amount of choice, which is why I’ve combed through the list to pick out the gems you should stream first. Because it’s now November, Prime Video’s latest movie drop is heavy on holidays, and I’ve picked a couple of Christmas classics to get you in the festive mood nice and early. However, I’ve also found some exciting thrillers for those who don’t start celebrating the holidays until December.

So, let’s get into my top picks; these are the five movies just added to Prime Video that should be at the top of your November 2026 watchlist.

Some of my fondest childhood memories of the festive season involve rewatching “Elf” so many times that the DVD was in danger of getting worn out. This 2000s holiday classic has it all: seasonal spirit, charming comedy, lovable characters and a message about the importance of family. Even now as a grown-up on the wrong side of 30, it’s still a holiday movie I watch every single year, and I’ve no plans to stop in 2026.

Will Ferrell plays Buddy, a human raised by Santa’s elves. Due to his human proportions and inability to make toys, he doesn’t quite fit in at the North Pole. So when Santa reveals to him that his father (James Caan), a New York City bigwig, is on the naughty list, Buddy travels to the Big Apple to meet his biological father and find his place in the world. Once in NYC, he discovers that humans are sorely lacking in holiday cheer.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The perfect movie doesn’t exist. Absolute perfection is an impossible goal. Even my favorite films of all time have some minor flaws. However, when it comes to a movie nailing exactly what it's trying to achieve, it’s hard to argue that “Mean Girls” doesn’t get pretty darn close to perfection. This movie is the quintessential teen comedy, packed with quotable lines, iconic outfits and legendary scenes. And yes, we’re talking about the original here, not the musical remake. Though for the record, I’m a defender of that movie; I think it’s very underrated.

Cady Heron (Lindsay Lohan) is a 16-year-old whose family has recently returned to the U.S. after spending 12 years in Africa. Now attending North Shore High School, Cady is introduced to a complex web of unspoken teenage rules and a strict social hierarchy. At the top of the food chain are The Plastics, a trio of ultra-cool mean girls led by queen bee, Regina George (Rachel McAdams). When Cady is invited into their inner circle, she hatches a plan to sabotage them from within.

This year will see the release of yet another big-screen spin on Charles Dickens’ enduring classic, “A Christmas Carol,” in the form of Ti West’s “Ebenezer.” But why trek out to your local theater when you can already enjoy the best movie adaptation of the timeless tale on Prime Video? Okay, so “Scrooged” is the best adaptation of “A Christmas Carol” that doesn’t feature The Muppets. It's still a great watch even if it doesn't include Kermit, Miss Piggy, and the gang. Plus, it stars Bill Murray at his sarcastic best.

You probably know the basic setup, but if you’re somehow unfamiliar with Dickens’ fable, it follows a cynical and selfish TV executive (named Frank Cross here rather than Ebenezer Scrooge), who is visited by three ghosts on Christmas Eve in an effort to convince him to change his self-centered ways. There’s a pleasant meta twist in “Scrooged.” Cross lives in a world where the “A Christmas Carol” story also exists, so when he starts living the tale for real, he’s not too happy about it.

Moving away from holiday classics and teenage comedies, another movie that’s just arrived as part of Prime Video’s huge November 1 drop is “The Manchurian Candidate.” This 1962 political thriller is one that fans of classic cinema definitely shouldn’t skip. It stars Frank Sinatra, Laurence Harvey, and Janet Leigh, alongside Angela Lansbury, Henry Silva, and James Gregory. And it is perhaps one of the sharpest American movies of the Cold War era.

Raymond Shaw (Harvey) is a U.S. soldier fighting in the Korean War, captured by the enemy, but then released three days later. Returned home, he receives the Medal of Honor, and on the surface it looks like a feel-good homecoming story. But Shaw is hiding a dark secret, a shocking memory that even he can’t recall. “The Manchurian Candidate” is a thriller that hasn’t lost its edge over the last 60+ years and has even inspired modern media like Showtime's “Homeland.”

Watch "The Manchurian Candidate" on Prime Video now

Staying on the theme of political thrillers, “WarGames” is an ‘80s techno ride that does feel a little outdated when watched in the 21st century. However, at the time of its release, it was a real cautionary tale about the dangers of technology and its potential uses in global conflict. Heavily influenced by the Cold War period in which it was released, it marked one of the first movie roles for Matthew Broderick, Ferris Bueller himself.

David Lightman (Broderick) is a smart but unmotivated high school slacker in Seattle. A computer whiz, he uses his aptitude for computers for teenage hijinks. But things get serious when he unknowingly accesses a military central computer with the ability to simulate and even launch a devastating nuclear attack against the USSR. He thinks he’s playing a game, but he might have just started World War III…

#3488. 3 Elite Prime Video Series to Binge This Week (Nov 2-6)

November is officially here, and The Terminal List is continuing its run at the top of Prime Video’s TV rankings for another week. Created by David DiGilio and based on the novels by Jack Carr, the action thriller series returned with a second season recently and has been performing quite admirably ever since. However, the Chris Pratt-starrer is hardly the only great show worth checking out on the streaming platform. Here’s a look at three great shows that we think you should binge this week on Prime Video.

For more recommendations, check out our list of the best shows and movies on Prime Video.

A Canadian police procedural series created by Michael Konyves, Wild Cards follows Cole Ellis, a detective demoted to patrol duty who is assigned to work with a spirited con artist, Max Mitchell, to solve cases. Cole’s by-the-book approach often clashes with Max’s street smarts and charisma, but they must find a way to work together and fight crime. The show stars Giacomo Gianniotti as Cole and Vanessa Morgan as Max, who appear in all seasons, alongside rotating recurring and guest stars like Martin Sheen, Jason Priestley, and Tamara Taylor.

Wild Cards follows the classic police procedural format and features a new case every week with underlying storylines revolving around the protagonists’ romantic dynamic and family secrets. The series has earned acclaim for reprising the trend of lighthearted, breezy crime procedurals of the 2000s, making the best of "opposites attract" and "mismatched detectives" tropes that fans might love to revisit. Since its premiere, the series has proven quite popular, with the first season becoming CBC's highest-rated new series and the show earning a steady 100% on Rotten Tomatoes across three seasons.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

A neo-Western crime drama, Longmire is a series adaptation of Craig Johnson’s mystery novel series featuring Sheriff Walt Longmire. The series focuses on the troubled ex-military law-enforcement officer who solves strange crimes in his community while dealing with the competing jurisdictional authority of the bordering native reservation and various other issues of contemporary Native American life. Robert Taylor stars as the titular character, with Lou Diamond Phillips, Cassidy Freeman, Katee Sackhoff, Bailey Chase, and Adam Bartley in main roles.

Longmire may have become more or less forgotten since it ended, but during its six-season run, the Western drama was a major success with both critics and fans, fascinating its audience season after season with its interesting mysteries and unconventional detective. The series combines the best of two popular television genres, traditional Westerns and modern crime procedurals, creating a narrative that appeals to fans of either. Longmire is praiseworthy for its grounded writing, compelling acting, and atmospheric visuals, and is often ranked among the best revisionist Western shows.

Created, written by, and starring Sharon Horgan and Rob Delaney, Catastrophe is a British sitcom that follows Sharon, an Irish primary school teacher in London who meets Rob, an American advertising executive on a business trip to the city. After a week-long whirlwind romance, Rob returns home to Boston while Sharon discovers that she is pregnant with his child, unleashing utter chaos in their respective lives. Besides Horgan and Delaney as the main characters, the series also stars Ashley Jensen, Mark Bonnar, and Carrie Fisher in her final television role.

Before the success and popularity of Bad Sisters, Catastrophe was Horgan’s most critically acclaimed work in television, earning her a BAFTA nomination for her performance. Raw, witty, and often brutally honest, Catastrophe excels in its sharp satire of the hard-hitting realities of modern parenting and marriage, finding its humor and heart in its flawed characters. Horgan and Delaney also earned BAFTA TV Awards and an Emmy nomination for their writing.

#3486. This High-Capacity Portable Power Station Is $550 Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. If you use DJI gear, that alone makes life easier in the field, notes this Mashable review. Recharging is also fast for a battery this size. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.
