#3485. Apple announces all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen Mac

Apple has officially announced the all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen laptop.

The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser. Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well.

Read on for all the details about the new high-end laptop…

The new machine features a light-up Apple logo, tandem OLED, and touch input on the display.

It runs on the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, like the existing MacBook Pro models without OLED touch displays.

John Ternus, who is rocking a new profile picture with the new Mac, shared the first look at the new machine on X:

We’re glowing with excitement over the new MacBook Pro. You’ve gotta touch it to believe it. pic.twitter.com/BLiGkGaefL

Apple previously used a glowing Apple logo on its notebook hardware for years until the 12-inch MacBook and 2016 MacBook Pro.

Pricing for the new laptop starts at $2899 for the 14-inch model. The 16-inch version starts at $3399.

Pre-orders are available starting today with deliveries starting November 6. You can find the product page for the new MacBook Pro here. The new machines are also available on Amazon.

Colors include silver or space black options with standard or nano-texture display configurations.

Beyond the new high-end laptop, Apple also announced the redesigned iPad mini, M6 iMac, and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro this week. Back in March, Apple upgraded the standard 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops to the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple calls the new design both thinner and lighter than the standard MacBook Pro models in the same size configuration.

The new MacBook Pros look awesome with glowing Apple logos. We’re so back. pic.twitter.com/Ce6G8EIVQF

The new MacBook Pro is the first to use what Apple calls a PROLED XDR display, replacing Mini-LED as the MacBook Pro display technology.

While Apple has innovated with multi-touch on the iPhone and iPad, the Mac has been resistant to touch input for years. The new MacBook Pro changes that with the first touchscreen Mac display. Here’s what Apple says about touch on the Mac.

MacBook Pro features Touch for the first time, bringing pros a whole new way to interact with their content. Crafted specifically for the Mac, every touch interaction feels incredibly responsive and refined. Everyday tasks are simple and intuitive, allowing users to scroll through a webpage with a natural swipe; pinch to zoom in on a photo; drag and drop slides from one presentation to another; and double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick to tile it into place. And the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it — reducing latency so users feel like they’re touching the content itself.

Apple also touts the use of a new hinge technology in the MacBook Pro, in part to support touch input without compromising on stability:

Touch also introduces entirely new ways of working for pro users. Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing; musicians can play software instruments right onscreen; and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display. And these new ways to interact with MacBook Pro work in tandem with the keyboard shortcuts and trackpad gestures pros know and love. In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.

In addition to touch as an additional input method, the new MacBook Pro also adopts the Dynamic Island in favor of the notch.

The Dynamic Island now comes to Mac, serving as the home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Not interested in touch? The existing MacBook Pro configurations from March stick around at the same prices. You just lose OLED, the glowing Apple logo, and the thinner and lighter design. Performance, however, is pretty much on par between versions as both offer M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

The new laptops can be configured with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of solid state drive storage.

Peak display brightness jumps from 1600 nits to 2000 nits for HDR content.

I honestly think this is a downgrade. Remember when Apple introduced the Touch Bar? It was supposed to be a big deal, but eventually Apple removed it. Now they’re adding a touchscreen to the MacBook. What’s the actual point?

If it supported the Apple Pencil, I could understand the appeal, especially for designers. But without it, I honestly don’t see much use for it. Maybe I’m wrong, but I’ve used touchscreen Windows laptops before, and I never really found it useful.

I can’t help wondering whether Steve Jobs would have approved of this direction. Apple needs a better marketing team that understands what people actually want, rather than adding a touchscreen that, in my opinion, offers very little practical use.

The 14-inch model is half a pound lighter at just 3 pounds even compared to 3.5 pounds for the same version of the previous design. The overall footprint is reduced as well with 0.59 x 12.24 x 8.52 inch dimensions compared to 0.61 x 12.31 x 8.71 inch dimensions when comparing 14-inch models.

The 16-inch model is notably lighter as well. The new design weighs in at 4 pounds even compared to 4.7 pounds for the previous design. Dimensions change to 0.63 x 14 x 9.62 inches compared to 0.66 x 14.01 x 9.77 inches between designs.

Playing piano on the touchscreen MacBook Pro pic.twitter.com/lDlwIeqErd

The new machines still use Touch ID with no Face ID support. Apple also doesn’t offer built-in cellular models of the new MacBook Pro. We’ll have to keep waiting for Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity.

You can find Apple’s press release for the new machines here. All configurations are available to order from Amazon.

#3483. All 66 Episodes Of Hulu's R-Rated Thriller Deliver Psychological Horror At Its Best

While Hulu’s greatest dystopian show is often listed among the best sci-fi series of the last decade, the adaptation rarely gets credit for just how great it is at pulling off psychological horror, too. If Blade Runner’s links to the Alien franchise prove anything, it is that the line between sci-fi and horror is often thinner than it might seem.

One need only look at the Star Trek franchise’s Borg or the earliest, eerily human Cylons from the Battlestar Galactica reboot to see that the uncanny line between man and machine can be mined for horror just as much as wonder or awe. Similarly, from the Xenomorph to its natural enemy, the Predator franchise’s Yautja, there are plenty of extraterrestrials in movies and TV that are a lot less friendly than Steven Spielberg’s awe-inspiring childhood favorite.

On occasion, sci-fi shows can also end up taking their dark dystopian plots so far that they essentially become psychological horror shows in disguise. For many fans of the genre, the term “psychological horror” will likely conjure up straightforward horror shows like Prime Video’s Stephen King adaptation Carrie or The Haunting of Hill House. However, with its oppressively bleak tone and truly terrifying sense of dread, Hulu’s Margaret Atwood adaptation, The Handmaid’s Tale, is just as scary as any of these titles.

Set in the Republic of Gilead, a totalitarian near-future America run by Christian fascists, The Handmaid’s Tale is loosely based on Atwood’s award-winning 1985 novel of the same name. While the book is an epistolary novel told mostly through the diaries of one “Handmaid,” the show’s sprawling narrative takes the perspective of various female characters to explore the horrors of its setting.

In Gilead, women like Elizabeth Moss’s Offred are held captive and have their bodies used as incubators to produce the offspring of the Republic of Gilead’s patriarchal zealots. The regime’s leaders are nightmarishly ruthless and the fate of these women is horrifying, but there is some hope despite the country’s fascist takeover as Offred spends season 1 plotting an escape to the Canadian border.

Suffice it to say that things are not quite that simple for Offred, and the horrors of The Handmaid's Tale’s setting don’t end when she escapes in the season 1 finale. This does, however, mark the moment that the show expands beyond the story of Atwood’s novel, with the remaining five seasons of the series expanding on the slight, sparse original story.

While ambitious sci-fi shows like HBO’s Westworld also depicted believable dystopian settings around the same time, The Handmaid’s Tale was notable for the sheer harshness in the show’s depiction of Gilead. Westworld had plenty of graphic violence, like so many shows that arrived after Game of Thrones and The Walking Dead, but lacked the overwhelming dread that defined every storyline in The Handmaid’s Tale.

That said, this wasn’t an unambiguously positive thing for the series. Later seasons of The Handmaid’s Tale were criticized precisely because the show was accused of relying on downbeat shock value to keep viewers invested, with some commentators claiming that the worst excesses of the series felt exploitative and gratuitous. For fans, The Handmaid’s Tale was an unblinking depiction of fascism’s cruelty.

However, for detractors, the show’s lingering focus on torture and public executions felt too lurid and grotesque to be justifiable. The Handmaid’s Tale seemingly addressed this critique when its final two seasons eased up on the brutality somewhat. This also resulted, inevitably, in the ending of The Handmaid’s Tale feeling less impossibly bleak and hopeless than seasons 2 and 3 of The Handmaid’s Tale might have led viewers to expect.

#3480. The 8 Most Amazing Horror Movies Ever Made, Ranked

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Horror lists built around the question “Which movie scared you the most?” are almost always bad. Fear is too personal and subjective for that. Sometimes the movie that follows me home is the one that barely raises its voice. Sometimes it is a face, a sound from another room, a character making one decision I desperately wanted them not to make.

That is what these eight have done to me. I have watched them enough times to know exactly where the bodies are buried, and somehow they still have power. The scares remain, obviously, but so do the performances, the moral ugliness, the ideas underneath the violence, and those tiny human reactions that make everything hurt more than a monster ever could. These are hands down, the 8 most amazing horror movies ever made.

Chris Washington (Daniel Kaluuya) spends a weekend meeting the wealthy white family of his girlfriend Rose (Allison Williams), expecting awkward questions and passive-aggressive liberalism. Get Out gradually turns those discomforts into something much worse when Chris notices that the Black people working around the estate behave strangely, Rose’s mother offers him hypnosis, and the family’s fascination with his body begins feeling considerably less innocent.

What destroys me is how long Chris is socially pressured into ignoring instincts that are completely correct. Jordan Peele wrote and directed the film, and he understands that politeness can become its own kind of trap. Chris keeps giving people opportunities to explain themselves because walking out would make him appear unreasonable. Then Logan (LaKeith Stanfield) briefly breaks character at the party and screams at Chris to “get out,” and suddenly every uncomfortable little interaction snaps into place. It is frightening, hilarious, furious, and so controlled that even the jokes sharpen the horror rather than interrupting it.

The Texas Chain Saw Massacre follows Sally Hardesty (Marilyn Burns), her brother Franklin (Paul A. Partain), and their friends through rural Texas, where an innocent detour eventually brings them to a farmhouse occupied by Leatherface (Gunnar Hansen) and his deeply disturbed family. There is barely any elaborate mythology. People enter the wrong house, and the nightmare starts almost immediately.

The first hammer killing is nasty. It happens abruptly with almost no ceremony. A door slides open, Leatherface appears, somebody collapses, and the door closes again. Tobe Hooper directed the film. He apparently made everything feel hot, dirty, exhausted, and horribly plausible even when the situation becomes grotesque. The dinner scene. Sally’s screaming becomes so constant. The entire movie feels physically oppressive. Then morning arrives, she escapes, and Leatherface dances with the chainsaw in the road while she laughs hysterically from the back of a truck. That ending does not feel victorious. It feels like somebody’s nervous system has snapped.

This film follows Marion Crane (Janet Leigh) who steals $40,000 from her employer and flees town, eventually stopping at the isolated Bates Motel. There she meets Norman Bates (Anthony Perkins), a shy young proprietor apparently dominated by his unseen mother. Alfred Hitchcock’s Psycho initially seems to be following Marion’s crime and guilt, then abruptly makes the motel itself far more important than the money she stole.

Perkins is the real weapon, though. Norman can appear fragile, embarrassed, friendly, and faintly wrong inside the same conversation. Watch him talk to Marion about his mother while birds loom around the parlor. Nothing outwardly outrageous is happening, but every sentence makes the room less comfortable. The shower murder became the icon. Norman’s nervous smile is what stays with me.

The Exorcist begins with actress Chris MacNeil (Ellen Burstyn) watching her daughter Regan (Linda Blair) undergo increasingly frightening physical and psychological changes that doctors cannot explain. Eventually, she turns to Father Damien Karras (Jason Miller), a priest and psychiatrist already struggling with his faith, who begins to suspect that Regan may be possessed.

I have never thought the pea soup was the frightening part. The horror is Chris exhausting every rational possibility and realizing none of them can help her child. William Friedkin directed the film with an almost clinical seriousness, which keeps the supernatural material from turning theatrical. Karras matters just as much because the demon attacks the exact wound he carries, especially his guilt surrounding his mother’s death. The final exorcism works because it is spiritual warfare conducted through incredibly human weaknesses. Everybody enters that room already damaged. That is why the possession feels personal rather than decorative.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The crew of the Nostromo is returning to Earth when Alien diverts them toward a mysterious transmission on a hostile planet. Kane (John Hurt) encounters an unknown organism, the crew brings him back aboard, and warrant officer Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) soon discovers that the creature now loose inside their ship is only part of the danger. Ridley Scott directed this like space travel had finally become a blue-collar job. On a lighter note, with all the reptilian aliens chit chatter, it is the perfect time to watch a horror film like this.

In Aliens, people complain about pay. Machinery looks used. Corridors feel practical rather than futuristic. Then the chestburster tears through Kane at dinner, and that normal working environment becomes impossible to trust again. I also love that Ripley survives partly because she was the person insisting on quarantine rules everyone else considered inconvenient. She is not “chosen.” She pays attention.

Stanley Kubrick helmed The Shining with an almost inhuman visual precision, making the Overlook feel too orderly to be safe. Writer Jack Torrance (Jack Nicholson) takes a winter job as caretaker of the isolated Overlook Hotel, bringing his wife Wendy (Shelley Duvall) and young son Danny (Danny Lloyd) with him. Danny possesses a psychic ability called “the shining,” which exposes him to the hotel’s violent past while isolation begins feeding something terrible inside Jack.

What gets me now is Wendy. People talk endlessly about the twins, Room 237, the elevator of blood, and Jack smashing through the bathroom door, but Shelley Duvall gives the film its bruised human reality. Wendy is the opposite of that control. She panics, cries, swings the bat awkwardly, and keeps moving because Danny needs her. Horror movies often make survival look cool. Wendy survives while looking absolutely terrified, which is far more convincing.

John Carpenter’s The Thing traps an American research team in Antarctica with an extraterrestrial organism capable of perfectly copying other living beings. Once MacReady (Kurt Russell) and the others understand what it can do, the problem becomes horrifyingly simple. The creature may already look exactly like somebody they trust.

I could recommend this movie purely for the blood test. Everyone is tied down. Nobody knows who is human. MacReady heats a wire and touches each blood sample because he believes every piece of the organism will instinctively protect itself. The waiting becomes unbearable. Rob Bottin’s effects are still magnificently disgusting, but the paranoia is why I keep coming back. Even the ending refuses to rescue us from it. MacReady and Childs (Keith David) sit together in the freezing ruins with no reliable way to prove either is human. After everything, distrust has outlived the monster.

FBI trainee Clarice Starling (Jodie Foster) is sent to interview imprisoned psychiatrist and serial killer Hannibal Lecter (Anthony Hopkins) because investigators hope his insight can help them catch another murderer, Buffalo Bill (Ted Levine). The Silence of the Lambs becomes a psychological duel between Clarice and Lecter while another woman’s life depends on Clarice understanding what Bill is doing before time runs out.

Jonathan Demme directed the film. The film has those extraordinary direct-to-camera close-ups that make conversation feel invasive. Lecter looks straight into Clarice and seems capable of reading whatever she hoped to conceal. Yet Clarice never becomes intellectually passive around him. Foster lets you see the nerves and the steel at once. Then the final hunt places Clarice inside Bill’s dark basement while he watches her through night-vision goggles, reaching toward her without her knowing how close he is. I still tense up even though I know every movement. That is why this sits at number one. The film gives me brilliant detective work, psychological warfare, genuine terror, and a great heroine without wasting a single minute.

Wet weather and warm homes are a recipe for mattress mold

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mattress mold is a problem that sneaks up on you. A slightly whiffy bed and small stains can quickly turn to itching, sneezing and watery eyes. And right now is primetime for moldy conditions.

A combination of cold, wet weather outside and warm heating inside increases moisture in the air. Your mattress soaks it up like a sponge and, trapped inside your warm bed, that damp helps mold spores to multiply.

Mattress mold doesn't have to spell the end of your bed, but you need to catch it early. We spoke to Dr Gareth Nye, Biomedical Sciences lecturer at the University of Salford working exclusively with M&S, about how to identify early signs of mold — and get rid of it.

Mold can completely ruin a mattress, but before you rush off to browse our best mattress guide for a replacement bed, look out for these early indicators of mold.

You won't necessarily see early signs of mold in your mattress, but you might be able to smell the problem has taken hold.

Dr. Nye describes the smell of mold as "a persistent musty, damp, or earthy odor" and notes that it can linger "even after the bedding has been washed."

If this new smell is accompanied by an uptick in allergy symptoms when you go to bed (itching, sneezing or watery eyes, for example) mold is the likely culprit. Noticed a sweeter musty smell? It might be bed bugs.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Big, dark stains are often a sign that your mattress is past saving. But before you get to that point, Dr. Nye recommends looking for "tiny, clustered pinpoint stains."

These small marks are the signs of an early mold infestation and they can be treated (we'll explore how below). And don't just look on the top surface of the mattress for stains. The underside of the bed as well as the sides can house mold as well.

Signs of mold aren't always visible on the mattress itself. Look in the surrounding area for indicators your bedroom is growing mold.

Dr. Nye describes "spaces up against a wall or behind units" as 'mold magnets' because they prevent airflow. So if your bed frame is pushed against the wall, move it forward when you clean and check for mold.

He also advices looking in any common sites for condensation, including anything pressed to the "external environment" (like radiators against a window).

"The space under the bed is also a prime spot for mold," says Dr. Nye. And if the mold is under the bed, it might not take long for it to move into the bed.

Mold is more than just an unwanted stain. Left to grow, mold in your mattress can have serious negative repercussions on your health.

"Mold reproduces by releasing microscopic spores and mycotoxins into the air, which are easily inhaled during the 7 to 8 hours you spend asleep," explains Dr. Nye. "This triggers an immune response, leading to allergic rhinitis (sneezing, congestion, runny nose, and itchy eyes) and significantly exacerbating symptoms for those with asthma."

And the longer the problem is allowed to grow, the worse the impact it can have on your health.

"Prolonged exposure can result in chronic illnesses," says Dr. Nye. "Mold spores can also severely worsen conditions like eczema and trigger contact dermatitis."

We previously asked the experts how to get rid of mattress mold. They advised spot treating any stains with ingredients you probably have in your kitchen: white vinegar and baking soda.

Begin by mixing equal parts white vinegar and water. Spray the solution lightly on the stain and leave for 20 minutes. Blot dry, then apply a thin layer of baking soda. Leave to sit for several hours and then vacuum thoroughly.

#3477. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3476. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR vs MacBook Pro: Here’s every difference

Apple unveiled its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR this week (pre-order here), which joins the lineup alongside the existing MacBook Pro using the same M5 Pro and Max chips. Here’s an in-depth comparison of the two models.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has an all-new industrial design. It’s the first design overhaul for the MacBook Pro since 2021.

You still get a 14.2-inch regardless of whether you choose PROLED XDR or not. On the 16-inch model, PROLED XDR is 16.3 inches, slightly larger than the standard 16.2-inch.

Apple’s new design is a bit sleeker and significantly lighter-weight. It also brings back the glowing Apple logo on the lid that was an iconic element in previous generations. Additionally, the PROLED XDR has a newly designed hinge that provides greater stability.

Here’s a breakdown of how each model compares in size and weight:

As the numbers show, the overall size difference is fairly minor, but the reduced weight should be obvious to anyone who upgrades.

The new MacBook Pro’s display technology is so important, Apple put it in the branding. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR features a tandem OLED that Apple says is “the world’s best laptop display.”

Again, it’s available in 14.2-inch or 16.3-inch sizes that are nearly identical to the standard MacBook Pro.

The PROLED XDR display is touch-enabled, with macOS 27 introducing a variety of optimizations for touch input. So if you want a touchscreen on your Mac, that’s a big advantage.

Tandem OLED means you’ll get deeper blacks, true-to-life color, and also a new max peak brightness of 2,000 nits (up from 1,600). And Adobe RGB is now supported, along with a host of industry-standard reference modes.

There’s also a Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro. It replaces the notch and serves as the home to software features like Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Apple is using the exact same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips in its two MacBook Pros, so performance should in theory be the same across models.

That said, real-world testing will reveal whether the new MacBook Pro design has an impact on sustained performance—for better or worse.

Memory options are also identical with the PROLED XDR model and standard MacBook Pro. That means:

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR largely retains the same storage options as the standard MacBook Pro, with one exception.

The only change here is that there’s now a high-end 16TB option when you choose M5 Max. Previously, 8TB was the most storage available in any MacBook Pro.

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers identical battery life and fast charging features as the standard MacBook Pro. That means:

All MacBook Pro models can fast charge up to 50 percent battery in 30 minutes.

Apple’s MacBook Pro models all feature the same 12MP Center Stage camera with support for Desk View, 1080p HD video recording, and an advanced image signal processor with computational video.

However, because of touchscreen support, the PROLED XDR model adds one new feature: Advanced Video Stabilization.

Essentially, this exists so that if you’re touching your display during a video call, it won’t have an impact on your camera feed.

The MacBook Pro PROLED XDR features largely the same speaker system as the standard model, but with a pair of key upgrades. Per Apple Newsroom:

The industry-leading six-speaker audio system in the new MacBook Pro features an all-new woofer design that provides 50 percent deeper bass and all-new tweeters that shape sound dispersion for remarkable clarity…And for the first time, dedicated audio tuning for closed-lid use delivers exceptional sound quality when MacBook Pro is connected to an external display, so users can enjoy a premium audio experience however they work.

Apple clearly learned from past mistakes of removing ports from pro users. With the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, you get all the same ports as on the standard MacBook Pro. Ports include:

One upgrade that will benefit some users is that Genlock is now supported by the Thunderbolt 5 ports as well.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch. That’s a $400 premium over the standard MacBook Pro.

Apple’s standard MacBook Pro starts at $2,499 for the 14-inch size and $2,999 for the larger 16-inch.

Warm fuzzies for the return of the glowing Apple logo but I won't need the other features so it's not worth the extra $400 to me.

Overall, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR offers a lot of upgrades over the standard model, but with the same basic performance and battery life. If you want a better display, touch support, a Dynamic Island, and various other smaller improvements, PROLED XDR is the way to go.

You can pre-order MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display here for launch-day delivery.

#3475. 26 Episodes Of Netflix's Best Time Travel Show Leave Zero Plot Holes

Most time travel movies and shows collapse under their own flawed logic and rules. They start strong and introduce compelling sci-fi concepts and ideas. However, the more they progress, the more their plot crumbles due to increasing paradoxes and narrative loopholes. A rare sci-fi series on Netflix, however, completely defies the norm and even turns its paradoxes into plot devices.

The show in question, Dark, is still remembered as one of the greatest modern additions to the sci-fi genre. When Dark first landed on Netflix in 2017, it was not driven by a hefty budget or a massive production. As a non-English series, even its reach was meant to be limited as it competed with other mainstream sci-fi shows like Stranger Things.

Yet, through its sheer brilliance alone, the Netflix sci-fi show managed to leave a legacy that remains far stronger and more long-lasting than most others in Netflix's catalog. From its background score to its immersive and atmospheric cinematography, a lot works in the time travel TV show's favor. However, its success can primarily be attributed to how meticulously it approaches time travel.

Time travel is not a flowing river in Netflix's Dark. The show does not merely adopt a one-dimensional cause-and-effect format where actions lead to rippling consequences. Instead, for two whole seasons, it sticks to strict determinism where time is a 4D block. The past, the present, and the future unfold all at once in Dark, with each dissolving into one another.

Owing to this, any attempt to change the past in the series is revealed to be a pre-existing part of history. The overarching timeline just cannot be altered because the mere attempt to intervene was already meant to happen. This is perfectly captured when Dark's main character, Jonas, attempts to save his late father by traveling to the past, but his very presence eventually triggers his father's death.

With this deterministic approach towards time almost throughout its runtime, Dark establishes how objects and information exist without any origins. Most time travel stories reverse-engineer their narratives as they reveal the origin of specific objects or devices. This often creates a paradox because their origins become impossible to establish.

Dark embraces these paradoxes by showing how knowledge perpetually exists in its closed temporal loop.

For instance, a book in the show's universe called A Journey Through Time by H.G. Tannhaus was never actually written by Tannhaus. A younger Tannhaus merely published and transcribed it after the main character's older version gave it to him. The same published copy then ended up going back in time to be handed to him.

Even the show's portrayal of family trees is intentionally loopy. There are no linear lineages. Instead of being pyramids that move from one generation to another, the family trees exist as webs where generations overlap and ancestors become their own descendants.

The Netflix sci-fi show features a compelling opening scene where a narrator makes viewers question their perception of time. "We trust that time is linear, that it proceeds eternally, uniformly, into infinity," he says before revealing how yesterday, today, and tomorrow "are all connected in a never-ending circle." These opening lines in Dark bring a spin on Albert Einstein's most profound quote about time:

"The distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion."

Albert Einstein penned the line in a letter he wrote to the family of his deceased friend, Michele Besso. He did not label time as a "stubbornly persistent illusion" to highlight humanity's lack of free will. Instead, he wanted it to be a reminder that even the dead eternally exist all across time even though we cannot help but grieve them in the present.

A similar sense of hope can be found in Dark's existential portrayal of time travel. The Netflix show's depiction of how the past cannot be altered and how the future is pre-determined can be incredibly harrowing. But there is some strange comfort in knowing that everything is already set in stone and one is exactly where one is meant to be.

By showing how even the most painful choices one makes perfectly tie into the grand scheme of things, Netflix's Dark captures how darkly beautiful time travel in sci-fi can be.

Dark is a German science fiction thriller focusing on four families in a small town impacted by the disappearance of a child. As they search for answers, they uncover a web of interconnected secrets, revealing complex temporal and familial relationships spanning multiple generations.

Recent news urges us all to prepare for sudden power cuts. I assumed I was fine, until an honest look around my house revealed I was woefully unequipped

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every time an emergency agency pops up on the news suggesting households keep a 72-hour emergency kit on hand, I do the same thing: nod knowingly, assume they’re talking to someone far less organized than me, and scroll on.

In my head, I’m a reasonably capable adult. The fridge is full, there are batteries rattling around in a drawer somewhere, and I have a phone flashlight. Surely that counts as disaster preparedness.

Curiosity finally won out, so I decided to run an honest, room-by-room audit of what would actually happen if our power lines went dark for three straight days. The verdict was... humbling.

It turns out my master survival plan was heavily reliant on an active Wi-Fi connection, an electric stovetop, and blind optimism. Here's five glaring blind spots I completely overlooked, and what you should do so you don't make the same mistakes.

Opening my junk drawer during the audit revealed two decorative candles, a lighter that took six clicks to spark, and I didn't have a flashlight. My entire plan, it seemed, was an iPhone and an ancient power bank that refused to charge past 12%. Using a phone flashlight burns through battery, leaving you without light, or a lifeline.

Retire your phone as a light source and stash dedicated LED lights or magnetic lanterns where you can grab them in pitch black, like a bedside drawer. Pair them with an inexpensive hand-crank AM/FM emergency radio: it pulls in vital civil broadcasts with zero Wi-Fi, and the built-in dynamo handle doubles as a manual charger as a last resort if your devices die.

I went looking for medical supplies and found a dusty tin with three sports bandages, one pack of ibuprofen, and a pair of blunt tweezers. That was the entirety of my home trauma unit. Navigating in the dark makes minor injuries inevitable, and local clinics won't be running at full capacity during a power cut.

Ditch the half-empty tin and get a proper, sealed multi-day medical kit stocked with sterile dressings, burn gel, antiseptic wash, and heavy-duty elastic wraps. Crucially, audit your prescription medications right now and set a reminder to refill them at least a week before they run dry.

When a storm knocks out power, pharmacies can't access electronic dispensary records, and nobody is handing out prescription pills over a dark counter.

A packed fridge gives you an immediate, unearned hit of confidence. But an unopened fridge only holds safe temperatures for about four hours, and my pantry was full of dry pasta, lentils, and rice — meals that require boiling water and an electric stove. Unless I fancied crunching raw fettuccine in the dark, I had zero edible food past day one.

Do a pantry check for foods that require zero heat and zero added water. Build a reserve of ready-to-eat staples: crackers, canned fish, pull-tab soups, peanut butter, spam, nuts. It won't win culinary awards, but it keeps you fed without burning precious cooking fuel or risking food poisoning on day three.

Municipal water relies on electric booster pumps. If the grid fails, pipe pressure drops fast, or contamination triggers boil-water alerts you can't comply with on a dead stove. My total water reserve was half a fridge filter carafe and a gym bottle on my desk.

Store the emergency baseline: four litres (one gallon) of water per person, per day, split between drinking and basic hygiene. For a 72-hour blackout, keep a minimum of 12 litres per person tucked into a dark cupboard or wardrobe, plus extra if you have pets. It's worth noting that your water heater has around 150-300 liters stored inside it too in case of an emergency.

Digital payments die the instant the power cut hits. Point-of-sale card readers, phone taps, and bank networks go dark, turning plastic and smartwatches into useless props. Checking my own bags, pockets and drawers produced exactly zero physical money.

If you're able, withdraw an emergency cash reserve and stash it. The guidance states between $100 and $500 depending on your family's size, covering essentials if card systems remain offline for several days. If you're like me and withdrawing in one go isn't feasible, simply start tucking away leftover change. Every little helps, and it adds up quickly.

#3472. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3471. 9 Dystopian Sci-Fi Shows That Are 10/10 Masterpieces

It seems like dystopian sci-fi shows are one of the fastest-growing sub-genres of late. Dystopian shows have been popular for some time, dating all the way back to the early The Walking Dead days and with shows like Lost.

Sci-fi shows, meanwhile, have also been popular for decades. But combining the two? That's a relatively new thing. Apart from shows like Studio One back in 1953 and its "Nineteen Eighty-Four" episode and, of course, iconic series like The Twilight Zone, sci-fi dystopia is a burgeoning space. A few specific shows from the last decade or so have really done it justice.

What makes Paradise especially brilliant is that it doesn't weave sci-fi into the plot until the second season. In fact, it doesn't even reveal the dystopian reality until the end of the pilot episode. The show also functions as an action-packed political thriller, mashing so many genres into one, yet blending them so well.

The story in one of the best thriller shows released since 2020 takes place in an underground bunker where survivors reside. In Season 2, it flips back and forth between the bunker and Earth above, where things are very different from what the few thousands who were saved are led to believe. The sci-fi angle throws you for the loop, suggesting the upcoming final Season 3 will lean more heavily into this side and reinvent the show for another exceptional season to complete the story.

Cryogenic chambers that keep people alive for centuries. Killer mutated insects called Radroaches. Fighters in heavily teched out robot armor. Undead ghouls roaming the streets. It's all par for the course in Fallout, a post-apocalyptic drama based on the video game series of the same name.

With two seasons under its belt and another on the way, Fallout follows naïve young Lucy (Ella Purnell) as she emerges from her underground bunker for the first time and realizes that life outside is far different from the sheltered one she has lived. She teams up with The Ghoul (Walton Goggins) to achieve a common goal, but the dangers they meet are a combination of fractured human nature and creepy sci-fi. It's so entertaining, even if you know nothing about the video games.

Another show where survivors from an apocalyptic event live underground. This time they're in silos in Silo. The towering floors are separated by endless loops of stairwells and people are divided by class; ironically, one aspect of the world before that hasn't changed. Everyone is led to believe that outside is a dangerous wasteland, proven through a projected image from a camera that reveals the immediate death of anyone who dares ask to leave. When Juliette Nichols (Rebecca Ferguson) starts to question things, however, the beginnings of a potential revolution emerge.

Like Paradise, the sci-fi element doesn't arrive in a big way until Season 3, when plenty of big revelations are presented for the story. But it is teased throughout. When the big reveal rears its head in the third season, however, you can't help but sit at the edge of your seat, desperate to find out how the story ends. Silo is based on a series of novels by Hugh Howey, but the show has carved a modified path, which means even fans of the books get surprises.

With a heavy spotlight on tech, Mr. Robot combines the dangers of technology with the challenges of mental health. Elliot Alderson (Rami Malek) is a talented and reclusive hacker who works for a cybersecurity company by day but uses his hacking skills to stop people from doing awful things at night. His main goal, however, is to take down the world's biggest corporation, E Corp (he calls them Evil Corp), believing that a financial reset that wipes out debilitating personal debt is the only way to save humanity.

Mr. Robot dives deep into sci-fi as the story progresses and Elliot discovers things about himself and his group's supposed leader, Mr. Robot (Christian Slater). He encounters cyberterrorist enemies, evil CEOs, and the dark implications of anarchy. The show is one of those series you benefit from watching twice.

Severance is one of the best shows of the last five years, a sci-fi psychological thriller about Mark Scout (Adam Scott), a man who undergoes an experimental procedure to divide his memories. The goal is to get through a mundane job without being consumed by grief over the death of his wife. But Mark's "innie" and "outie" are still technically the same person, even if they know nothing about one another.

The show gets bizarre yet gripping as it further explores the concept of personal agency, and the nefarious plans of Lumon Industries, the biotechnology company that performs these procedures. It's an intense thriller show worth watching over and over, obsessing over every detail in Reddit forums with other fans. Both seasons will have you wide-eyed, Season 2 especially upping the ante. By the end of both seasons to date, you'll be screaming at the TV.

Unequivocally the best sci-fi dystopian show of this generation, Black Mirror tells a unique story in every episode of its anthology format. There are admittedly some weak episodes among the bunch, but even the weakest ones are better than the totality of some other shows of the genre. And the best ones? They will blow your mind.

Black Mirror serves as a cautionary tale, a warning of the dangers of rapid technological innovation and our reliance on it. From AI to social media, the monetization of everything, parental controls, and more, each speculative fiction story is like a piece of art. Often, you don't quite understand the point until towards the end, leaving your jaw on the floor. That's especially so with some of the episodes from early seasons, like Season 2's "Be Right Back," fan favorite Season 3's "San Junipero," and the horrifying Season 3 episode "Shut Up and Dance."

From the mind of Breaking Bad creator Vince Gilligan, Pluribus explores the sci-fi and dystopian angle from a completely new lens. The world as we know it has come to an end. But survivors have become part of a hive mind. They aren't out to murder and maim, they want to create a utopian society. Carol Sturka (Rhea Seehorn) is one of only a few survivors who are immune to the virus, and she has no interest in joining. It's a race against time to stop the madness before the hive mind uses its vast knowledge to figure out how to bypass her immunity.

Pluribus is subtle. There aren't flashy scenes. It's mostly dialogue driven with compelling discussions that make you ponder if individuality is more important than literal world peace. Is world peace really achievable anyway, and at what cost? Plus, there's the big question of what caused this virus in the first place. The answer leads to somewhere in the stars and potential other life forms.

Sometimes, the best shows in the eyes of viewers aren't necessarily the ones that continue beyond a few seasons. Such is the case with Raised by Wolves, which debuted to positive reception, was even more revered in Season 2, then was shockingly canceled by HBO Max. Even so, the sci-fi drama is still worth your time.

Set in the future following the destruction of Earth, Father (Abubakar Salim) and Mother (Amanda Collin) are androids raising human children on their home planet. A colony of human survivors is forming on Kepler-22b, but political and social views don't always align. This threatens the entire race and leaves the androids struggling to figure out how to deal with this foreign species. The show is so original, wonderfully exploring not only dystopia and sci-fi, but the implications of religion and integration with a completely different world. It's one of the best shows that's no longer available to stream.

Unlike the others, Upload takes a more comedic sci-fi slant. Though it's not a traditional end of the world scenario, it's a story about what happens when the world ends for specific people. Before you die in this future world, you can decide to have your consciousness uploaded to an afterlife community, like a retirement home for the dearly departed. But the system has become heavily monetized as corporations fight to sell their communities as the best, or most affordable. While there, people in their host bodies are inundated with virtual purchase options, their guilty living relatives compelled to buy more credits to show their love by ensuring their dead relatives are able to "live" in comfort.

At the heart of Upload is the story of life and philosophical questions about its finality. Nathan Brown (Robbie Amell) is uploaded by his wealthy girlfriend before he dies from injuries sustained in a car crash. Now, he's forever tied to her purse strings. Heavy on sci-fi, we see humans communicating with the dead through VR headsets and holograms. The story grows to explore how humanity has been able to make this happen and the societal and greed-fueled implications of those who stand to benefit. Upload is a charming, sweet show. It's one of the best Prime Video shows everyone has been sleeping on.

There are few things I enjoy more than settling in for a good soapy period drama, preferably one involving extravagant gowns, vicious social maneuvering, forbidden romances and people getting spectacularly worked up over who gets invited to dinner. So of course, I'm a big fan of “The Gilded Age.” Four seasons in, I'm still thoroughly invested. I've been looking forward to this new chapter for months, and I'm happy to report that HBO's lavish historical drama has delivered another delicious helping of everything I love about it.

Verdict: “The Gilded Age” season 4 is another lavish, deliciously soapy treat, with juicy new conflicts and a terrific ensemble that makes even the smallest social squabbles entertaining. A few storylines stumble, but I'm still more than happy to spend another season among New York's most extravagantly dressed troublemakers.

Release schedule: Episode 1 on Sunday, Nov. 1 at 9 p.m. ET

The new season picks up several months after the events of season 3, with the usual assortment of New York's elite navigating romance, family squabbles, and the delicate business of maintaining their social standing. Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon) and George (Morgan Spector) are facing serious marital difficulties, while their daughter Gladys (Taissa Farmiga) is preparing for motherhood in England.

Across the street, Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) is adjusting to a household where she no longer calls all the shots; Peggy Scott (Denée Benton) is balancing her writing ambitions with her relationship with Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica); and Marian (Louisa Jacobson) and Larry Russell (Harry Richardson) remain frustratingly complicated.

There's plenty happening across these interconnected households, and while some storylines are more compelling than others, season 4 finds the show giving its best characters fresh reasons to scheme, spar, and occasionally make me want to yell at the television. I've seen all eight episodes, but I promise not to reveal too much, as this is a show's plot turns are best enjoyed weekly.

Warning: Light spoilers ahead (not much beyond the trailer)

Kelly most recently reviewed "Nobody Wants This" season 3 and "The Diplomat" season 4."

One of the things I've always loved about “The Gilded Age” is its ability to make seemingly trivial matters feel enormously consequential. A dinner invitation can become a declaration of war.

Season 4 also introduces some genuinely compelling stakes, particularly for the Russell family. I've always enjoyed watching Bertha and George operate as an unstoppable power couple, with her social ambition and his business acumen making them practically invincible. So, seeing them at odds is painful. At the same time, I have to admit that their relationship was in danger of becoming a little too perfect. Now, with their marriage under strain, both have to reckon with what happens when their greatest ally becomes their biggest obstacle.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Coon remains an absolute force as Bertha, who is accustomed to getting what she wants and isn't particularly good at taking no for an answer. Spector gets some terrific material, too, as George grapples with the consequences of getting shot and mounting professional pressures. Their chemistry remains one of the show's biggest assets, and I desperately want these two crazy kids to work things out. But I'm also enjoying the fact that the show isn't making it easy for them.

Meanwhile, Agnes has her own ambitions to pursue, setting up a delicious clash of wills as she and Bertha vie for the opportunity to host President Grover Cleveland (guest star Jim Gaffigan). Baranski is always a treat, particularly when Agnes has a reason to be indignant and mouth off. Seeing these two formidable women competing for the same prize is exactly the sort of society skirmish I break out the popcorn for.

One of the best facets of “The Gilded Age” is its exploration of the world of upper-class Black Americans, and season 4 blessedly gives us more of that. Peggy's growing success as a writer brings new complications as she navigates her upcoming marriage to William and the expectations of his family, particularly his mother, Elizabeth Kirkland Phylicia Rashad), who would make everyone in the r/JustNoMIL subreddit quake. Rashad is simply divine in the role, and I relish seeing her face off against both Peggy and Peggy's mother, Dorothy (Audra McDonald).

Then there's Oscar van Rhijn (Blake Ritson) and Enid Winterton (Kelley Curran), whose unconventional partnership is quickly becoming a favorite storyline. The two make a formidable team, and I love watching them scheme their way toward greater influence in New York society. They're a bona fide power couple in the making; long may their unholy alliance reign.

The show also continues to get plenty of mileage out of the household dynamics between Agnes and Ada (Cynthia Nixon). Baranski and Nixon are such a wonderfully entertaining pairing that I could watch them bicker over curtains for an entire episode. Even the lighter storylines involving the servants and their increasingly complicated lives add to the show's rich ensemble feel. Not every subplot lands with equal force, but there's rarely a dull moment.

My biggest frustration remains Marian and Larry, whose romantic entanglement continues to test my patience. I understand that a TV romance needs obstacles, but at some point, the writers have to give these two a break. Their continued complications seem so contrived. Come on, already!

Still, I have few complaints about "The Gilded Age" season 4. The production design and costumes are a feast for the eyes. This is the kind of show where I want to pause every few minutes just to admire someone's dress or the sheer extravagance of a dinner table. The performances are equally strong, with Coon, Baranski, Benton and Rashad among the standouts.

What I appreciate most is that “The Gilded Age” knows exactly what it is. It can explore serious subjects like race and women's independence while also giving us extravagant parties, romantic scandals and enough high-society backstabbing to fill several lifetimes. Sometimes I want challenging prestige television; other times, I just want to watch Christine Baranski deliver a devastating put-down in a spectacular hat. There's room for both. So, take a glass of champagne and enjoy.

Kelly is the managing editor of streaming for Tom’s Guide, so basically, she watches TV for a living. Previously, she was a freelance entertainment writer for Yahoo, Vulture, TV Guide and other outlets. When she’s not watching TV and movies for work, she’s watching them for fun, seeing live music, writing songs, knitting and gardening.

#3468. The Elder Scrolls: Valenwood Officially Releases This Month

After more than eight years of near silence, The Elder Scrolls 6 is finally beginning to show some serious signs of life. Bethesda first announced the long-awaited successor to Skyrim back in 2018, and while updates have been few and far between, a new report claims the sequel will officially be titled The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Although Bethesda has yet to confirm the name, an official announcement could arrive as early as November, coinciding with Skyrim's 15th anniversary.

Of course, one of The Elder Scrolls franchise's greatest strengths has always been its incredible world-building, with each new installment introducing players to another iconic region of Tamriel. From the snow-covered mountains of Skyrim and the volcanic landscapes of Morrowind to the Imperial heartland of Cyrodiil, these locations have become practically synonymous with Bethesda's legendary RPG series.

However, there are still plenty of fascinating regions deserving of more attention, which is largely why Sentinel rumors had been circulating, looking at the region of Hammerfell. However, ahead of TES6's launch, players can head to Valenwood, the sprawling forest homeland of the Wood Elves, in an exciting new release that will officially bring fans back to this beloved corner of Tamriel.

Fans looking to explore Valenwood before The Elder Scrolls 6 finally arrives have a great opportunity thanks to The Elder Scrolls: Betrayal of the Second Era, the officially licensed tabletop adventure game from Chip Theory Games. Its Valenwood expansion, which originally debuted alongside the base game in 2025, is once again available for preorder through Zatu Games for approximately $43, launching later this month.

For those unfamiliar, Betrayal of the Second Era (or BOTSE) is a cooperative strategy game for one to four players, taking place during Tamriel's tumultuous Second Era. Players create their own adventurers, join guilds, explore different provinces, complete quests, and battle enemies across three connected sessions. Character progression is a major component, with players spending experience points to develop unique abilities and prepare for increasingly difficult encounters.

The Valenwood expansion introduces the homeland of the Bosmer, better known as the Wood Elves, with an entirely new map, quests, encounters, enemies, and equipment. Its storyline explores the disappearance of Falinesti, tensions involving independent Wood Orc tribes, and the growing influence of the mysterious Deslandra.

Players can also access three additional classes, including Arcanist, Burglar, and Ranger, alongside the Illusion, Legerdemain, and Light Armor skill lines. The expansion contains new skill dice, enemy chips, encounter cards, and a detailed regional gazetteer. However, Valenwood isn't the only exciting addition to BOTSE. Chip Theory Games has five major expansions in its latest wave, with fulfillment expected to begin in November 2026.

Two of these introduce additional regions: Summerset, featuring the Mage and Assassin classes alongside unpredictable magical anomalies, and Elsweyr, which explores the Khajiit homeland and introduces Thieves, Berserkers, and a dragon that can pursue adventurers across the map.

Meanwhile, Heroes of Tamriel expands character customization with Warriors, Witchhunters, and new combat skills. Fur and Fang introduces werewolf and vampire abilities, while Shadows of Oblivion brings five Daedric Princes into the adventure, each offering unique blessings and curses.

Additional accessories and character packs are also available for preorder. With so much new content arriving, Betrayal of the Second Era is giving The Elder Scrolls fans plenty of ways to return to Tamriel while Bethesda continues developing its next major RPG.

#3467. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.
