#3465. I tested the Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential Mattress and it delivered plenty of cushioning for side sleepers — but here's who should steer clear

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The CopperFlex Essential is Brooklyn Bedding's most affordable adult mattress, with a 10" model regularly priced under $600 for a queen. I found its pressure relief excellent for side sleeping, with no pressure whatsoever mounting in my shoulders and hips. Stomach sleepers will need something firmer for more back support, and hot sleepers should look elsewhere for effective cooling. However, couples will detect minimal motion transfer from a restless co-sleeper, and strong edges mean you'll sleep securely. Sure, there are much cheaper mattresses out there that offer better value for money, but the CopperFlex Essential is still worth considering if you're a side sleeper looking for a super-comfortable mid-market bed.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

We conduct seven robust tests in our lab to capture objective data on the four areas of a mattress that most affect your sleep comfort: pressure relief, temperature regulation, motion isolation and edge support. We also sleep on a mattress for at least three weeks before subjectively rating it. This data is fed into a scoring system, along with feedback captured by our testing panel, to create an overall score. Read our full mattress methodology.

When Brooklyn Bedding's most affordable mattress, the Dreamfoam Essential, was discontinued, it was swiftly replaced by the CopperFlex Essential Mattress. While both models sport a navy-and-grey appearance, come in multiple height options, and are marketed as entry-level, affordable beds, there is one key difference: the addition of copper-infused gel.

With the addition of copper-infused memory foam, the CopperFlex Essential dovetails into Brooklyn Bedding's CopperFlex collection, a cooling line-up of beds that includes the CopperFlex Pro Hybrid Mattress (which rivals some of the year's best mattresses thanks to its luxurious comfort). The CopperFlex Essential is also a mid-range bed, but at the lower end of the spectrum, usually sold for under $600 in a queen.

But while the CopperFlex Essential, like the Dreamfoam, is billed as a budget-friendly, no-frills alternative to the brand's more premium beds, its price still isn't low enough to fit into the budget tier.

So, when compared with the best cheap mattresses out there, including the Siena Signature Mattress and the SweetNight CoolNest Mattress, does the CopperFlex Essential offer good value for money? And does its addition of cooling copper gel mean it's the right fit for hot sleepers?

To find out, we vigorously tested a full-sized 10" CopperFlex Essential Mattress in our sleep lab and slept on it at home for three weeks. Here are our honest thoughts...

It's easy to tell when you're getting a good deal at Brooklyn Bedding, as the Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales are split into two discounts: a regular 25% discount and a holiday-related 30% off sale. If you see a 25% discount on the CopperFlex Essential, then you're looking at the standard price (it's never sold at MSRP).

If there's a 30% off sale, however, then that means you're getting a fantastic discount. This 30% discount typically coincides with the biggest holidays and sale events, including the Black Friday mattress sales, the Cyber Monday mattress sales, and the Presidents' Day mattress sales. This is brand's biggest price drop, and the only time it's ever been topped was a 32% discount during the Labor Day mattress sales in fall 2025.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

So, how much is the CopperFlex Essential when these discounts are applied? The price of the CopperFlex Essential varies depending on the height you choose. For the 10" model (which is the model I tested for this review), a queen size is $699 at MSRP and $524.25 with the regular 25% off deal. During 30% off sale, a queen-sized 10" CopperFlex Essential drops down to $489.30.

We define a "budget" or "cheap" mattress as one that's regularly under $400 in a queen, which means that the CopperFlex Essential isn't in the budget price tier (despite being marketed as a budget-friendly option). Instead, it sits in the lower mid-range price tier, along with mattresses such as the Nectar Classic and Bear Original.

The CopperFlex Essential is also a cheaper alternative to mattresses found at the more expensive end of the mid-range tier, such as the Nectar Premier and the Leesa Original (both typically $999 for a queen).

That said, there are plenty of mattresses out there with a similar, if not better, construction. The top-rated 10" Siena Signature Memory Foam Mattress, now $329 in a queen at Siena Sleep is a prime example, as is the cooling 12" CoolNest Memory Foam Mattress, which is regularly $399.99 in a queen at SweetNight.

However, one department where the CopperFlex Essential stands out is its generous benefits, including a free shipping, a 365-night sleep trial, and a lifetime warranty. The only downside is that returns come with a fee of $99.

Thanks to a regular 25% off sale, a queen 10" CopperFlex Essential is always under $600. However, 30% discounts during the biggest mattress sales of the year take a queen 10" model down to $489.30. Whether you buy it for 25% off or 30%, you always get generous benefits, including a 365-night sleep trial and a lifetime warranty (shame about the returns fee, though).

The design of the CopperFlex Essential varies (but not hugely) depending on the height option you choose, with the shortest height (6") containing only two layers with the thicker models (12" and 14") contain four layers.

While the 6" and 8" models are the cheapest, they are not thick enough for most adult sleepers and should only be used as a temporary bed (such as for guests, RVs, and growing children). That's why I opted to test the 10" model, as mattress thickness should be at least 10" to support most adults and sleep styles.

However, all height options have a fiberglass-free all-foam build that features a "Nano Stain Terminator Protector" cover (which safeguards against stains and spills) and a top layer of memory foam infused with antimicrobial copper.

The 10" model I tested features a 1" comfort layer of copper-infused memory foam on top and a durable 5" base layer for stabilizing support at the bottom. In between the comfort and base layer, a 4" transition layer acts as a buffer between the softer and firmer materials for balanced support.

For full context, I'm a side and back sleeper weighing under 130lbs, so I need a mattress that's supportive but has enough softness to soothe my side-sleeper pressure points (namely, my hips and shoulders).

The CopperFlex Essential is not the first all-foam mattress I've tested, as I've also written full reviews for the EGOHOME Black 12" Memory Foam Mattress and the SweetNight CoolNest Memory Foam Mattress. Both impressed me with their body-contouring comfort and support, but the former did trap some body heat (which is far from atypical for all-foam beds).

So, on the one hand, I was looking forward to testing a memory foam bed, as I know they can make the best mattresses for side sleepers, but I also didn't want to put up with any heat build-up (the testing period coincided with an unseasonably warm fall).

While the CopperFlex Essential didn't deliver the cooling prowess of the SweetNight CoolNest or the universal support of the EGOHOME Black, it still kept this side sleeper comfortable.

Let's see why I recommend the CopperFlex Essential to side sleepers and how it scored in other areas...

Temperature regulation refers to how well a mattress maintains a comfortable sleep temperature and prevents body heat retention. It's a key testing area, as a mattress that doesn't regulate temperature well can lead to night sweats and 3 a.m. wake ups.

While the best cooling mattresses feature top-of-line cooling tech to regulate temperature, most conventional mattresses today feature some degree of thermal regulation.

The CopperFlex Essential is definitely not a dedicated cooling model (and it isn't marketed as one), and the only form of temperature regulation it has is the addition of heat-dispersing copper. That being said, the Siena Signature features very little cooling materials (just a breathable cover) and it performed incredibly well in our temperature tests.

To test how well the CopperFlex Essential regulates temperature, we used a thermal imaging camera to measure how much of my body heat the mattress absorbs and dissipates. To do this I laid on the CopperFlex mattress for 15 minutes while the temperature of the bed was recorded every minute using a thermal imaging camera.

At its hottest point, we observed a maximum temperature increase (MTI) of 11.1°F — that means it was over 11.1°F warmer than before I laid down on the mattress. We generally rate an MTI over 9°F as "poor" and a 1 out of 5. This result was unsurprising, as the CopperFlex Essential isn't a cooling mattress.

That said, the all-foam Siena Signature had an MTI of 9.8°F, despite possessing no specialist cooling materials. Meanwhile, the mid-range all-foam Nectar Premier had an MTI of 8.1 9°F.

I also know from testing the SweetNight CoolNest (which is a dedicated cooling model) that MTI isn't always the best indicator of cooling ability. Despite being a cooling mattress, the CoolNest actually had a much higher MTI of 15.2°F, but redeemed itself through an ultra-fast cooling rate (CR)

The CR refers to how well a mattress dissipates heat during the first five minutes after the MTI. In the CopperFlex's case, the bed shed my body heat at a rate of 1.32°F per minute, a rapid cooling rate considered to "best in class".

The lower the maximum temperature increase (MTI) and the faster the cooling rate, the cooler you'll sleep.

It wasn't the fastest cooling rate displayed by a memory foam mattress (that distinction goes to the SweetNight CoolNest and the Siena Signature, which had a rapid cooling rate of 1.52°F per minute), but it's still relatively fast when you consider that the Nectar Premier dissipated heat at 0.9°F per minute.

15 minutes after I left the mattress, the CopperFlex Essential still hadn't returned to its baseline temperature. However, I should point out that none of its all-foam rivals did either.

In fact, when comparing the way the CopperFlex regulates heat versus its rivals, I was struck by how similarly it performed to the Leesa Original Mattress (usually between $999 and $1,100 for a queen). Both had an MTI of just over 11°F and had an identical rapid cooling rate 1.32°F per minute, which was surprising as Leesa refers to the Original as a "cooling memory foam mattress".

Based on the thermal imaging camera tests alone, we awarded the CopperFlex Essential an objective temperature control score of 3.8 out of 5.

How effectively the CopperFlex Essential absorbed, managed and dissipated heat compared to its closest rivals

In addition to the objective thermal imaging camera tests, we also conduct subjective tests to see how I (and the wider testing panel) perceive the mattress's sleep temperature.

Our subjective feedback was slightly lower than the objective results, with our testing panel awarding a score of 3 out of 5. This score means the mattress offers generally good thermal comfort, but felt mostly neutral with some heat build-up.

I slept on the CopperFlex Essential for three weeks during an unseasonably warm fall in a bedroom with no AC, and while I wouldn't say I overheated or experienced night sweats, I did feel some patches of heat build-up every now and again. I never experienced this while testing the SweetNight CoolNest during the sweltering summer months.

When you're sleeping on a mattress, certain body parts will come into contact with its surface, creating pressure. These body parts are known as pressure points (for example, pressure points when side sleeping include the hips and shoulders), and the way a mattress cushions and supports these pressure points is known as pressure relief.

While each height option comes with a different feel — mattress thickness as a big impact on firmness — Brooklyn Bedding recommends the 10" version I tested to combination back, side, and stomach sleepers.

During our subjective tests, my fellow testers and I agreed that the CopperFlex suits side sleeping the most, as it cushions the hips and shoulders. We also think it could suit some back sleepers, too, even if it doesn't offer the best lumbar support.

I felt I was the ideal candidate to test the mattress, as I'm a combo side and back sleeper. From the first night, I felt ample cushioning when sleeping on my side, especially in the shoulder region. In fact, I found the CopperFlex to be one of the softest mattresses I've ever tested — and I've tested the ultra-plush Helix Sunset Luxe.

Do I think it's one of the best mattresses for back sleepers? No, but I still felt supported when sleeping on my back, and I didn't wake up with lower back pain. Overall, if you're a side sleeper, or predominantly a side sleeper who also sleeps on your back from time to time, then I recommend the CopperFlex Essential.

The deeper the indentation and faster the response time, the better the ability of a mattress to relieve pressure

A mentioned above, Brooklyn Bedding also recommends the CopperFlex Essential to stomach sleepers. For stomach-sleeping tester Ruth Jones, the CopperFlex Essential did cause some lower back strain when lying on her front, and she warned that back sleepers could feel some lower back pressure.

"When back sleeping, I could feel strain on my core," Jones told me.

However, she agreed that its gentle contouring makes the CopperFlex Essential a top pick for side sleepers.

"Side sleeping was far and away the most comfortable position to lie in," she said. "I wasn’t expecting this as the mattress didn’t initially appear to have much contouring but it was soft at the shoulders and hips which meant no pressure build up."

Thanks to its comfort for side sleepers, we awarded the CopperFlex a subjective pressure relief score of 4 out of 5 ("Very Good").

We also performed objective pressure relief tests using a 25kg weight. We placed the weight at the hip and shoulder areas of the mattress, and then measured how deep the weight sank and how quickly the mattress bounced back when the weight was removed.

The CopperFlex had an average Indentation Depth (ID) of 3.6" and Recovery Time (RT), of 2.25 seconds, achieving an objective pressure relief score of 3.4 out of 5, which is a "Good" objective final rating. The weight test results indicate that the CopperFlex is a responsive bed (I agree, as I found it easy to move around on) but I was surprised that the weights didn't sink further on what I perceive as a cushioning bed.

Even more surprising is that Siena Memory Foam had a higher ID of 3.63", despite being a firm bed that is recommended to anyone but side sleepers. The CopperFlex's RT, on the other hand, was one of the quickest. A quick RT is especially important in a memory foam mattress, as they can be notorious for their "quicksand" sinkage.

Combining subjective and objective feedback, we awarded the CopperFlex Essential's pressure relief a score of 3.76 out of 5, indicating a "Strong Performance".

We rate a mattress's firmness on a standardized scale of one to 10, with 10 being the firmest and 1 being the softest. We don't use any objective tests to measure firmness, as this key area is highly subjective and is dependent on body weight, sleep position, and personal preference.

To get a good idea of the CopperFlex's firmness level, I asked each member of our diverse testing panel to rank the firmness of the CoolNest on a scale of one to 10. I then created a collective rating based on everyone's feedback.

The Brooklyn Bedding calls the firmness of the CopperFlex Essential "medium-firm", which indicates a score of 6-7 out of 10 on the standardized scale. As a team, we mostly agreed with the brand's rating, and awarded the CopperFlex Essential a 6 out of 10 on the firmness scale.

Motion isolation refers to a mattress's ability to prevent a co-sleeper's movements from traveling to your side of the bed and waking you up. Its especially important for couples, co-sleeping families, and anyone who shares a bed with their pets.

Memory foam mattresses tend to be better at absorbing motion than other mattress types, such as innerspring and hybrid mattresses, as they contain dense, slow-moving foams and no springs or coils.

To see how well the CopperFlex Essential isolates motion, we conducted an objective slam ball test and a subjective co-sleeper test.

In our subjective tests, my fellow testers and I evaluated the impact of each other's movements by manually performing motions classed as low, moderate and high force to replicate real-life co-sleeping scenarios.

The faster the decay rate, the better the mattress is at reducing motion transfer (which means you'll be disturbed less by a restless co-sleeper)

During the subjective tests, I felt the high-force movements of my fellow tester, but I would not say the high-force movements were as disruptive as they've been on other mattresses I’ve tested.

My fellow testers were also impressed with the perceived motion isolation, with one panelist saying they could hardly feel the low-force movements. "There was some small motion transfer when the tester moved but I would have slept right through it and it wouldn’t have bothered me as I was falling asleep," they said.

Overall, the CopperFlex Essential earned a subjective score of 3.75 out of 5 for motion isolation.

For for our objective lab-based tests, we dropped a 5kg slam ball on one side of the CopperFlex Essential and measured its impact absorption via an accelerometer on the other. The initial impact average (IIA) was 14.569, which is relatively high when compared to Siena's IIA of 5.527 m/s2 and the Nectar Premier's IIA of 7.961.

However, the CopperFlex Essential redeemed itself with a short decay rate (MDS). So, while the IIA was sizeable, its motion transfer only lasted for 1.72 seconds on average. While not as quick as the Leesa Original's 1.116 second MDS, it still shows that the CopperFlex is adept at deadening the slam ball's motion.

Overall, we rate the CopperFlex's motion isolation as "Strong", with an overall motion isolation score of 3.5. This means that, while you'll feel more moderate and high-force movements, they won't last long enough to cause too much disruption.

Edge support refers to how sturdy the edges of your mattress are, with strong edge support indicating that the sides and foot of the bed will make you feel supported when sitting, sleeping, or getting in and out of bed.

To test the CopperFlex's edge support, we placed a 25kg weight 3" away from the edge of the mattress and measured how far it sank.

After five minutes, the average indentation of the weight was 5.25", which we rate as "strong." The sinkage at the foot of the bed was a little deeper than at the sides of the bed, but we should point out that the edge support at the foot of the bed will only affect sitting rather than sleeping.

To measure the available sleep space, we also performed a roll-off test. For this, our reviewer lies near the edge of the bed and another tester records how close they get to the edge before they feel unstable and are going to roll off. The CopperFlex Essential has a roll-off distance (ROD) of 0.5", a measurement which gets a score of 5 out of 5 as it indicates that most of the mattress can be used for sleeping.

Combing the weight and roll-off test scores, the overall edge support score of the CopperFlex Essential is 4 out of 5, which we rate as "Very Good".

Less compression means better support for sleeping close to the edge or climbing in and out of bed

On the brand's website, the CopperFlex Essential has an overall user score of 4.6 out of 5 from over 800 reviews, which is a pretty glowing score.

Five-star reviews praise how comfortable the mattress is, which many customers buying it for their RVs (it's one of the rare mattress that come in a range of RV sizes). As for negative reviews (which are in the minority) customers criticize the mattress for not being as firm as they expected.

In terms of Brooklyn Bedding's trustworthiness, you can look on review platform TrustPilot website for customer feedback. At the time of writing, the brand has an overall "Excellent" rating of 4.6 out of 5 stars from a total of 210 reviews.

Let me start by saying that there are cheaper memory foam mattress out there that offer better value for money than the CopperFlex Essential. That being said, I would definitely recommend this body-contouring mattress to a certain group: side sleepers.

The CopperFlex Essential's pressure relief, is a standout feature that makes this all-foam bed a top pick for anyone who sleeps on their side.

I tend to perceive mattresses as being firmer than my fellow testers do, and I often require good mattress break-in period to feel comfortable. However, I felt well-cushioned from night one on the CopperFlex Essential, and felt zero pressure build up in my shoulders.

Edge support is good, too, and I always felt secure even when sleeping close to the edge. For couples, motion transfer from a restless partner shouldn't be an issue, and the sleep temperature should remain neutral enough for the average person.

That said, hot sleepers will need to look at a model with more cooling ability, such as the SweetNight CoolNest or the Siena Siena Signature, which are both cheaper than the lower mid-range CopperFlex Essential. I wouldn't recommend this soft mattress to stomach sleepers wither, as the lack of firmness won't keep their hips and lower back supported.

However, I do think this is a mid-range mattress worth considering if you're a side sleeper looking for a mid-market bed for your home, guest room, or even your RV.

Like the CopperFlex Essential, the EGOHOME Black 12" Memory Foam Mattress is a conventional all-foam bed designed for medium-firm comfort. However, I found it to be much more supportive than the CopperFlex Essential, and I slept comfortably on it in all sleep positions. Plus, it's always under $400 for a queen.

If you're looking for an affordable memory foam bed, but the CoolNest seems a little too soft for your sleep position, check out the Siena Memory Foam Mattress as a firmer (and cheaper) alternative. It also regulates temperature surprisingly well, but side sleepers will find it way too hard.

If you want something that sleeps cooler than the CopperFlex, check out this cooling model from SweetNight. The SweetNight CoolNest is one of those rare budget mattresses (always under $400 for a queen) equipped with specialist cooling tech.

Frances Daniels is a PPA-accredited journalist and Sleep Staff Writer at Tom's Guide with an MA in Magazine Journalism from Cardiff University. Her role includes covering mattress and sleep news and writing sleep product reviews and buyer's guides, including our Best Hybrid Mattress 2025 guide. She is interested in the relationship between sleep and health, interviewing an array of experts to create in-depth articles about topics such as nutrition, sleep disorders, sleep hygiene, and mattress care. She is also our specialist on mattress toppers — producing bed topper reviews and taking care of our Best Mattress Toppers 2025 guide — and leads content relating to fiberglass-free beds for a non-toxic sleep. #3464. All-new MacBook Pro brings back beloved design feature from the past

Apple unveiled its MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR today, and the all-new model features the return of a beloved design feature: a glowing Apple logo on the lid.

One of the MacBook’s most iconic design features in the past was its glowing Apple logo on the lid.

Among a sea of other laptops in coffee shops and offices around the world, the glowing Apple logo made the MacBook stand out.

But Apple started phasing out the illuminated logo in 2015 with its 12-inch MacBook. The non-glowing logo then spread to redesigns of the MacBook Pro and MacBook Air in the years that followed.

Today though, the glowing Apple logo returns with the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display,

Here’s a hands-on look via 9to5Mac’s Chance Miller:

Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro 🤩 pic.twitter.com/EmBFQTJ6ob

It’s just one of the many changes with the all-new MacBook Pro, but it’s a significant one for longtime Apple users.

For a lot of users, the glowing logo represents a fond, nostalgic period in Mac computing.

CEO John Ternus clearly knew this, as he teased the new feature in a video this morning.

This is literally the best and most exciting feature of the new MBP

Its reintroduction in the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is a good sign that the illuminated logo could start spreading to other models in the future. Though it won’t happen right away, Apple is likely to bring back the glowing logo on redesigns of its other models in the years ahead.

Read more: MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR vs MacBook Pro: Here’s every difference

#3463. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3462. Goodbye 'Ocean's Eleven,' Ben Affleck's Heist Thriller Is Now Officially Streaming

A holiday-themed heist thriller released in 2000 that never found an audience, didn't even make back its budget, and was savaged by both critics and one of its own stars, Reindeer Games has fallen largely into obscurity. Still, the star-powered oddity is due a re-evaluation, and that's for two reasons: It's strange enough that you have to see it to believe it, and it was helmed by legendary director John Frankenheimer. And one thing Frankenheimer has never done is phone it in.

Ben Affleck and Charlize Theron head up the film's cast, with Affleck playing an ex-con named (yes) Rudy impersonating a man named (also, yes) Nick. There's snow, ice and Santa suits aplenty amid the borderline nonsensical twists and gunfire, but the man who once directed The Manchurian Candidate and Seven Days in May plays it straight all the way through. For the curious, the Christmas heist film no one really needed is now streaming on Paramount+, after long being only available as a rental — and it's a lot more fun than you'd expect.

Written by Hollywood veteran Ehren Kruger, whose credits run the gamut from several Transformers films to Top Gun Maverick, the story for Reindeer Games seems almost deliberately hard to follow. To keep things simple: Affleck plays Rudy, an ex-con who, upon his release from prison, impersonates his dead cellmate Nick and shacks up with Ashley (Theron), the dead man's pen pal girlfriend, who has never met him in real life. Ashley's got a brother, though, played by a terrifically villainous Gary Sinise, and he wants "Nick" to help him rob a casino, run by the incomparable Dennis Farina.

A series of double and triple-crosses follow, as well as a shootout on a frozen lake, a sex scene between Affleck and Theron that reportedly had to be cut to get an R-rating, and eventually, for some reason, everyone ends up wearing Santa suits. The film is also packed to the gills with brief appearances by actors like Danny Trejo, Isaac Hayes, and even Ron Jeremy. It's frankly a mess that works best if you let it just wash over you — and likely wash it down with a few cocktails.

Theron herself even admitted in a later interview that the whole thing was a bit of a disaster, saying: "That was a bad, bad, bad movie. But even though the movie might suck, I got to work with John Frankenheimer. I wasn't lying to myself — that's why I did it. I mean, he directed The Manchurian Candidate, which is like the movie of all movies. Fuck regret. Just fuck it."

Affleck's movie sees a mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped.

That's a hard question to answer but, depending on your tolerance for lackadaisical performances and nonsense plotting, it could well be yes. Frankenheimer brought the world The Manchurian Candidate and the action-thriller classic Ronin, which features one of the greatest car chases of all time, and he doesn't slouch behind the camera here, no matter how ridiculous the material. Reindeer Games clearly takes delight in its ludicrous number of plot twists, excessive violence, and groan-worthy Christmas references. And Frankenheimer manages to pack in some booming, bloody, and impactful gunplay that keeps things moving at a crisp pace. He also later admitted that he wanted the film to be even racier and more violent, having been made to cut over 20 minutes by the MPAA.

Notably, Frankenheimer was also unapologetic about the sheer number of twists in the film, later saying that he would have liked the story to have been even thornier. In an interview, he said: “Let’s get a reality check here. Today’s audience may not be confused by how fast a film like Reindeer Games moves, but the intellectual level of the person watching this movie is not nearly what it was for the person watching The Manchurian Candidate.”

Even in its compromised form and with its cringe-worthy holiday nods, Reindeer Games is the kind of nasty, unapologetic Hollywood failure we rarely get anymore.

#3461. Alien Meets Interstellar In Netflix's 8-Part Lovecraftian Sci-Fi Series

While a blend of Alien and Interstellar might sound tough to pull off, one Netflix series managed this mix admirably. The scope and scale of a sci-fi story can often end up defining its tone. Even though both Ridley Scott’s Alien and Blade Runner are technically dystopian thrillers where major characters are revealed to be uncannily human-like robots during the narrative, the two movies could not feel more different.

The sprawling cityscape of Blade Runner makes Scott’s adaptation of the seminal Philip K. Dick novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep feel massive and overwhelming. The movie’s setting is a dark, anonymous, rain-drenched city, one that calls to mind the lonely post-human setting of author William Gibson’s iconic cyberpunk novel Neuromancer. In stark contrast, Alien takes place almost entirely on the Nostromo, and the claustrophobic setting makes the movie feel more like a slasher set in space than an immersive, futuristic saga like Blade Runner.

Blade Runner offers viewers an absorbing city to get lost in, while Alien offers the audience a setting so small that it leaves nowhere to hide. Right in between these two extremes is director Christopher Nolan’s 2014 blockbuster Interstellar. While the stakes of its story are existential, the setting is fairly small, with much of the movie taking place on a lone spaceship. Netflix’s underrated sci-fi series The Silent Sea managed to take the high stakes of Interstellar’s story and reintroduce some of the claustrophobic horror of Alien to the mix.

Released in 2021, The Silent Sea follows a crew of astronauts to the Moon’s Sea of Tranquility. The group is trying to retrieve the samples that were left behind at Balhae Station, an abandoned research facility five years earlier, since a dried up earth needs access to water by any means. Of course, the sister of the lead researcher, Doctor Song Ji-an, was one of the researchers who mysteriously disappeared from Balhae Station, so the mission is more than a little personal.

Across The Silent Sea’s eight episodes, the mystery of what happened at Balhae Station, and why the government covered it up and sent another crew to the abandoned site, comes to light. While the basic setup might remind viewers of shows like Stargate and Firefly, thanks to the tight-knit spaceship crews and their high-risk missions, The Silent Sea instead starts out feeling like Interstellar and gradually grows more similar to Alien.

Initially, viewers and Doctor Song Ji-an alike are worried about the Earth’s desertification, so the biggest concern is ensuring that the crew obtains the all-important samples from the abandoned site. At this stage, The Silent Sea still feels like The Martian, Gravity, or even the real-life storyline of Apollo 13. It is only when the crew learns the truth about Balhae Station that things take a turn into another genre.

Much like The Descent is a survival thriller about a caving mishap until suddenly it isn’t anymore, The Silent Sea has a few big twists that radically change the show’s genre and tone. Fortunately, unlike HBO’s similarly ambitious sci-fi series Westworld, these twists never feel jarring or explained.

Instead, the further the crew explore the eerie empty research facility, the clearer it becomes that viewers are watching a body horror/creature feature, rather than just a space exploration story. This was a great choice on the part of the creators, since there was a deluge of similar space exploration shows arriving around the same era.

The Silent Sea needed to stand out in a crowded marketplace, as Apple TV’s alternate history series For All Mankind and its spinoff show Star City, the Star Wars spinoff Andor, and Netflix’s ambitious sci-fi anthology Love, Death, & Robots all explored similar settings. Luckily, The Silent Sea’s blend of Alien's claustrophobic horror and Interstellar’s stakes makes the show a must-watch.

#3458. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

#3457. Ternus addresses Apple breaking touchscreen Mac taboo: ‘Who knew?’

In an interview with WIRED, Apple executives including CEO John Ternus, hardware chief Johny Srouji, and marketing chief Greg “Joz” Joswiak discussed the company’s decision to bring touch to the Mac. Here are the details.

For years, online commenters countered rumors of touchscreen Macs with quotes from Steve Jobs and other Apple executives, including Phil Schiller, arguing that touchscreens had no place on the Mac.

Shortly after Apple announced the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, journalist Steven Levy published an interview with Apple executives in WIRED discussing the company’s decision to reverse its longstanding stance on touchscreen Macs.

I ask if Apple is about to break a long-imposed taboo and introduce a Macintosh with a touch screen.

In the interview, Ternus notes that while indirect input through the trackpad and keyboard remains central to the Mac experience, “there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.”

He also stresses that Apple sees touch as an add-on, rather than a feature that should require compromises to the MacBook Pro’s design.

Throughout the interview, much of Apple’s reasoning for finally bringing touch to the Mac revolves around the fact that it reworked and developed several hardware and software components to make touch possible without compromising the Mac experience.

“We needed to get to a point where adding touch didn’t make the product lesser in any way. It didn’t make it heavier. It didn’t make it thicker. That came together with the OLED screen, the best display we’ve ever put into a Mac,” Ternus told me. “All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.”

As for Srouji, he argued that advances in technology over the past decade had finally made it possible for Apple to meet its standards for a touchscreen Mac.

Thank God the touch support is very basic and limited to specific situations, and there’s no redesign of macOS that would make it something like a hybrid device. I'm fine using it occasionally for very specific tasks, but the Mac should remain a touchpad/mouse device.

That included custom silicon, a redesigned thermal system to keep the display from feeling hot to the touch, and a reworked hinge to minimize screen wobble when users interact with it.

“Ten years is a very, very long time,” says Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer. “Many things have changed, whether it’s the display technology, the custom silicon, et cetera.” Eventually, he told me, the confluence of chips, display tech, and software architecture “met our bar.” “I like my engineers to be gated by physics, not imagination or timelines,” he says.

Joz, in turn, noted that part of Apple’s decision was driven by a new generation of touch-first users who expect to interact directly with their screens:

“Most pros own an iPad, and almost every pro owns an iPhone,” Joswiak says. “So this is something that they’re natural with. There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch.”

He added that professional users, including “engineers, scientists, software developers, and media creators,” had also been asking Apple to bring touch to the Mac.

The full interview also touches on (no pun intended) how Apple adapted macOS for touchscreen interactions, the new gestures for Dynamic Island, and whether touch might eventually make its way to other Macs. You can read it in full here.

#3456. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3455. The new MacBook Pro has everything I wanted, minus one thing

Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is an exciting upgrade that delivers nearly every feature I was hoping for, with just one exception.

I’ve been waiting a long time for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR. I haven’t used a Mac as my primary computer in years, but rumors about this new model made me think that might finally change.

The iPad Pro has been my main computer of choice since 2015, but lately I’ve grown increasingly curious about revisiting the Mac full-time.

This is largely due to Apple making the Mac, to me at least, a lot more exciting than it was in 2015. The Mac’s hardware and software are advancing in compelling new ways, and today’s new MacBook Pro brings an especially big leap.

As a longtime iPad Pro user, I’ve come to expect features like touch support and OLED in a relatively thin, lightweight device. I also love how iPadOS tends to advance in lockstep with iOS, a trend that has recently started extending to macOS too.

Until recently, it seemed like Apple’s latest and greatest tech—with the exception of pro-focused chips—has been in the iPad and iPhone.

I don’t need an extremely powerful chip, as my computing needs are pretty basic. But I do value having a great display, touch support, and modern OS features like the Dynamic Island.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR delivers those things. I’ve ordered one and can’t wait to give it a legitimate shot to be my full-time computer. But my biggest hesitation is the lack of cellular.

I use cellular all the time on my iPad Pro. I tend to work from coffee shops and random outdoor spots for at least a few hours every day. And in my experience, public Wi-Fi options aren’t reliable enough for my needs.

Having a persistent cellular connection on my iPad is a killer feature. I very much wish Apple provided the option of cellular on the MacBook Pro too.

I’m hoping that personal hotspot has become a lot more reliable since I last tried it. Apple does say its N1 wireless chip makes the feature better.

I’m very surprised that they didn’t include cellular. They can fit it in an Apple Watch, so why not a laptop computer? I think more buyers would want it than not want it. And given the price of the machine, nobody’s going to not buy it because it has a cellular modem that they’re not going to use.

I’ll stick with my MacBook Air and 13" iPad Pro.

Additionally, I wonder if the need for cellular will be mitigated some by having a tablet-sized iPhone Duo in my pocket soon. So if I need to stop in the middle of nowhere and get work done quickly, maybe the Duo will suffice.

In any case, the MacBook Pro looks like a fantastic product regardless. It’s not for everyone, and the high price hurts, but I’m excited to give it a try.

What are your thoughts on the new MacBook Pro? Would you use cellular if it was offered? Let us know in the comments.

#3454. The 8 Heaviest Gangster Movies of All Time, Ranked

Lots of gangster movies are heavy-going, obviously, but not all. Pulp Fiction has a couple of intense scenes, for example, but it’s not really a super heavy or depressing movie. And then you’ve got something like Scarface, which is very much a tragedy and has bad things happening to its main character (and most of the other characters, honestly), but the style and bombast there makes it all go down a little easier and honestly feel kind of fun.

As for the actually super downbeat movies about organized crime, that’s what you’ve got below. These are some of the darkest and heaviest gangster movies ever made, all of them going the extra mile to stress that whole notion of crime not paying, at the very least. Some of them go further and get more upsetting still, but usually with good reason. And, for what it’s worth, all of these depressing gangster movies are pretty great quality-wise, too.

Battles Without Honor and Humanity was a movie that kicked off the series of the same name, and it’s a yakuza movie more than it is a strict gangster movie, if you're a stickler for definitions, but the yakuza is a kind of criminal organization, so this movie counts. It’s also the best movie in its series, though all of them are pretty downbeat, chaotic, and unapologetically violent, all the while telling something of an overarching story, though it can be hard to keep up, by design.

Broadly speaking, there’s a complicated gang war being fought throughout this one, and a whole lot of people double-cross each other and end up dead. It’s a series of tense situations and sometimes violent ones, or sometimes a bit of both at the same time. Battles Without Honor and Humanity (1973) is a lot, and maybe even close to too much, but in a good (and admirable) way, for the most part. And it is absolutely downbeat and cynical, too.

Though he gained attention for making some later crime films (namely, Drive and, perhaps more infamously, Only God Forgives), Nicholas Winding Refn’s Pusher came first, and it’s a bit more straightforward. It’s still challenging, though, just in a different way, as while it’s about a criminal in a deadly situation following a deal that goes wrong (so, easy to follow), it’s got some rather intense violence and is undeniably gritty.

The extent to which that main character is in danger also makes things feel hectic and heavy, and if all that’s not enough, it’s the first part of a very heavy-going trilogy, too. Pusher does work wonders with what might sound like a slightly too lean premise and what seems like a pretty slim budget, though you do probably need a decently strong stomach to get through it in one piece.

Seeing the words “an Andrew Dominik film” should tip you off that you're in for a likely feel-bad time, since he was behind both Blonde and The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford, and so it’s not too surprising that him tackling the gangster genre with Killing Them Softly made for a pretty downbeat time. It is still an engaging film, and maybe even a slightly darkly funny one at times, but all of that is found alongside some serious nihilism, and also, no one in this film comes anywhere close to feeling morally sound.

It’s all very dark, gritty, and largely compelling, and while it’s entertaining to some extent, you're unlikely to come away from it with your spirits raised.

Narratively, Killing Them Softly is about the aftermath of a card game robbery that was supposed to be protected by the mob, so it being targeted has serious consequences, with Brad Pitt’s character being tasked with cleaning up the whole mess as best as possible. It’s all very dark, gritty, and largely compelling, and while it’s entertaining to some extent, you're unlikely to come away from it with your spirits raised, to say the least.

When breaking down the two fast-paced gangster epics Martin Scorsese directed in the 1990s, it’s safe to call them both – Goodfellas and Casino – quite brutal and relatively unromanticized, at least in some regards. But Goodfellas feels gentle if you're directly comparing it to Casino, since this 1995 film is far more cynical, it contains a good deal more explicit violence and language, and the characters are almost entirely without redeeming qualities. Concerning the last of those, some characters in Goodfellas do feel human and are at least a little endearing.

Well, okay, the characters in Casino are also human, with many based on – or inspired by – actual people, but they are meaner and crueler people than what you'll find in most gangster movies. It also doesn’t pull punches in showing Las Vegas as (at least for a time) a violent and totally corrupt city, all because the mob could run the place through owning so many casinos. Casino is pretty much three hours of betrayals, beatings, murders, arguments, threats, and robberies. It is relentless, but maybe it has to be.

Infernal Affairs is a Hong Kong gangster movie that has a premise you might be more familiar with thanks to The Departed being a remake. And sure, The Departed is plenty intense, and also fairly downbeat, but it does have a slightly neater ending than Infernal Affairs. It’s hard to elaborate without going further, but what can be said is that the story is the same either way: there are two people who’ve gone undercover, with one being a detective who’s undercover in a gang, and the other a gang member who’s gone undercover in the police force.

It’s all cat-and-mouse stuff, and it’s also the kind of story that can’t end well for everyone, though there’s a ton of suspense in anticipating whether it can end well for anyone. And if you know what’s coming, or if you think you know what’s coming (like, if you’ve seen The Departed first), it’s still great... just don't expect anything too uplifting here. To further compare it to The Departed, Infernal Affairs might be more straight to the point and perhaps faster-paced, too, for what that’s worth.

Once Upon a Time in America does what a lot of great epic movies do by feeling sprawling in some ways, but then it also manages to achieve a feeling of being quite personal and intimate in other regards. If you look at things chronologically, it’s about a group of young boys who grow up to be ruthless gangsters, making much of their money during the Prohibition era, and then at least one lives into old age, and he grapples with various memories of his violent past.

That’s simplifying things for sure, because Once Upon a Time in America does not play out chronologically, with the previously alluded-to old man looking back on his life, and these play out in a series of sometimes strange flashbacks… and then things get even more unusual – and even surreal – in the film’s “present.” All the while, Once Upon a Time in America works as a deconstruction of the whole gangster genre, so it’s deeply upsetting, oftentimes violent, and totally unafraid to have its main characters do numerous terrible things throughout.

When The Godfather (1972) ends, it’s definitely not happy, but it still feels lighter in comparison to The Godfather Part II. There was a good deal of murder and tragedy to be found in the first movie, sure, though it’s the sequel that bumps things up a notch in those regards, especially because the family side of the first film is on its way to being broken by that film’s end, and then you see the Corleone family (and crime empire) well and truly break down in The Godfather Part II.

It’s a downfall for Michael Corleone, mostly, and he suffers a sort of death in every regard but physical (since The Godfather Part III exists, so he kind of has to make it to there). The Godfather Part II is about him losing friends, family, and much by way of hope of becoming legitimate. The film also contrasts Michael’s downfall with his father’s rise in the past, so that adds another layer to things in terms of it being a tragedy and all.

While The Irishman isn't as violent as Casino, it is a more harrowing and overall sadder film, and you can use it to help make the argument that age has made Martin Scorsese a better filmmaker, in some ways, alongside being a more brutally honest one. Not that his earlier films were lacking those things either, yet if you look at Silence, The Irishman, and Killers of the Flower Moon… like, come on. They're all pretty despair-filled movies.

As a gangster movie, The Irishman is about as dark as things get, and the whole movie pushes things further than Once Upon a Time in America, looking at a person affiliated with the mob aging and looking back on the most violent and life-changing events from his past, usually with regret. All the characters either die suddenly (and usually gruesomely) or they live overlong ages and deal with losing everyone else. The final act of The Irishman is particularly concerned with such things, and it’s an absolute downer in ways that are hard to put into words.

#3453. Prime Video's 32-Episode Action Series Deserves Kudos For Successfully Adapting The Source Material

There is nothing inherently wrong with an adaptation changing its source material. After all, a different medium demands its own storytelling devices and liberties. However, many TV adaptations, especially in the action genre, usually take things a little too far. They embrace so much creative freedom that they almost become unrecognizable from their source material.

Fortunately, one of the best TV adaptations on Prime Video does not tread the same path. Based on Robert Kirkman's comic book series of the same name, Invincible is a rare adaptation that respects its source material while carefully improving its story for the small screen. The Prime Video action series is already four seasons in, and it seems to be showing no signs of slowing down.

Most book or comic book adaptations end up going completely off the rails after two seasons. Prime Video's Invincible, in contrast, has only grown from strength to strength with each new season. It still boasts a near-perfect Rotten Tomatoes score of 99% and sets a perfect example of how action comic books should be translated to the screen.

The Invincible comics' earlier volumes are driven by a slice-of-life superhero story. As a reader, it becomes impossible to suspect how dark it will eventually become until a major twist reveals Omni-Man's true nature. Prime Video's take on the comics does not take the same slow-burn approach. It throws all caution into the wind and immediately establishes high stakes by the end of episode 1.

This approach works incredibly well for the show because, in the streaming era, attention spans run low, and a series must find creative ways to instantly hook audiences.

Despite disclosing one of the best twists from the comics a lot earlier, Prime Video's Invincible does not compress its source material storyline. It only restructures it in a way that makes it seem more coherent and continuous. Even the subplots and fillers from the comics, including Cecil’s covert operations and the Flaxan invasions, are perfectly woven into the overarching storyline.

Even side characters from Invincible, like Debbie Grayson and Amber Bennett, get more expansive arcs in the series, making them seem more relatable than their comic book counterparts. Omin-Man is incredibly terrifying in the comics as well, but the show further elevates his menacing presence. The show achieves this by making him look more like a tragic anti-hero and adding more layers to his relationship with Debbie.

In terms of action, Ryan Ottley’s art does an incredible job of immersing readers into the comics gore and scale. The show perfectly translates this to the screen by borrowing the original art style and giving it a more visceral edge. Even action sequences, like the subway scene between Mark and Nolan, are extended in the show to reveal how brutal and destructive superhero showdowns can realistically be.

All these aspects are further elevated by Invincible's talented voice cast, which includes many big names like J.K. Simmons, Walton Goggins, Steven Yeun, and Sandra Oh, among others.

The original Invincible comics' author, Robert Kirkman, also serves as the Prime Video show's creator. It is hard not to see how the Prime Video superhero series benefits a lot from Kirkman's power of hindsight. Since Kirkman understands his work far better than anyone else, he also sees all the pacing missteps and narrative issues that originally marred the comics.

His ability to look back and revise his comics allows him to flesh out underused characters like William Clockwell and even subtly foreshadow some of the better story beats from the source material. Owing to this, even the show's deconstruction of superhero tropes seems far more progressive and well-thought-out in the series than the comics.

Invincible also refines the source material's black comedy, while bringing more realism to its coming-of-age themes. While the action series on Prime Video can also be incredibly gruesome, it perfectly balances its darker aspects with many wholesome story beats. This balance in tone further cements the show as one of the greatest adaptations of our time.

Based on the comic book character by Robert Kirkman, Invincible follows Mark Grayson,  a seventeen-year-old who leads a seemingly average life save for the fact that he lives behind the shadow of his superhero father, Omni-Man. Mark goes on to develop superhuman abilities, but he must also learn that his father's legacy isn't as glitzy and glamorous as he's been led to believe.

#3452. Apple fined $15.5 million as South Korea orders changes to App Store rules

Apple and Google were fined today in South Korea over their app payment practices, with regulators also ordering both companies to change several policies. Here are the details.

South Korea’s Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) announced today a series of fines and corrective orders against Apple and Google over violations of the country’s Telecommunications Business Act.

Specifically for Apple, the KMCC imposed a fine of 20.81 billion won (approximately $15.5 million) and ordered the company to revise its App Store policies regarding payment methods and app review procedures, as well as prevent what it referred to as “discriminatory commission” practices from recurring.

This is the first enforcement case under the 2021 amendment to the Telecommunications Business Act, which introduced prohibited acts for app market operators, such as forcing specific payment methods and unfairly delaying app reviews.

In essence, the decision centers around three violations: forcing specific payment methods, unfairly delaying app reviews, and imposing discriminatory commissions.

On the payment methods front, the KMCC said Apple and Google “effectively forced” developers to use their own in-app payment systems by imposing a 26% commission and additional restrictions on third-party alternatives.

“This constitutes an act in which an app market operator unfairly uses its position in transactions to force mobile content providers and others to use a specific payment method,” the KMCC said.

As a result, Apple and Google must revise their policies to allow external payment methods and address restrictions imposed on developers using alternative payment systems.

As for the app review process, the KMCC found that Apple and Google “delayed app reviews, for example by not providing specific reasons when reviews were delayed or not clearly responding to individual inquiries about the reasons for delays and expected timelines.”

Accordingly, Apple and Google must revise their app review procedures to address these issues.

Finally, on the discriminatory commissions, which applied only to Apple, the KMCC found that between July 2015 and January 2023, the company calculated its 30% commission differently for South Korean and overseas developers. While overseas developers were charged based on prices excluding value-added tax (VAT), South Korean developers were charged based on prices including VAT.

“KMCC determined that this constituted an act of unfairly providing rates, numbers, telecommunications facilities, or other economic benefits for telecommunications services or bundled services in a discriminatory manner compared to other users […].”

The KMCC said Apple will also have to take measures to prevent discriminatory commission practices between South Korean and overseas developers from recurring.

According to Reuters, Apple said it “‌disagreed ⁠with the decision and was evaluating options in accordance with South Korean ​laws.” ​Apple added that “⁠it has worked with outside developers ​to enable innovation ​through ⁠its App Store.”

Today’s decision comes on the heels of similar regulatory pressure in other markets, including Brazil and Japan, where Apple has introduced alternative app distribution and payment options in response to local competition rules.

The company has also faced years of scrutiny in the European Union, where it recently overhauled its App Store fees and business terms to address concerns raised by the European Commission.

To read the KMCC’s full announcement, follow this link.

#3451. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.
