#3448. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3447. Apple and OpenAI trade secrets lawsuit now has an official trial date

Judge Edward Davila today formally established the schedule for Apple’s trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, including a trial date. Here are the details.

A couple of weeks ago, during an October 14 case management conference, Judge Edward Davila instructed Apple and the defendants to agree on a proposed schedule for the lawsuit, working toward a tentative trial date of July 19, 2027.

The parties were given until October 23 to submit their proposed schedule, which the judge has now formally established.

As we’ve been covering since July, Apple filed this lawsuit accusing the defendants of improperly accessing or using confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts.

In recent days, Apple scored two procedural wins in its efforts to obtain expedited discovery, with Judge Davila granting the company access to additional documents and information from the defendants ahead of the normal discovery process.

In a case management order issued today, Davila established July 19, 2027, at 9 a.m. as the official trial date, with additional deadlines for discovery, motions, and pretrial proceedings in the meantime.

Notably, the schedule includes a June 1 deadline for the lead attorneys on both sides to meet and discuss a potential settlement.

To be clear, this is a common procedural step in federal civil lawsuits and does not necessarily indicate that Apple and OpenAI are considering settling the case.

#3446. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3445. Russia now requires Apple to store user communications and hand them over if requested

As Bloomberg reported today, Apple and Microsoft are now subject to Russian regulations requiring companies to store users’ communications and provide them to security agencies if requested. Here are the details.

Apple and Microsoft are now in Russia’s state surveillance registry, joining companies and services such as Google Meet, WhatsApp, Telegram, Snapchat, Cloudflare, and Blizzard Entertainment, all of which are required to store users’ messages, audio and video communications, and provide them to Russian security agencies if requested.

According to Bloomberg, Apple and Microsoft were added on October 2 to the “organizers of information dissemination” registry, which is maintained by Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor.

Companies on the list are required under Russian law to store local users’ correspondence, audio and video messages and turn that data over to security services if asked. They must also store in Russia information about users and the transmission of their communications for three years.

Companies that fail to comply can face fines and ultimately have access to their services restricted in Russia. Google and its Google Meet video-calling service were added to the same registry in January.

The move comes as Russia continues to tighten restrictions on foreign messaging services, having already blocked or limited access to platforms such as WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, and Apple’s FaceTime.

Specific to Apple, the company’s relationship with Russia has become increasingly complicated since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, prompting Apple to suspend product sales and exports while limiting services such as Apple Pay.

However, Apple continued operating the App Store in Russia, which has led to several disputes with local authorities.

In April, Russian users lost the ability to make new App Store purchases or renew subscriptions without an existing Apple Account balance, following government-imposed payment restrictions.

Apple might get away with it by simply exit Russia's market. It won't impact its economy much, afterall.

But what will happen when China will ask to do the same?

In June, the Kremlin demanded an explanation after Apple removed several apps developed by Russian state-controlled company VK from the App Store. Around the same time, Apple also removed banking apps linked to sanctioned Russian financial institutions.

More recently, in August, Russia’s antitrust regulator opened formal proceedings against Apple over its failure to preinstall the state-backed MAX messaging app and the RuStore app marketplace on its devices.

All of that said, neither Apple nor Microsoft has publicly commented on its inclusion in the registry or indicated whether it intends to comply with the requirements.

#3444. This Sci-Fi Kids' Series Captures the Horrors of War Better Than Most Adult Books

Scholastic has come a long way since its founding in 1920. Its content ranges from fun, educational adventures like The Magic School Bus to light horror stories like Goosebumps. Then you have more unique and out-there works, like Animorphs, which ran from 1996 to 2001. Written by Katherine Applegate and her husband Michael Grant with the aid of a team of ghostwriters, this was a science fiction series about alien parasites called the Yeerks invading Earth in the hopes of enslaving humans to use in their galactic war against the Andelites, an advanced race of space-centaurs. Earth's only hope comes in the form of five teenagers who use Andelite technology to transform into animals, and a young Andelite cadet who is the sole survivor of a deadly space battle.

What set Animorphs apart from Scholastic's other series wasn't just its creative sci-fi setting, but the level of detail and maturity put into it — namely, its approach to war. The fact that the books were written for kids did not stop the husband-wife duo from writing about gory battles, genocide, paranoia, and propaganda, among other horrors of war. This honesty gave Animorphs a unique identity in the world of children's literature, and even thirty years after the first book was published, it has aged like fine wine for its nuanced handling of such heavy topics.

Most children's media try to keep their depictions of war simple. You'll generally have one side portrayed as the aggressor with aspirations of conquest, and another as the victim or underdog trying to fight against them. At first, Animorphs follows this trend. The six protagonists are underdogs forced to use their morphing powers to keep their identities safe from the Yeerks, a ruthless galactic empire that has already subjugated other species. The kids are forced to use guerrilla tactics to avoid open warfare until the Andelites arrive with reinforcements.

However, the series is very quick to throw a wrench in this perception. The noble and heroic Andelites are soon revealed to be vain, arrogant, and paranoid, as it was one of their scientists who gave the Yeerks the technology to take to space. We even see them use propaganda to cover their tracks. In Book 8, The Alien, the Andelites are furious when they learn their morphing technology is known by the humans and force a young cadet to take the fall for the leak of information. It's just the first of many instances where Applegate and Grant delve into how governments try to control the narrative in wars, showing that often, your allies in a war are only so because they hate your enemy as much as you.

Likewise, the Yeerks are full of nuances. Yes, they are parasites who take away the autonomy of their hosts, but to not do so is to live a blind, deaf life eternally swimming in the pool of your birth, all while possessing a mind as complex as any human's. Their expansionist war occurred partially because they were overwhelmed by this impossible reality they had been exposed to, and partially because the Andelites were trying to contain them on their home world. Several Yeerk characters are complex individuals, with wants, goals, aspirations, and even loved ones. Many of them even sympathize with the plight of their hosts and would gladly try to find a way to peacefully coexist, but they are bullied into silence by the military and the ruling Council of Thirteen. More than an evil alien species out to conquer humanity, the Yeerks are a young empire hated by an established power and internally divided, hampered by their biology and inexperience.

Perhaps the best example of this complexity can be seen within the protagonists themselves. While everything they do is to save humanity from enslavement, they often have to step into morally dubious territory. One example happens early in the series in Book 7, The Stranger, when the Animorphs destroyed a device that allowed Yeerks to feed when outside their hosts every three days. While a major victory that slowed down the Yeerks' plans, it also caused hundreds of Yeerks to die an agonizing death by starvation, to say nothing of all the human hosts who were also quietly killed off. The protagonists would also use torture as needed and had a horrible track record when it came to recruiting members. This makes sense in a lot of ways; what teenager is going to fight a secret war for years and not go a little crazy? It all shows the reader that wars are almost never simple good vs. evil, and that everyone has the chance to be a hero or a villain.

Applegate and Grant vividly detail the atrocities of the conflict. The battles between the Animorphs and Yeerk controllers leave very little to the imagination when it comes to body horror. The Yeerks might have access to advanced technologies and strong alien hosts, but a blow from the paw of an adult grizzly bear or the bite force of a Siberian tiger is enough to cause major damage. These clashes are bloody and hectic, with plenty of severed limbs, torn-out eyes, broken bones, and worse. The morphing technology protects their bodies, but the psychological effect weighs heavily on the kids.

Many times, the kids are reduced to tears when they change back to human form due to close calls with death. They can also get stuck in animal form if they don't change back within two hours. Some, like the athletic fashionista Rachel, end up embracing the violence and become hardened killers. Others, like the animal-loving Cassie, are repulsed by it, leading them to make drastic choices in the name of finding a resolution to the conflict. The longer the conflict goes on, the greater the mental strain becomes, leading to tragic consequences for the characters and their loved ones.

In Book 1, The Invasion, de facto leader Jake learns that his older brother, Tom, is a controller, and he is unable to rescue him. Thus, he is forced to be on his guard constantly. His best friend, Marco, later learns that his mother, who was presumed to have died in a boating accident, is actually Visser One, the highest-ranked member of the Yeerk military. And while the other Animorphs don't have controller family members, it highlights how terrifying the Yeerks are: they can literally be anyone, and you won't know until it's too late. This reinforces a deep sense of isolation and paranoia. When enemies could be anywhere, how do you go about making allies?

In the end, all these qualities make Animorphs such a mature and nuanced series. Sure, it still has plenty of silly adventures and the infamous covers are decidedly goofy, but at its core, the books introduced kids to war by highlighting the human cost, not just in the lives lost, but in how the psychology of those living through such horrors is slowly eroded. Here, good people are forced to do terrible things in order to survive, and atrocities can come from anywhere and anyone. In doing so, Animorphs created one of the best children's sci-fi series that is still remembered and celebrated to this day.

#3442. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

Can the Busy Bar bring Flipper Zero-like hacking to your workday?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The right gadget on your desk can make all the difference for the task at hand, and I think I’ve finally found a smart display that’s more helpful than distracting.

Sure, my monitor and computer will always be the main fixtures on my desk, but the smaller accessories I swap in and out of my setup can make a real difference in my day-to-day routine.

For instance, I added a Google Nest Hub Max underneath my ultrawide monitor a few years ago. While it was great for getting answers to quick questions, controlling my smart home, and checking feeds from my security cameras, having videos, music, and media just a voice command away made it easy to drift off task.

Although I eventually swapped out that smart display for a portable monitor to gain extra screen real estate, part of me still missed having a dedicated clock right on my desk. What I didn’t expect, though, was to find a simple desk clock with the smarts of a display and a built-in Pomodoro timer.

To top it off, the Busy Bar I’ve had on my desk for the past few months comes from Flipper — the same company behind the iconic Flipper Zero pentesting tool. Here’s everything you need to know about this unique gadget that works just as well on your desk as it does mounted on your monitor.

If you’re looking to swap out noisy touchscreens for a simple, focus-first desk display, Flipper’s Busy Bar brings a tactile edge to staying on task. Packing dual front-and-back screens, a built-in Pomodoro timer, mechanical switch controls, and automatic macOS meeting sync, it offers a surprisingly fun desk companion. Add in its fold-out monitor feet, open-source API, and 3D-printable design files for custom mounts, and you get a uniquely hackable status light that fits right into any modern workspace setup.

At 6.64 x 2.17 x 1.61 inches, Flipper’s new Busy Bar won’t take up much space on your desk at all. Just like the Flipper Zero, it comes in white with orange accenting, which I found to be just playful enough without being overly distracting.

In the box, you get the Busy Bar alongside a color-matched braided USB-C cable. While the device can run on its battery for around eight hours — or up to two weeks on standby — I found it easiest to leave it plugged into a USB power adapter underneath my desk. (If you use a Mac, you can also connect it directly to your computer, but more on that later.)

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The front of the device features a bright, pixelated dot-matrix display, but the real star of the show sits right on top: tactile physical controls for adjusting settings and running your timers. There’s a selector switch on the left to toggle between different modes, a giant Start/Pause bar in the middle, and a rotary knob on the right to add time or scroll through menus.

Coming from touchscreen devices like the Nest Hub Max and Echo Show 5, these physical controls offered a refreshing change of pace. I particularly like that the main Start/Pause bar uses the same mechanical switch mechanism you'd find in a mechanical keyboard. While the switches and dials aren’t totally silent, the quiet click they produce is soft enough for an office environment while making the whole experience of using the device genuinely fun.

On the bottom of the Busy Bar, there’s a USB-C port for charging or connecting it to your computer, right alongside two fold-out feet that let you mount it on top of your monitor like a webcam. Before trying that out, though, I wanted to see how it performed sitting directly on my desk.

Unlike the Flipper Zero — which has gotten a bit of a bad rap as a "hacking tool" — the Busy Bar is designed to help you hack your workday. Others can clearly see its large pixelated display and know not to bother you when it’s flipped to Busy. Alternatively, you can switch it to "Custom," which by default displays a "Keep Out" message complete with animated yellow warning tape.

Given that I work from home and don’t sit in a crowded office, my favorite thing about the Busy Bar so far has been its built-in Pomodoro timer. When you switch to Busy mode, the timer defaults to a 20-minute focus period followed by a five-minute rest break. The device’s built-in 0.8W speaker emits a clean chime to let you know when your interval is up, leading into a second work period with another short break in between.

What I like about this hardware-first approach is that I don’t have to pull out my phone — which usually ends up distracting me with notifications when I'm supposed to be focused. Plus, physically slamming down on the Start/Pause bar between work and rest intervals is surprisingly satisfying. Using the Busy Bar throughout my workday has genuinely helped me stay on task, especially when plowing through administrative work that would normally leave me bored out of my mind.

It isn’t just a glorified Pomodoro timer, though. Like other smart displays, it also features built-in apps. My favorite is the standard clock, which shows the current time and date. While that was essentially the only first-party app available for most of my testing period, a recent firmware update added a dedicated Weather app that includes a clock interface.

I initially tested the Busy Bar out in my game room sitting on top of my BlueAnt Soundblade soundbar, where it fit into my setup seamlessly. Eventually, I moved it into my office underneath my desk shelf where I’ve been using it ever since. At just over two inches tall, you can tuck it almost anywhere. However, mounting it on top of my monitor is what truly sold me on it as a companion gadget for a busy workspace.

With the feet pulled out, the Busy Bar perches easily on top of a monitor, just like one of the best webcams or a monitor lightbar. If your desk sits in an open workspace rather than facing a wall, people walking by can instantly see whether you’re available or wrapped up in focus time.

My favorite feature, though, is how it handles virtual meetings. When connected to my Mac with Flipper’s macOS app running, the display automatically flips to "On Call" the instant I join a meeting. Once the video call ends, it seamlessly drops back to your clock or timer.

How do you know what the Busy Bar is showing everyone else while it's resting on top of your screen? Flipper thought of that, too.

Unlike the 6.35-inch RGB LED pixel matrix on the front, the back of the Busy Bar features a secondary 1.54-inch monochrome OLED display. It mirrors whatever is showing on the main screen so you always know what people looking at your monitor are seeing. Flipper also used the extra space on either side of the back panel to include helpful quick-start guides — computer connection instructions on the left, and companion app info complete with a QR code on the right.

At the moment, Flipper hasn’t released its Windows companion app yet, though the website notes it's "Coming soon." That wasn't a dealbreaker for me since I regularly jump between operating systems when testing gear, so I downloaded the macOS app on my Mac mini M6 to get started. Just like the mobile app, the desktop software makes tweaking settings and digging into menus much easier, even if it’s a bit less tactile than using the physical dial and knob.

To get that automatic "On Call" status working when you drop into a meeting, you do need the desktop app running with the Busy Bar tethered to your computer over USB. In practice, it worked reliably, and having quick control right from the macOS Menu Bar made making adjustments effortless.

While I didn’t get a chance to test this feature out with my family at home — the school year is in full swing, after all — I could easily see it being a lifesaver during summer break when the kids are home. Plus, because you can also wall-mount the Busy Bar, it feels like a natural fit for podcasters, streamers, or anyone else who needs a clear "do not disturb" indicator while recording.

With most consumer electronics seeing price hikes lately due to the ongoing effects of RAMaggedon, I was still a bit surprised when I saw the Busy Bar’s price tag. At $249, it costs more than both the Echo Show 8 and the Google Nest Hub Max. Fortunately, the Busy Bar has been available for 20% off for the past month or so, and I hope its discounted $200 price becomes permanent.

Even at $200, you’re paying quite a bit for a device with deliberately fewer features — though that’s kind of the point, right? In Flipper’s defense, the Busy Bar is as customizable and hackable (in the best way) as the Flipper Zero.

For instance, you can integrate it with the rest of your smart home devices to turn on lights, lock your door, or pause your music the second you switch your status to "Busy". It’s a remarkably developer-friendly device too, and there’s already a growing collection of custom-made apps for it. Flipper even released a 1:1 model of the Busy Bar so you can 3D print your own custom mounts and accessories.

While its software ecosystem is still in its early stages, I’ve really enjoyed the simplicity of having the Busy Bar on my desk. It’s a great digital clock, a solid Pomodoro timer, and an ambient focus tool that lets me keep an eye on my day without getting bogged down by endless notifications.

Given how open Flipper has made the platform from the outset, the sky is truly the limit. Here’s hoping Busy Bars end up on more people’s desks and that the tinkering community has as much fun with this device as they did with the Flipper Zero — I know I have.

#3438. Apple seems to have the right approach to the first touchscreen Mac

Steve Jobs famously dismissed the idea of a touchscreen Mac back in 2010 when he said that it “gives great demo” but turns out to be “ergonomically terrible” in real-life use.

It was inevitable that eyebrows would be raised when the company did a U-turn on this by launching the first touchscreen Mac. But while I have no interest myself, I do think the company’s counterargument some 16 years later makes sense …

We thought about this years ago. We’ve done tons of user testing on this and it turns out it doesn’t work. Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical. It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue – and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off. It doesn’t work, it’s ergonomically terrible. Touch surfaces want to be horizontal […] that’s why we’ve perfected our multi-touch trackpads over the years.

Current CEO John Ternus addressed this change of heart directly. Specifically, he said that touch was intended to be a supplementary way of interacting with the machine rather than a primary one.

The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.

He suggested that it isn’t the headline feature of the new model.

All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.

I’m a Mac guy through and through, right from the original Macintosh back in 1984. I’m also a massive trackpad fan, using the Magic Trackpad on my desk setup rather than a mouse. To me, it’s just the perfect way to control a Mac.

There was a period when I quite frequently used a 12.9-inch iPad with Magic Keyboard as a mobile alternative. Like the new MacBook Pro, that setup offered the choice of using the trackpad built into the keyboard or the touchscreen.

What I noticed about my own usage in this laptop-like configuration is that I almost exclusively used the trackpad. The only time I used the touchscreen was for scrolling, especially when I wanted to scroll a significant way down a page. That absolutely tracks with Ternus’ perspective of trackpad first, touchscreen sometimes.

However, when an M1 MacBook Air replaced my iPad with a Magic Keyboard, I didn’t miss the touchscreen at all.

One of the many things that’s changed over the years, in large part because of Apple’s launch of the iPhone way back in 2007, is that almost an entire generation has grown up with a touch interface. For them, the idea of a laptop without a touchscreen seems somewhat archaic.

However, I do very much suspect that even this generation will still use the trackpad as the primary control mechanism for the very reasons Steve outlined 16 years ago.

I use a 2 in 1 Yoga for years and loved it. So, I’d prefer that the MacBook had a hinge like the Yoga to allow it to fully fold into a “tablet” or “tent” mode. But a touchscreen Mac, even only being allowed to use vertical, is a Giant Leap for mankind! 😄

The nightmare scenario for Mac users was Apple compromising the interface in order to support touch. None of us wanted to lose the high resolution UI elements and see them replaced with giant cartoon-like equivalents. None of us wanted to lose the precise control we get from a trackpad. Thankfully, that hasn’t happened.

So no, I won’t be buying one personally, but I can see why Apple added the feature, and I do think the company has the right attitude to it.

Do you agree, or have a different view? Please share your own take in the comments.

#3437. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3436. Every Jane Austen Love Interest, Ranked

Jane Austen fans have enjoyed a plethora of characters to dissect over the years, especially romantic ones. This is quite fortunate because in Austen's books there are a lot of them. Every main character has at least two romantic interests: one that they secretly love and one that is recommended to them by others.

Diving into this rich and varied territory, there is a kaleidoscope of personality traits to admonish and admire. Austen does a fantastic job of making her characters feel real and paints them so vividly in readers' minds that familiarity with them feels like second nature. Out of the bouquet of leading men who won the hearts of Austen's main characters, here is how they stack up against one another.

Edmund Bertram is the beige of Jane Austen romantic interests. He is neither hot nor cold, but lukewarm in many respects. He is a kind person and takes care of his younger cousin Fanny when she arrives to live with him and his family in Mansfield Park. Even though Fanny develops romantic feelings for Edmund, he spends the majority of the story pining for Mary Crawford.

Edmund's admiration for Fanny feels like an afterthought. He only decides he likes Fanny when he has a falling out with Mary and is determined not to love her anymore. Edmund's last-minute pivot to Fanny feels more like a rebound than a realization. Even though Edmund is more virtuous than the lustful Henry Crawford, he is consistently infatuated with Mary. Though Fanny gets her happily ever after, and they end up together, readers are left to wonder how true his affections for her really are.

Henry Tilney is a great match for Catherine in Northanger Abbey. They share similar interests and love to read, especially Gothic novels. They have different manners, and the sarcastic and charismatic Henry comes to admire the candid and genuine, straightforward nature of Catherine.

Henry was close to his late mother and has a good relationship with his sister. This gives him a keen insight into female feelings, and he expresses knowledge of topics that men of the era had little interest in, like fabric choices for dresses. He empathizes with his mother and sister's plights and recognizes how his father's treatment of them was cruel. Unlike other characters in Austen's novels (Willoughby, Frank Churchill, cough, cough), Henry stands up to his father and proposes to Catherine, despite his objections based on her lack of fortune.

An influence over a person can be a powerful thing, and that subject is brought to bear in Persuasion. Although Captain Frederick Wentworth and Anne Elliot are in love, Anne is persuaded by her father and her mentor not to marry him. Captain Wentworth is snubbed by her family as being poor and beneath them socially, and they want Anne to wait and marry a wealthy gentleman instead. After a successful career in the navy, Captain Wentworth comes back into Anne's life, and they both eventually confess that they have never stopped loving each other.

When Wentworth returns, he is wealthy, successful, and a respected naval officer. His social status has changed, and he is looking for a wife. Although he secretly still loves Anne, he takes the opportunity to get back at her by treating her with indifference and flirting with Louisa Musgrove. Wentworth doesn't seem to realize that his actions could be misinterpreted by Louisa and her family. Luckily, her feelings for him cease, and he eventually proposes to and marries Anne.

It is hard to blame Wentworth for being a little spiteful around the woman who broke his heart, but doing it at the expense of the young and naive Louisa was careless. Luckily, it ended up in everyone's favor, and all's well that ends well. Despite his moody overreaction upon his return, Wentworth is one of Austen's most endearing heroes because of his fidelity to Anne. Persuasion examines long-lost love from both a male and female perspective, and Wentworth is a figure many can identify with.

When readers first meet Edward Ferrars, they wonder if he will be as petty and materialistic as his sister Fanny, but he turns out to be quite the opposite in Sense and Sensibility. Unlike his other two siblings, Edward is humble, kind, and a genuinely nice person. He forms an attachment to Elinor as they spend time together before she and her mother and sisters move out of Norland Park. However, things seem hopeless and complicated for Elinor when she finds out that he has secretly been engaged to Lucy Steele for several years.

For much of the rest of the novel, it appears as though Elinor and Edward will never be together, until a shocking plot twist towards the very end! Austen knew how to keep her readers on the edge of their seats, and Elinor and Edward's delayed gratification is one of the best. Although Edward did not purposefully mislead anyone, it was harsh for Elinor to hear about his engagement from Lucy instead of him. When eventually confronted by his strict and resentful mother about the engagement, Edward was willing to marry Lucy or set her free since he was disinherited, and he would not go back on his word, which is admirable. Fans rejoice along with Elinor when she and Edward get to be together at last in a surprising twist near the end of the book. Edward is as happy as Elinor to be free to marry her, and their bond based on friendship makes a solid foundation for a happy marriage.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

To quote the 1995 film version of Sense and Sensibility, Colonel Brandon is "[…] the kindest and best of men." Suffering numerous heartbreaks, Colonel Brandon perseveres and continues to display love, loyalty, and honor. Brandon is betrayed and conspired against by his father and brother. They force his sweetheart Eliza to marry Brandon's brother and send him into the army. When he returns, Eliza's life has taken a tragic turn, and before she dies, he promises to care for her illegitimate daughter, also named Eliza. Brandon again has to pick up the pieces when the younger Eliza is left pregnant and abandoned by Willoughby.

In spite of all of his setbacks, betrayals, and wounds from others, Brandon does not become harsh or cruel. He develops a strong admiration for Marianne Dashwood and wants to marry her. Marianne is not attracted to Brandon at first because he has a more reserved and quiet nature. As she spends time with him, she starts to realize that there is more under the surface, and he does care deeply about passions and pursuits, like music.

It is completely understandable why Brandon keeps his feelings close to the chest. The last time he openly loved someone, everything went wrong, and he was stabbed in the back by those closest to him. Towards the final chapters of the book, Marianne comes to see all the admirable character traits Brandon possesses, and they marry. It will likely take some time for Brandon to be able to let his guard down fully, but a feeling and open person like Marianne is the perfect partner to help him. He is also unfailingly kind to their family and gets along well with Elinor.

If there is a man who can take notes, it's Fitzwilliam Darcy in Pride and Prejudice. An aristocrat since birth, Darcy has been largely influenced by the affluent crowd around him and has strict opinions on wealth, social standing, and rank. However, all of these long-held ideals get challenged when he falls in love with the socially less endowed Elizabeth Bennet. In perhaps one of the worst marriage proposals ever, Darcy, who has already persuaded his friend not to propose to Elizabeth's sister, makes notable mention of her inferior status as he asks for her hand. After being verbally scorned and put in his proper place by Elizabeth, Darcy leaves, but does not retire to sulk in idleness.

As the novel goes on, Darcy takes several significant steps to change. He becomes more civil towards Elizabeth and her family and comes to the rescue of two of her sisters, including poor Jane, who finally gets to marry Mr. Bingley. Darcy starts out as a very prideful and stubborn character but becomes much more open and humble by the end. He allows Elizabeth's thoughts and observations to influence him, and he doesn't just talk the talk; he sets about making things right time and again. Darcy and Elizabeth are one of the best enemies-to-lovers in literature and a favorite for movie and TV adaptations.

If anyone deserves the blue ribbon for being the best role model for a Jane Austen romantic interest, it is George Knightley in Emma. Knightley proves over and over again in the book how he is sensible, kind, and selfless. He calls Emma out when she behaves rudely toward an older friend and persuades Harriet to reject Robert Martin's proposal. At every opportunity when Emma makes a blunder, Knightley is there having warned her before, during, or after. Despite his frustrations, he is always respectful and honest with Emma.

Knightley continually puts Emma's needs ahead of his own. Even though he disliked Frank Churchill, he did not say anything because he thought Emma cared for him. At the end of the book, Knightley agrees to leave his home and move in with Emma and her father after they are married because she does not want to leave him alone. Knightley only ever loved Emma for exactly who she was, first as a friend and then as a romantic partner.

Happy Sunday! Halloween weekend is winding down, and nothing snuffs out the "Sunday Scaries" quite like a cozy night on the couch with a movie to take your mind off things.

Netflix added 30 new movies at the top of the month, including several heart-warming movies to wile away a weekend afternoon. Headlining this Sunday's lineup is a rare Stephen King adaptation that won't scare the crap out of you: Rob Reiner's coming-of-age drama "Stand By Me" for a whopping dose of '80s nostalgia. It's not the only movie on this list that brings the good vibes though. Netflix also got Kristen Wiig's hilarious comedy "Bridesmaids" as well as a Christmas movie led by "Yellowstone's" Dave Annable called "No Sleep 'Til Christmas."

Read on for everything you need to know about the best feel-good films streaming right now on Netflix to end your weekend on a high note.

Rom-coms usually aren't my thing, but "Bridesmaids" is the rare one I'll watch again and again. A big part of its enduring appeal comes down to pitch-perfect performances from Kristen Wiig (who also co-wrote the script), Maya Rudolph and Rose Byrne. More than a decade after seeing it in theaters with the girlies, I'm still quoting it regularly — and laughing just as hard at all the gags.

Paul Feig's breakout comedy dives into the surprisingly cutthroat world of pre-wedding planning. When a well-meaning but increasingly frazzled maid of honor (Wiig) finds herself competing with an effortlessly perfect bridesmaid (Byrne) for the attention of her best friend (Rudolph), things quickly turn ugly. Neither woman is willing to back down, and their petty attempts to one-up each other threaten to derail the entire wedding. Melissa McCarthy, Ellie Kemper and Wendi McLendon-Covey round out an excellent ensemble, each bringing their own unforgettable comedic moments to the mix.

Halloween only just ended, but all the stores have already whipped out Christmas decorations because what is time anyway these days? Netflix added a few yuletide flicks at the top of the month, and while there's no real winners among the bunch, you could do far worse than "No Sleep ’Til Christmas." This romcom stars real-life couple Odette Annable and Dave Annable of "Yellowstone" fame as two strangers who have one very unusual thing in common: neither can fall asleep alone.

Lizzie (Odette Annable) is an engaged wedding planner struggling with insomnia, while Billy (Dave Annable) is a bartender who can't get a decent night's rest without someone beside him. When the two unexpectedly discover that they can sleep peacefully next to each other, they strike up an arrangement to help one another get some shut-eye. Watch "No Sleep 'Til Christmas" on Netflix now

While it's not a strictly feel-good movie, "Stand By Me" packs enough nostalgia that just seeing the opening is enough to take me back to simpler days. Based on Stephen King's novella "The Body," Rob Reiner's 1986 coming-of-age drama follows four boys growing up in a small Oregon town in the 1950s. Gordie (Wil Wheaton), Chris (River Phoenix), Teddy (Corey Feldman) and Vern (Jerry O'Connell) set out on an adventure through the woods after Vern's iconic line: “You guys wanna go see a dead body?”

As the boys travel together, they run headfirst into one challenge after another, all the while opening up about what's weighing on them. Gordie is grieving the loss of his older brother, Chris is trying to escape his troubled family's reputation, Teddy is dealing with an abusive father, and timid Vern is often picked on by bullies. Through it all, the boys lean on one another and face the difficult realities of growing up head on, the adventure ultimately becoming a bittersweet turning point in their lives.

#3431. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3429. iOS 27.3 release date: Here’s when to expect new iPhone features

Apple released iOS 27.2 this week with new features for Messages, Siri AI, and Photos, plus an Apple Music rebrand and more. But work on iOS 27.3 is already well underway, here’s when to expect the next big iPhone update.

If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.

For example, iOS 27.2 launched this week right around the same time as Apple’s previous releases in years past.

The only difference is that normally we would have expected iOS 27.1 in the last week of October rather than 27.2. But due to Apple making iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.

That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.

iOS 27.3 is expected to arrive in beta within the next few days—Monday, November 2 is likely.

As for the public launch, here’s what past years have shown for comparable x.2 updates:

27.3 should automatically hide the iPhone Dua dock like ipadOS. And add a new left left-hand user interface with the dock at the left.

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release in mid-December.

Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.

As for new iPhone features in iOS 27.3, we’ll know a lot more after the beta arrives. So far though, at a minimum we’re expecting the additional Siri AI languages Apple announced this week, plus the return of the all-new Health app.

Will you install the iOS 27.3 beta or wait for the release version? Let us know in the comments.

#3427. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

The 65-inch LG Evo C6 OLED TV has dropped to $1,399.99 from $1,599.99, a $200 price cut that brings it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers—and the savings aren't limited to this particular size either, with discounts extending across the C6 lineup, from the compact 42-inch model to the massive 83-inch version, although the 65-inch screen is particularly appealing if you want a larger OLED without spending more than $1,500. Nocturne stars Liev Schreiber, Zazie Beetz, and Stephen Graham, with Graham as a serial killer who makes the show “impossible to stop watching” per The Guardian.

Reviews for the show praise Graham’s chilling performance, which follows his award-winning turn in Adolescence last year on Netflix. Here are a couple quotes:

Not every review is effusive, as some found the series too slow in the early episodes. But by and large, critics find the show compelling.

Here’s Apple’s official series summary, followed by the trailer:

The series tells the story of Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber), an ex-soldier turned homicide detective who, tired of working the tough streets of Philadelphia, moves to a small town in western Pennsylvania for a quiet life. But, as the town and his family come under attack from the diabolically cunning serial killer Jurek Walter (Stephen Graham), Jonah must protect all that he holds dear. When the desperate search for Jurek’s last missing victim forces Jonah to send his surrogate daughter, FBI Agent Saga Bauer (Zazie Beetz), up against Jurek, how far will Jonah go?

Nocturne is based on the bestselling crime novels “Lazarus” and “The Sandman” by Lars Kepler.

The first two episodes of the show drop tonight, followed by weekly releases through December 25.

Have you watched Nocturne’s premiere yet? Let us know what you thought via the comments.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month, or you can get it discounted through the Apple One bundle.

#3422. Brad Pitt's Daughter Vivienne Officially Drops His Last Name

Brad Pitt has officially been dropped from another one of his kids' names ... his 18-year-old daughter Vivienne has legally ditched her famous father's surname ... TMZ has confirmed.

A Los Angeles judge approved Vivienne's petition Monday, changing her legal name from Vivienne Marcheline Jolie-Pitt to Vivienne Marcheline Jolie.

The judge signed off on the request after no objections were filed.

As we reported ... Vivienne filed paperwork in July, shortly after turning 18, citing "personal" reasons for wanting to remove "Pitt" from her name.

She had already been using her mom Angelina Jolie's last name professionally, receiving credit as "Vivienne Jolie" in the Playbill for the Broadway production of "The Outsiders," which she worked on alongside Angelina.

Vivienne is now the fourth of Brad and Angelina's six children to legally drop their dad's surname.

Her older sister Shiloh officially changed her name in 2024, while siblings Maddox and Zahara received court approval for their own name changes earlier this year.

Vivienne's twin brother Knox also left "Pitt" off his high school diploma, though he has not legally changed his name.

As TMZ previously reported ... sources close to Brad have claimed Angelina is responsible for the growing rift between the actor and his children, describing the name changes as part of an ongoing effort to alienate them from their father.

Brad and Angelina finalized their divorce in December 2024, but remain locked in a separate legal battle over their French winery, Château Miraval.

#3420. These Surprisingly Powerful Soundcore Earbuds Are Under $35 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

#3418. Disney Star Erik von Detten: Company From Elder Abuse Lawsuit Owes Over $60 Million

The company Disney star Erik von Detten worked for when he allegedly played an "instrumental" role in finding customers to buy gold says it owes over $60 million to creditors ... TMZ learned.

According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Rosland Capital, where Erik worked for years, revealed the massive figure as part of its ongoing bankruptcy.

Rosland Capital listed debts of $63,695,061. The company's business involved selling precious metals to retail customers.

As we previously reported, Rosland filed for bankruptcy months after the company and Erik were sued for elder abuse by a couple, Sheila Greenberg and Norman Greenberg. The couple claimed Erik worked for Rosland, where he sold them gold.

The couple said they bought the gold for over $2 million, but later learned it was only worth $1.3 million. The lawsuit claimed Erik of took advantage of the couple due to their age.

Erik did not respond to the suit before the company filed for bankruptcy.

As TMZ first reported, the creditors in the bankruptcy claim Erik has been a "roadblock" in obtaining information about Rosland. The case is ongoing.
